docs.title: Budapest food and markets: first-time guide to cafés and local flavours
docs.description: Discover the Great Market Hall, famous Budapest cafés, classic Hungarian dishes and practical tips for a food-focused city break.

heroImage.alt: Shoppers walking between stalls under the iron roof of the Great Market Hall
heroImage.caption: Budapest city panorama — not a photograph of the food venues in this article.

docs.intro: A good Budapest food day does not need a perfect checklist. Try a market, make time for a café and order a dish that interests you. This guide focuses on a small number of documented venues already in our directory, plus useful pointers for discovering Hungarian flavours at your own pace. It is not a restaurant ranking or a personal tasting review.
highlights: Go to the Great Market Hall to browse food stalls and ingredients
Consider Café Gerbeaud and New York Café for very different historic interiors
Check menu prices, allergens and reservations with each venue

sections.title: Start with the Great Market Hall

children.text: The Great Market Hall is an easy introduction to Budapest's market culture. Browse before buying and take time to compare stalls. Traditional ingredients, everyday produce and food-to-go can share the same building, but traders and selections change.

Market hours may differ from typical restaurant hours and can change around holidays. Verify the official opening information for your visit; avoid planning a final-day market stop around a guessed schedule.

sections.title: A café stop near Vörösmarty Square

children.text: Café Gerbeaud is a well-known historic café in central Pest. Its location makes it a convenient addition to a stroll around Vörösmarty Square and Váci Street.
The atmosphere may be a reason to visit as much as the menu. Check the current menu and booking arrangements directly, and decide whether the experience fits your budget and appetite.

sections.title: The theatrical interiors of New York Café

children.text: New York Café offers an ornate setting away from the compact District V core. It works best as a deliberate stop in a wider city walk rather than an assumed quick detour from the river.
Popular historic cafés may have waits or their own admission and reservation policies. Always verify the current arrangements with the venue instead of relying on old travel videos.

sections.title: What to look for on a Hungarian menu

children.text: Gulyás is a familiar starting point, alongside paprika-seasoned dishes, lángos and pastries such as rétes. These names describe broad traditions, not a promise that every café or stall will serve them in the same way.
If you have food allergies or other dietary requirements, ask the venue about the specific preparation and ingredients. Translations and menus can be incomplete.

sections.title: Leave room for your own discoveries

children.text: A market breakfast, riverside walk and afternoon coffee often make more sense than travelling across the city for three famous venues in one day. Choose stops close to where you already plan to be.
Treat this guide as an editorial starting point. GoToBudapest currently has three detailed food-and-market attraction entries, and those are not an exhaustive account of Budapest dining.

sections.title: Hungarian dishes explained

children.text: Gulyás is the dish visitors most often get wrong. In Hungary it is a soup, even though English-language menus often call it a stew. It is described as a one-pot dish seasoned with paprika, usually built on beef or mutton with onion, caraway, potatoes, carrots and small pinched noodles called csipetke. The word means cattle herder, which points to its origin on the plains. Pörkölt is its thicker cousin: a stew of meat, onion and sweet paprika that can be made with chicken, pork or other meat, and paprikás is the version finished with sour cream. If you want the soup, ask for gulyásleves; if you want a stew on rice or with dumplings, look for pörkölt or paprikás.

Lángos is fried yeast dough, traditionally eaten warm, with toppings such as sour cream, grated cheese, sausage, bacon or garlic. It began as a way of using leftover bread dough and is sold at markets, fairs and fast-food counters. Kürtőskalács, the chimney cake, is a strip of sweet yeast dough wound around a spit, rolled in sugar and roasted over charcoal until the sugar forms a crisp caramel crust; it is associated with the Székely people of Transylvania, and the first written record dates from 1679. Dobos torte, a sponge cake layered with chocolate buttercream under a hard caramel top, was introduced by the Budapest delicatessen owner József C. Dobos at the 1885 national exhibition.

Two more names to know are túrós csusza, egg noodles with túró (a fresh curd cheese, similar to quark), served savoury with bacon or sweet with sugar, and halászlé, a hot paprika fish soup whose recipe varies between the Danube and Tisza river regions. Rétes, the strudel, is the traditional pastry. Menus and recipes differ from place to place, so treat these descriptions as a guide to what to expect, not a rulebook.
Gulyás is a soup; pörkölt is a thicker stew; paprikás adds sour cream.
Lángos and kürtőskalács are snacks to share while walking.
Ask staff how a dish is prepared if you have a food allergy.

sections.title: How a Hungarian meal works, and what to drink

children.text: Traditionally, lunch is the main meal of the day and may have several courses: soup first, then a main dish, then dessert. Dinner is described as less important, and there is no single typical Hungarian dinner. Traditional cooking rests on meat, seasonal vegetables, fruit, bread and dairy, with chicken, pork and beef the everyday meats. Paprika is the defining spice, and both sweet and hot varieties are common, so a Hungarian menu is not automatically fiery.

Hungary has several wine regions. Tokaj in the north-east is the best known, famous for the sweet Tokaji aszú, made from individually picked grapes affected by noble rot, and also for dry Furmint; the Tokaj wine region was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2002. Eger is associated with the red blend Egri Bikavér, and Etyek-Buda, close to Budapest, is known for fresh white wines. Ask a wine bar or restaurant for a glass of a region you have not tried.

Pálinka is a fruit brandy, usually from plums, apricots, apples, pears or cherries. Under Hungary's 2008 law only a spirit made from Hungarian-grown fruit and distilled and bottled in Hungary may carry the name, and it has had EU protected status since 2004. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company from a secret blend of herbs and aged in oak casks; it is usually taken as a digestif and is described as an acquired taste. Drink both slowly: they are strong spirits, not table wines.

sections.title: The Great Market Hall and other markets

children.text: The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér is Budapest's largest and oldest indoor market. It was designed by Samu Pecz and opened on 15 February 1897, and its roof is covered in coloured Zsolnay tiles. Inside, the ground floor is mostly produce, meat, pastries, spices and spirits, an upper level holds food stalls and souvenirs, and the basement has fish and pickled vegetables. The hall was badly damaged in the Second World War, and a renovation begun in 1991 led to its reopening in 1997. Walk the whole hall before you buy: prices and quality differ from stall to stall.

Other markets give a more local picture. The Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII was one of the big halls of the 1890s. It was destroyed by fire in 1988 and rebuilt, reopening in 1991; it is a working neighbourhood market, mostly meat and groceries. The Lehel Market Hall in District XIII at Váci út, designed to look like a ship, is described by local-food writers as a neighbourhood hall for fresh produce, cheese, sausages and lángos. The Fény utca market, on the Buda side near Széll Kálmán tér, is described as a semi-open-air, multi-storey market with produce, baked goods, wine and seasonal events.

Sources disagree on details such as the opening year of the Rákóczi tér hall, which is given as 1894 in some places (when building began) and 1897 elsewhere, and on traders and hours, which change. Check each market's current arrangements before a special trip, and note that market halls are working shops first and sightseeing stops second.

sections.title: Coffee houses and pastry, with their history

children.text: Café Gerbeaud on Vörösmarty tér has a long story. Henrik Kugler founded the business in 1858 and moved it to what is now Vörösmarty tér in 1870. He invited the confectioner Émile Gerbeaud to Budapest in 1884, and Gerbeaud eventually took over the business and kept the name. Today its own website highlights its pastry selection, its coffee blend and classic sweets such as cognac sour cherries and cat's tongues.

The New York Café on Erzsébet körút opened on 23 October 1894 on the ground floor of a New York insurance company building, and was long a meeting place for Hungarian writers and poets. After the Second World War the café was renamed Hungaria in 1954 and regained its original name in 1989. The building was later restored and reopened as a hotel with the café inside. Because it is both a historic interior and a popular stop, allow extra time and read the venue's own page for seating and reservation rules.

A practical approach: choose one historic café for atmosphere and eat the rest of your pastry at neighbourhood confectioners, where the focus is on the cake itself. Order a Dobos torte, a rétes or a slice of whatever the display case recommends, and let the coffee house be a rest from sightseeing rather than a race through the sights.

sections.title: Special diets and food experiences

children.text: Traditional Hungarian cuisine is built on meat, so vegetarians may find the classic menu limited, and traditional sweets often contain a lot of egg and dairy. Dedicated vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and kosher kitchens exist in Budapest, especially in the central districts and in Erzsébetváros, the old Jewish Quarter, where a glatt kosher Hungarian-Jewish restaurant is listed by one city directory. On menus, look for the words vegán, gluténmentes and kóser. Listings of such places are compiled by third parties and details differ, so confirm certification, kitchen practice and halal or kosher status directly with the venue.

If you would like help with orientation, food experiences come in several types. Guided culinary and wine walks, sommelier-led wine tastings and visits to food markets are all offered by local companies, and some multi-day programmes include baking Hungarian holiday desserts. Read what each experience actually covers before choosing, and remember that none of these is needed: a market stroll and a coffee-house stop already give you a fair taste of the city.

faqs.question: Is this a list of the best restaurants in Budapest?
faqs.answer: No. It is a curated introduction to markets and historic cafés, not a quality ranking or first-hand review of every venue.

faqs.question: Do I need a booking for a famous café?
faqs.answer: Reservation rules vary by venue and date. Use the official venue site for current details.

faqs.question: Can I rely on fixed food prices in travel guides?
faqs.answer: No. Check the venue's current menu and any service charges before ordering.

faqs.question: Is gulyás in Budapest a soup or a stew?
faqs.answer: In Hungary gulyás is a paprika-flavoured soup, usually made with beef, onion, potatoes and small noodles. The thicker dish that English speakers often call goulash is closer to pörkölt, so check the menu wording if you want a stew.

faqs.question: What are Hungarian pálinka and Unicum?
faqs.answer: Pálinka is a Hungarian fruit brandy, often from plums, apricots or pears, and the name is legally protected. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company and usually drunk as a digestif. Both are strong, so sip slowly.

faqs.question: Is Budapest food hard for vegetarians?
faqs.answer: Traditional Hungarian cooking is meat-heavy, so classic menus can be limited for vegetarians. Dedicated vegetarian and vegan restaurants exist, and many places can adapt, but ask staff about ingredients and check the venue's own menu.

faqs.question: Which markets can I visit besides the Great Market Hall?
faqs.answer: Local-food writers and market sources mention the Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII, the Lehel Market Hall in District XIII and the Fény utca market near Széll Kálmán tér. Hours and traders change, so check current details before going.

docs.name: Chain Bridge
docs.description: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge, opened in 1849, was the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary. Designed by an English engineer and built under a Scottish one, it carries stone lions at its abutments, was blown up in 1945 and rebuilt, and ties Pest's Széchenyi Square to Buda's Adam Clark Square.

children.text: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge links Buda and Pest across the Danube, anchored at Széchenyi Square on the Pest side and Adam Clark Square on the Buda side. It is a chain suspension bridge of wrought iron and stone, with cast-iron decoration. It opened on 20 November 1849 and was the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary. Its centre span of 202 metres was among the largest in the world at the time, and the whole structure measures about 375 metres in length and 14.8 metres in width.

The design was drawn up in 1839 by the English engineer William Tierney Clark, and construction ran from 1840 to 1849. A Scottish engineer, Adam Clark, who was no relation to the designer, supervised the work on site and spent about ten years on it. Much of the funding came from the Greek merchant Georgios Sinas, whose name is inscribed on the base of the south-western foundation on the Buda side.

The building years were turbulent. During the 1848 revolution Clark helped the army of Lajos Kossuth cross the unfinished bridge; one estimate puts the number at 70,000 men and 300 artillery pieces in a single day. In early 1849 he flooded the anchorage chambers and disabled pumps to protect the bridge from an Austrian plan to blow it up, and only one of four gunpowder canisters detonated. In June 1849 he persuaded the Hungarian commander, General Henryk Dembiński, not to destroy the whole bridge. The platform was dismantled instead so that construction could resume later.

The sculptor János Marschalkó carved the stone lions at the abutments, installed in 1852. The bridge received its present name in 1898, and its iron structure was strengthened in 1914. Retreating German forces blew it up on 18 January 1945 during the Siege of Budapest, leaving only the towers standing; it was rebuilt and reopened in 1949. A popular story says the lions have no tongues, but Wikipedia calls this untrue and says the tongues are simply not visible from below.

On the Buda side, Adam Clark Square was renamed in 1912 in the engineer's honour and contains Hungary's Zero Kilometre Stone. The Buda Castle Tunnel, commissioned by the Hungarian government in 1850 and opened to foot traffic in March 1856, runs beneath the castle hill and comes out opposite the bridge. The Castle Hill Funicular also starts from the same square, so the crossing is a natural start for a walk up to the castle district.
Good to know
Walk across for views of Buda Castle and the Pest riverbank; the Pest end is at Széchenyi Square and the Buda end at Adam Clark Square.
Adam Clark Square holds the Zero Kilometre Stone, the mouth of the Buda Castle Tunnel and the lower end of the Castle Hill Funicular.
Look at the stone lions at the abutments and judge the tongue story for yourself; the tongues are said to be there but not visible from below.

historySections.heading: The bridge that changed how the city crossed the Danube

children.text: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge was the first permanent bridge connecting Buda and Pest across the Danube. It helped replace seasonal crossings with a reliable link between the growing communities on either bank.
The suspension bridge and its stone gateways remain central to the city's urban identity. The bridge was destroyed during the Second World War and later rebuilt.

docs.name: St. Stephen’s Basilica
docs.description: Budapest's largest church, named for Hungary's first king, took more than fifty years to build. Its 96-metre dome has a panoramic viewing platform, and the building is also a venue for organ concerts, so it works as both a place of worship and a lookout.

children.text: St. Stephen's Basilica is dedicated to Stephen I, the first king of Hungary, whose mummified right hand is kept in a reliquary inside. Construction began in 1851 and continued for fifty-four years. The first architect, József Hild, designed it in the neoclassical style; after his death in 1867 Miklós Ybl altered the plan toward the neo-Renaissance, and the work was completed by József Kauser. A dome collapse during construction forced much of the work to be rebuilt from the ground up, which is part of why it took so long.

At 96 metres the basilica is as tall as the Hungarian Parliament Building, and the two are often described as the city's equally high landmarks. The ground plan is a Greek cross. Pope Pius XI gave the church the title of basilica minor in 1931, and it is a co-cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Esztergom–Budapest.
Visitors can also go up to the dome: it can be reached by lift or by 304 steps, and from the top there are panoramic views over the city.

The basilica is also one of the city's regular concert venues, with organ concerts and other music programmes. Ticket options for the dome and the concerts differ, so check the official source for the current programme.
Good to know
The dome is reached by lift or 364 steps; the view is wide in clear weather.
Concert and dome tickets are separate from entering the church: check the current options before you go.
The Danube and the Hungarian Parliament are a short walk away.

docs.historyIntro: One of Budapest's grandest churches, St Stephen's Basilica brings together nineteenth-century architecture and the story of Hungary's first king.

children.text: Construction extended across several generations and changes in architectural leadership. The building was completed and dedicated in 1905, becoming an unmistakable landmark of central Pest.
Its dome and richly decorated interior helped establish it as one of the city's major ceremonial spaces. Repairs and restoration have followed damage during the twentieth century.

The basilica is dedicated to Stephen I, the first king of Hungary. It houses the Holy Right, a relic traditionally identified as the king's preserved right hand, which remains important to Hungarian Catholic devotion.

stories.title: The Holy Right: a centuries-old religious tradition

children.text: The basilica tells the remarkable story of the Holy Right: according to Catholic tradition, the relic survived successive relocations and periods of concealment before being returned to public veneration.
This is a religious tradition associated with a preserved relic; claims of miraculous qualities belong to the tradition, not to verified scientific findings.

docs.name: Matthias Church
docs.description: Matthias Church is Buda's coronation church: a Gothic building of the 13th century, a mosque under Ottoman rule, and a showpiece of 19th-century restoration with a richly painted interior, beside Fisherman's Bastion on Castle Hill.

children.text: The church that crowns Castle Hill has served more than one faith and several rulers. Béla IV, between 1255 and 1269, replaced an older, smaller church with a three-nave basilica. Tradition credits an earlier foundation by Saint Stephen in 1015, but the sources note there is no clear evidence for it. The church takes its popular name from Matthias Corvinus, whose coat of arms on the south-west bell tower dates its rebuilding to 1470 (the earlier tower had collapsed in 1384), and who married here in 1463 and 1476.

It was also the coronation church of Hungary's later monarchs. Franz Joseph I and Elisabeth were crowned here in 1867, when Franz Liszt's Coronation Mass was first performed, and Charles IV and Queen Zita followed on 30 December 1916.

After the Ottomans took Buda the church was converted into a mosque, which it remained from 1541 to 1686. After the siege of 1686 the Jesuits restored it in Baroque style. The building you see today is largely the result of the restoration led by the architect Frigyes Schulek between 1874 and 1896, which gave it its steep Gothic spire and gargoyles.

Inside, the walls and vaults are covered with painted decoration, including murals by Bertalan Székely and Károly Lotz, with stained glass designed by them. The Ecclesiastical Art Museum begins in the crypt, and the church is also a concert venue, so a visit can combine sightseeing with music.
Good to know
Check opening arrangements before you go: the church is a place of worship and can close for services and events.
Fisherman's Bastion and the equestrian statue of Saint Stephen are directly beside the church.
Look up: the painted vaults and the pulpit reward a slow visit.

docs.historyIntro: Behind Matthias Church's patterned roof is a long history of coronations, royal celebrations, religious changes and painstaking restoration on Castle Hill.

children.text: The Church of Our Lady on Buda Castle Hill is documented as under construction in the mid-thirteenth century. King Matthias Corvinus was closely associated with the church and celebrated both of his marriages here.
During Ottoman control of Buda in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the church was used as a mosque. It was returned to Christian worship after the reconquest of Buda in 1686.

historySections.heading: A church rebuilt for a new age

children.text: In the nineteenth century, architect Frigyes Schulek oversaw a major restoration that reshaped the building's appearance. Franz Joseph and Elisabeth were crowned Hungarian king and queen in 1867, and Hungary's last king, Charles IV, was crowned here in 1916.
Damage during the Second World War led to further restoration. The church remains both an active place of worship and a major historical landmark.

stories.title: A coronation crown that mattered

children.text: In 1309 Charles I was crowned in the church; the church's own chronology calls the crown provisional, while other sources describe a newly consecrated crown. His coronation with the Holy Crown of Hungary followed at Székesfehérvár in 1310.
The episode reflects how the correct crown and ceremony were central to the legitimacy of medieval Hungarian rule.

docs.name: Buda Castle District
docs.description: Castle Hill is the historic heart of Buda: a UNESCO-listed ridge of palace, churches and museums above the Danube, rebuilt after sieges and war, with views across the river to Pest. The Royal Palace, Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion all lie within a short walk of one another.

children.text: The first royal residence on Castle Hill was built between 1247 and 1265 under King Béla IV. Over the following centuries the palace was extended again and again: under Sigismund in the 1410s and 1420s, and, after his marriage to Beatrice of Naples in 1476, by Matthias Corvinus, who rebuilt it in an early Renaissance style.

Buda fell to the Ottomans in 1541, and the siege that ended Ottoman rule in 1686 destroyed the medieval palace. A small Baroque palace followed in the 18th century and was enlarged under Maria Theresa, finished in 1769. After fires in the 1849 siege the palace was rebuilt and expanded in the late 19th century to designs associated with Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann, and the Royal Palace was officially inaugurated in 1912.

The siege of Budapest in 1944–45 left the palace in ruins. Its post-war reconstruction, externally complete by 1966 although the interiors were finished only in the 1980s, took a simplified Baroque form and gave the building the outline and the dome you see today. Some medieval rooms were also uncovered and reconstructed.

Today the palace houses the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. The streets around it, with Matthias Church, Fisherman's Bastion, Trinity Square and the Hospital in the Rock, form the Buda Castle Quarter, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue', inscribed in 1987.

The district is compact and best explored on foot. Many visitors spend a half-day on the terraces, Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion, and add a museum or the Hospital in the Rock to make a full day.
Good to know
The Castle Hill Funicular climbs from Clark Ádám tér beside the Chain Bridge; walking up from the river is the alternative.
The museums in the palace have their own tickets and opening days: check each one before you go.
Matthias Church, Fisherman's Bastion and the Hospital in the Rock are all within a few minutes' walk of the palace.

Today the palace courtyards, historic lanes, churches and viewpoints preserve different moments of Budapest's history in a compact area.

docs.name: Buda Castle Funicular
docs.description: The Buda Castle Funicular, known in Hungarian as the Sikló, climbs a short, steep slope from Adam Clark Square to the castle terrace. First opened in 1870 as a steam-powered line, it was destroyed in the Second World War, rebuilt and reopened in 1986, and is run by BKV as part of city transport.

children.text: The Buda Castle Funicular, known in Hungarian as the Budavári Sikló, connects Adam Clark Square at river level, beside the Chain Bridge, with the castle terrace above. The ride is short: the track is about 95 metres long and climbs roughly 51 metres, with a maximum gradient of 31.75 degrees. Two cars, each carrying up to 24 passengers, run on a double track of standard gauge, and a trip takes about a minute and a half.

The line was an early piece of urban transport engineering. According to the Industrial Heritage Hungary site, Count Ödön Széchenyi proposed a steam-powered funicular to the city authorities in 1867 and received a 40-year concession to build and run it. Ödön Juraszek developed the first plans and Henrik Wolfarth supervised construction from 1869. Building began in July 1868, the first test run took place on 23 October 1869 and the line opened to the public on 2 March 1870. Budapest's funicular is described as the second in Europe, after Lyon's.

A steam engine of about 30 horsepower drove the cars for nearly 75 years, and the line carried more than two million passengers in 1943. Bombing in December 1944 severely damaged it; the cars and terminal buildings were destroyed and the remains were later cleared. The city has owned the line since 1920, and rebuilding was decided in 1965. After 42 years of closure it reopened in 1986. Sources differ on the exact day in 1986, so this guide gives only the year.

Two pedestrian footbridges cross above the track. They existed when the line opened, were removed in 1900 when the castle garden was extended, and were rebuilt to the original design in 1983. Today the funicular is electric and operated by BKV, the Budapest transport company. Its short run makes it both a practical link to the castle terrace and a small piece of Budapest's transport history.
Good to know
Check the BKV or Budapest Info pages for current running days, hours and fares, because they can change with the season and for maintenance.
The lower end is at Adam Clark Square beside the Chain Bridge, the same square as the Buda Castle Tunnel and the Zero Kilometre Stone.
The Buda Castle Tunnel, which opens beside the Chain Bridge, is another landmark in the same square.

docs.name: Hungarian Parliament
docs.description: The neo-Gothic seat of Hungary's National Assembly stands on the Pest bank of the Danube. Designed by Imre Steindl and completed in 1904, it is one of Budapest's most recognisable buildings, and its interior can be seen on a guided visit.

children.text: Few buildings define the Budapest riverfront as clearly as the Hungarian Parliament. Its long, lace-like facade, steep spires and central dome stand on the Pest bank of the Danube, facing Buda across the water. The building was designed by Imre Steindl, who won an international competition for the commission. Work began in 1885, the building was inaugurated in 1896, the year of Hungary's millennium celebrations, and it was fully completed in 1904.

The style is Gothic Revival, crowned by a dome in the Renaissance Revival manner. The scale is easiest to grasp in the commonly cited figures: about 268 metres long, 123 metres wide and 96 metres high, with 691 rooms, ten courtyards, 29 staircases and some 242 sculptures inside and out. Construction is said to have used around 40 million bricks and 40 kilograms of gold, and the stained glass and glass mosaics are the work of Miksa Róth.

At the heart of the plan is a sixteen-sided domed hall. On one side lies the chamber of the lower house, where the National Assembly meets; on the other, the former upper house chamber, now used for conferences and ceremonies. Since 2000 the Holy Crown of Hungary has been displayed in the central hall, and it is the main reason many visitors join a guided tour.

Inside, a visit takes you up the ornamental main staircase beneath painted ceilings, past a bust of the architect, and into the ceremonial hall. Visits are arranged through the official visitor centre, which sets the languages, times and prices, so check its website before you plan the day.
Good to know
For the best photographs, stand on the Buda embankment or look from the river; from Kossuth Lajos tér you see only the entrance side.
Guided visits are arranged through the official visitor centre (latogatokozpont.parlament.hu): check languages, dates and ticket conditions there.
Kossuth Lajos tér station (Metro line 2) and tram line 2 stop beside the building.
Nearby: the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial and St. Stephen's Basilica are both a short walk away.

historySections.heading: A purpose-built home for the legislature

children.text: Parliament's building programme began in the 1880s following an architectural competition won by Imre Steindl. The neo-Gothic design combined a dramatic riverside facade with ceremonial chambers and extensive interior decoration.
The legislature held special sessions in the partly completed complex for the 1896 millennium celebrations. The keys to the building were handed over in 1902, and it was fully completed in 1904.

stories.title: An architect who did not live to see his building completed

children.text: Imre Steindl went blind before the building was completed and died in 1902, two years before it was fully finished in 1904.
His design nonetheless became one of the most recognisable symbols of Budapest.

docs.name: Heroes’ Square
docs.description: Heroes' Square is Budapest's great ceremonial space: the Millennium Monument with the seven chieftains and kings of Hungary, flanked by the Museum of Fine Arts and the Műcsarnok at the head of Andrássy Avenue and at the entrance to City Park (Városliget).

children.text: At the end of Andrássy Avenue, Heroes' Square marks the thousandth anniversary of the Magyar settlement of the Carpathian Basin in 896. Construction of the Millennium Monument began in 1896 and was mostly completed by 1900, though the monument was inaugurated in 1905. The square has been officially called Heroes' Square since 1932.

At the centre rises a 36-metre column topped by a bronze statue of the Archangel Gabriel holding the Holy Crown of Hungary and the apostolic double cross, by the sculptor György Zala. It won the Grand Prix at the 1900 Paris Exposition. At the base of the column ride seven mounted figures of the Magyar chieftains, led by Árpád.

Behind the column, a curving two-part colonnade carries statues of Hungarian rulers and leading figures. The line-up has been changed by history: the Habsburg statues were removed during the Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919, rulers' statues were restored in the Horthy era, some were destroyed during the siege of Budapest in World War II, and after the war the Habsburg places were given to leaders of Hungary's struggles for independence, including Imre Thököly, Francis II Rákóczi and Lajos Kossuth in 1954–55.

In front of the column is the Memorial Stone of Heroes, a cenotaph first erected in 1929, removed in 1951 and rebuilt on the same spot in 1956. It is often called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but no remains are buried there. The square has also been the stage for national moments: Imre Nagy was reburied here on 16 June 1989.

The square is framed by the Museum of Fine Arts on one side and the Műcsarnok (Hall of Art) on the other, and the municipal park, with its Vajdahunyad Castle copy, begins right behind the monument. Heroes' Square is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Andrássy Avenue and the Underground' within the wider Budapest site, inscribed in 1987 and extended in 2002.
Good to know
Metro line 1, the Millennium Underground, stops at Hősök tere: it is the quickest way here from the city centre.
Combine it with the Museum of Fine Arts, the Műcsarnok, City Park, Vajdahunyad Castle and the Széchenyi Thermal Bath, which are all within walking distance.
Statues and restoration works change over time: check recent news if a particular monument matters to your visit.

docs.historyIntro: Heroes' Square is a monument built for a national anniversary and then rearranged by every political era that followed, which is why its statues tell as much about the twentieth century as about the Middle Ages.

children.text: The Millennium Monument commemorates the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin, dated to 896. Construction began in 1896 and was mostly completed by 1900, and the monument was inaugurated in 1905. The monument was designed by the architect Albert Schickedanz, and the original sculptural commission went to György Zala, who made the statues of the rulers with several assistants. His bronze Archangel Gabriel, holding the Holy Crown and the apostolic double cross, was installed in 1901 on a 36-metre column, after the work had won the Grand Prix at the 1900 Paris Exposition. The square has officially been called Heroes' Square since 1932.

historySections.heading: Statues that followed the politics of the day

children.text: The colonnade was planned with Habsburg rulers among its figures. During the Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919 the Habsburg statues were removed, the monument was draped in red on 1 May 1919 and a red obelisk replaced the Gabriel statue. The rulers' statues were restored in the Horthy era, and the statues of Maria Theresa and Leopold II were destroyed during the siege of Budapest. After the Second World War the Habsburg places were given to figures from Hungary's struggles for independence, including Imre Thököly, Francis II Rákóczi and Lajos Kossuth, added in 1954–55.

historySections.heading: The Memorial Stone and a national funeral

children.text: In front of the column stands the Memorial Stone of Heroes, a cenotaph first erected in 1929, removed in 1951 and rebuilt on the same spot in 1956. It is often called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but no remains are interred there. The square has also been a stage for national moments: on 16 June 1989 Imre Nagy, the prime minister of the 1956 revolution, was reburied here.

stories.title: The archangel, the crown and a royal dream

children.text: A tradition about the first Hungarian king tells of the Archangel Gabriel appearing in a dream and encouraging the creation of a Christian kingdom. The figure atop the Millennium Monument holds the Holy Crown and a double cross in reference to that national and religious story.
The dream belongs to a historical religious tradition, not to a documented eyewitness account. The monument illustrates the story through symbolism.

docs.name: Hungarian State Opera
docs.description: A neo-Renaissance opera house by Miklós Ybl on Andrássy Avenue, opened in 1884. Its horseshoe auditorium, grand staircase, painted ceilings and bronze chandelier were restored in a project completed in 2022, and the company also uses the Erkel Theatre as a second venue.

children.text: The Hungarian State Opera House stands at Andrássy út 22 and was designed by Miklós Ybl, whom one account describes as one of the greatest architects of European historicism. It is a neo-Renaissance building, begun in 1875 and funded by the city of Budapest and Emperor Franz Joseph I. It opened to the public on 27 September 1884 as the Hungarian Royal Opera House. One account says Ybl won the tender that Frigyes Podmaniczky called in 1873.

The facade is meant to show the link between European and Hungarian music. Statues of Ferenc Erkel and Franz Liszt by Alajos Stróbl stand in niches beside the main entrance. Erkel composed the Hungarian national anthem and was the opera house's first music director. Károly Lotz's two sphinxes beside the entrance are made of Carrara marble. The original facade sculptures grew mouldy within a few decades and new ones were made in the 1960s, so the figures seen today are not the first set.

Inside, the horseshoe-shaped auditorium seats around 1,261 people according to Wikipedia. According to Wikipedia, the vast, sweeping main staircase allowed ladies to show off their new gowns. A bronze chandelier weighing about three tonnes, made by craftsmen from Mainz, hangs beneath Károly Lotz's fresco of the Greek gods on Olympus. Murals by Bertalan Székely and Mór Than on the foyer vaults depict the nine Muses, and the boxes beside the royal box carry sculptures representing the four operatic voices. A former smoking room near the artists' entrance holds a gallery of portraits and caricatures of about 600 backstage workers and orchestra musicians, and a rumour says the painters were paid a beer for each.

The house was technically ambitious for its time. A 2014 article notes a hydraulic device for moving the stage and says electric lighting was added from 1895. Gustav Mahler was director of the opera from 1888 to 1891, and Otto Klemperer was music director from 1947 to 1950.

The building has been restored twice in recent decades. A major renovation from 1980 to 1984 ended with a reopening on 27 September 1984, exactly a century after the original opening. A second restoration, lasting nearly five seasons, restored the gold paint and other original decorative surfaces, improved the basement waterproofing and building services, rebuilt the orchestra pit to improve the acoustics and replaced the stage machinery installed in 1984. The house reopened on 12 March 2022. The Opera's second venue is the Erkel Theatre, which opened in 1911 as the Népopera and has been part of the Hungarian State Opera since 1951.
Good to know
Check the official Opera site for the current performance calendar, tours and tickets, and confirm whether your performance is at the Opera House or at the Erkel Theatre.
The Erkel and Liszt statues flanking the main entrance are on the street side, so they can be seen without entering the building.
The house is on Andrássy Avenue, so it pairs naturally with a walk along the avenue.

historySections.heading: A palace for a growing capital

children.text: The Neo-Renaissance opera house was designed by Miklós Ybl and opened on 27 September 1884. Its position on Andrássy Avenue helped establish the new boulevard as a showcase of modern Budapest. It gave the opera company a dedicated home; until then opera had been staged at the National Theatre alongside drama.

Painters, sculptors and craftspeople contributed to its celebrated interiors. Károly Lotz's painted ceiling and the ceremonial staircase are as much part of the experience as the stage. A major restoration culminated in the venue's reopening in 2022.

stories.title: An opening night the crowd could not resist

children.text: The Opera House's own account recalls spectators pushing past guards on the opening day in 1884, eager to see the new building. The excitement became part of the institution's history.
This is an anecdote documented by the opera company, not a local ghost legend.

docs.name: Dohány Street Synagogue
docs.description: The Dohány Street Synagogue, built in 1854–1859 in Moorish Revival style, is the largest synagogue in Europe. It is the centre of Budapest's Jewish quarter, with a museum, memorial park and Heroes' Temple, so a visit covers both architecture and history.

children.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue was built between 1854 and 1859 and consecrated on 6 September 1859. Ludwig Förster designed the exterior in the Moorish Revival and Romantic Historicist style, and Frigyes Feszl was responsible for part of the interior design. The twin towers, striped brickwork and rose window make it one of the most distinctive buildings in the city centre.

It is described as the largest synagogue in Europe, seating about 3,000 people, with separate seating for men and in the women's galleries. The original organ, built in 1859, was played by Franz Liszt and Camille Saint-Saëns; the current mechanical organ was built in 1996.

The synagogue stands at the edge of the area that became the Budapest Ghetto in 1944, and it sheltered many people during that winter. More than two thousand people who died in the winter of 1944–45 are buried in its courtyard. The Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park at the rear holds the Holocaust Tree of Life memorial (the Memorial of the Hungarian Jewish Martyrs) by the sculptor Imre Varga.

The complex also includes the Heroes' Temple, added in 1931 and designed by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó to commemorate Hungarian Jews who died in World War I, and the Jewish Museum, attached in 1931 and standing on the plot where Theodor Herzl's house once stood.

A visit combines a place of worship with a memorial. Check the current visiting rules before you go, since the complex is closed to visitors every Saturday and, according to visitor guides, on Jewish holidays, and the community asks visitors to cover their shoulders and knees, men to cover their heads, and everyone to pass a security check at the entrance.
Good to know
Check the current opening times, ticket options and visiting rules on the official source before you go.
The streets around the synagogue formed the edge of the Budapest Ghetto in 1944; the Jewish Museum and the memorial park are part of the same complex.
Heroes' Temple, the Jewish Museum and the Wallenberg Memorial Park can be visited as part of the same site: ask what your ticket includes.

The synagogue and surrounding memorial spaces now connect worship, historic preservation and remembrance of Jewish life and the Holocaust.

docs.name: House of Music Hungary
docs.description: A City Park building by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto, topped by a roof perforated with 100 openings. Exhibitions on the history of music, a sound dome, a concert hall and an open-air stage are spread across three levels in the Liget Budapest museum quarter, with a separate calendar of events.

children.text: The House of Music Hungary, in Hungarian the Magyar Zene Háza, stands in Budapest's City Park and was designed by the Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto. It is part of the government-funded Liget Budapest project, which aims to create a museum quarter in the city's oldest public park. Fujimoto was one of three winners selected in the Liget Budapest museum competition. The house opened to the public in January 2022, with Apollo Magazine giving 23 January as the date, after almost six years of construction according to Archinect.

The building is topped by a large white roof canopy perforated with 100 openings, which channels light deep into an open floor plan. Panels of glass blur the boundary between the interior and the park, and plant life rises from the core of the building. Fujimoto said his team was enchanted by the multitude of trees in City Park. The programme is spread across three levels, and Archinect puts the building at about 97,000 square feet.

According to Archinect, the subterranean level holds permanent and temporary exhibitions as well as a sound dome that creates a hologram-like aural environment, inspired by a concept from the composer Karlheinz Stockhausen. The House's own site describes the Sound Dome, Hangdóm in Hungarian, as an immersive 360-degree cinema room with a dome screen and a surround-sound system. Apollo Magazine describes a gallery of about 1,000 square metres, a permanent exhibition on the history of music in Europe and an inaugural temporary exhibition on Hungarian pop music from 1957 to 1993. The ground level has a concert hall and an open-air stage for performances.

The top level is devoted to educational spaces that present Hungary's musical heritage and draw on the ideas of Klára Kokas and Zoltán Kodály. Archinect names András Batta as managing director and says museum projects by Napur and SANAA were due to follow within the Liget Budapest development. Because exhibitions and concerts change, the official site is the place to see what is currently on.
Good to know
Check the official House of Music site for current exhibitions, concerts and tickets, as the programme includes temporary exhibitions and performances.
The building sits within City Park, so it combines easily with a walk through the park.
The open-air stage is on the ground level, so some performances may depend on the weather; confirm on the event page.

The institution combines the history of music with exhibitions, education and live events. Its themes reach beyond classical composers to sound technology and popular music, placing Hungarian traditions in an international story.

docs.name: Margaret Island
docs.description: Margaret Island is a 2.5-kilometre park in the middle of the Danube, largely closed to cars, with gardens, a music fountain, a Japanese garden, a water tower, pools and a running track. It lies between Buda and Pest and is reached from Margaret Bridge.

children.text: Margaret Island lies in the Danube in central Budapest, between Margaret Bridge to the south and Árpád Bridge to the north. It is about 2.5 kilometres long and 500 metres wide, with an area of around 0.965 square kilometres. In its present form it was created at the end of the 19th century by joining three smaller islands, the Festő, Fürdő and Nyulak islands, to control the river's flow.

Before the 14th century it was known as the Island of Rabbits. Its modern name comes from Saint Margaret (1242–1270), the daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent on the island. Religious houses dominated the island until the 16th century; during the Ottoman wars the monks and nuns fled and the buildings were destroyed. It became a resort of the palatines in the 18th century and was declared a public garden in 1908.

Today it is a public park in the middle of the city. Motor traffic is restricted: you cannot drive through the island, driving in needs an entry permit, and bus line 26 runs through it, so you can walk, run or cycle in relative peace. A rubber-coated running track is about 5.35 kilometres long. You can rent four-person pedal carts and small electric cars.

Among the sights are the Music Fountain and the Music Well, the Japanese Garden, a small zoo, the Centennial Memorial of 1973 by István Kiss, and the octagonal Art Nouveau water tower of 1911. The island also has large sports and bathing facilities, including the Palatinus open-air swimming complex and the Alfréd Hajós sports pool, and an open-air theatre.
Good to know

The island lies between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge; you cannot drive through the island and entering by car needs a permit, so plan to arrive on foot or by public transport; the only parking is a paid car park at the northern end, and the access rules are best checked before you travel.
Pedal carts and small electric cars can be rented on the island if you do not want to walk its whole length.
Bring a swimsuit if you plan to use the Palatinus open-air complex: check the current opening dates.

docs.name: St. Stephen's Hall
docs.description: A reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace, designed by Alajos Hauszmann around 1900 and gutted in the Second World War. Rebuilt over decades from photographs and plans, with a large Zsolnay ceramic fireplace, it opened to visitors in 2021.

children.text: St. Stephen's Hall, Szent István-terem, is a reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace. It is named after Saint Stephen, founder of the Hungarian state, and was one of the most important interiors of the palace during the Dual Monarchy. Budapest.com says it was part of the palace's expansion after the Compromise of 1867, with architect Alajos Hauszmann designing it as the showpiece of the state rooms.

According to We Love Budapest, the original room had a carved ceiling, a large ceramic fireplace with Zsolnay depictions of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints, gilded furnishings and large chandeliers. Vilmos Zsolnay made the ceramics, Endre Thék the carved furniture and interior, and the Neuschloss brothers the parquet inlay. Budapest.com gives the fireplace as about 4.5 metres high and 2.5 metres wide, made of more than 600 pieces, with a bust of Saint Stephen by Alajos Stróbl on the mantelpiece. The interior was shown at the 1900 Paris World's Fair, where it won a top prize, before being installed in the palace. Emperor Franz Joseph called it very beautiful on his visit.

The hall hosted royal audiences and working lunches and served as a card room during balls. In December 1916, the day before the coronation of Karl I, the chest holding the Holy Crown was opened in the hall before the crown was taken to Matthias Church; this was the last ceremonial use of the room.

The Second World War ended the hall's life. The palace was bombed and fire gutted the interior, and the southern connecting wing suffered the most damage in the siege of 1944 and 1945. The room then stood unrestored and was used as storage for decades. Reconstruction began only in the post-communist era and took a long time, using archive photographs, plans, old invoices, duplicate ceiling pieces from the Zsolnay Quarter in Pécs and a transcript found in a villa on Lendvay utca. It was carried out under the National Hauszmann Program.

The reconstructed hall opened to the public in 2021, and We Love Budapest says visits are by guided tour. The accompanying exhibition, The Miracle of Buda Castle, includes a ten-door installation by Sam Havadtoy based on The Admonitions, a Latin text attributed to a foreign cleric and dated to around the 1010s. The hall also displays a very large herm, a sculpted likeness of Saint Stephen.
Good to know
Visits are by guided tour, according to a 2021 report; check the official St. Stephen's Hall site for current tours, languages and tickets.
Look first at the Zsolnay ceramic fireplace and the portraits of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints around the walls.
The hall is in the Buda Castle palace area, where the Matthias Fountain and the Savoyai Terrace also lie.

historySections.heading: A royal interior from the turn of the century

children.text: The room originally belonged to the expanded Royal Palace complex and was designed to celebrate Hungarian craftsmanship and the legacy of the country's first king. Rich timber decoration, ceramics and historical ornament gave the room a ceremonial character.

The palace suffered severe wartime damage, and the original hall was lost. The reconstructed room is presented to visitors as part of the Castle Museum's palace heritage, with a separate exhibition and ticketing arrangement from other museum spaces.

docs.name: Museum of Fine Arts
docs.description: Hungary's principal art museum, housed since 1906 in a neoclassical building on Heroes' Square. Its collections range from Egyptian antiquities and Greek and Roman art to Old Master paintings by Raphael, El Greco and Goya, sculpture, drawings and prints, shown alongside temporary exhibitions.

children.text: The Museum of Fine Arts, Szépművészeti Múzeum, is described by Finestre sull'Arte as the largest art museum in Hungary. It stands on Heroes' Square facing the Műcsarnok exhibition hall, and its holdings are organised into departments including Egyptian antiquities, classical antiquities, Old Master paintings, sculpture, graphics and art after 1800. Figures vary by source, but the collection runs to well over a hundred thousand works.

The decision to found the museum was made in 1896, and the site chosen was the square in front of the Műcsarnok. Albert Schickedanz and Fülöp Herzog designed both buildings, and the museum's eclectic neoclassical building was built between 1900 and 1906. It opened on 1 December 1906 in the presence of Emperor Franz Joseph, and the public could enter from 5 December. Its origins lie in collections from noble Hungarian families such as the Esterházy, Pyrker, Ipolyi and Jankovich, which the state acquired in the late nineteenth century.

The Old Master paintings number about three thousand and include Raphael's Esterházy Madonna, Correggio's Madonna of the Milk and works by Titian, Giorgione, Tintoretto, Dürer, Rubens, El Greco, Velázquez and Goya. The Egyptian collection includes painted mummy sarcophagi, and the classical collection includes 135 marble works acquired from Paul Arndt in 1908. Drawings and prints are shown in rotating exhibitions. A Giorgione painting was stolen in 1983 and recovered in Greece in 1984.

The twentieth century left its mark. The building was bombed in the Second World War, and part of the collection was taken to Germany. Works recovered in 1946 and 1947 were often damaged, and We Love Budapest notes that works taken by the Red Army remain in Russian museums. In 1957 the Hungarian artworks moved to the new Hungarian National Gallery, and the two institutions were reunited in 2012.

The museum closed on 15 February 2015 for a renovation led by the Mányi Studio. Its main aim was to restore the Romanesque Hall, which had been a storeroom for decades. Check the official museum site for the current galleries and exhibitions rather than relying on older reports.
Good to know
Heroes' Square and the Műcsarnok are directly beside the museum, so they combine naturally in one visit.
Check the official museum site for current opening times, tickets and temporary exhibitions before you go.
The collection is large; choose two or three departments, such as the Old Masters or the Egyptian collection, rather than trying to see everything.
The Romanesque Hall was restored as part of the museum's renovation; check which galleries are currently on show.

docs.historyIntro: The Museum of Fine Arts anchors Heroes' Square with a collection that puts Budapest's artistic identity in a wider European and ancient-world context.

children.text: The museum was established in the era when Budapest's public institutions were growing rapidly around the Millennium Monument. Its monumental classical-style building faces Heroes' Square, alongside the Kunsthalle exhibition hall.

historySections.heading: Collections from Egypt to European painting

children.text: The museum now brings together ancient Egyptian and classical objects, old masters and later works. Its historic and modern galleries allow visitors to follow contrasting artistic traditions rather than only Hungarian painting.

docs.name: Andrássy Avenue
docs.description: Andrássy Avenue is Pest's grand boulevard, laid out in the 1870s to link the inner city with City Park. Lined with Neo-Renaissance palaces and built over the Millennium Underground, it runs past the Opera House and the Oktogon to Heroes' Square and forms part of Budapest's UNESCO World Heritage listing.

children.text: Andrássy Avenue is the long, tree-lined boulevard that links the inner city of Pest with City Park. It was decreed in 1870 to relieve traffic on the parallel Király utca and to connect the centre with the park. Construction began in 1872, and the avenue was inaugurated on 20 August 1876. It was named after Gyula Andrássy, the Prime Minister described as the main supporter of the plan, in 1885 or 1886 depending on the source, and most of the palaces along it were finished by 1884.

The layout blended proposals from three competitors: Lajos Lechner, Frigyes Feszl, and the firm Klein and Fraser. The palaces were designed by leading architects of the day, led by Miklós Ybl. A summary of the UNESCO listing says that from 1872 the avenue radically transformed the urban structure of Pest. It is part of the World Heritage Site Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue, which was extended to include it in 2002.

Under the avenue runs the Millennium Underground Railway, today Line M1 of the Budapest Metro. It was built in 1894-1896 and is described as the first underground railway in continental Europe. It opened on 2 May 1896 with its southern terminus at Vörösmarty Square, to carry visitors to the millennium celebrations in the Városliget. The avenue's outer end is Heroes' Square, which belongs to the same heritage listing.

Notable buildings along the avenue include the State Opera House, the former Ballet School, the Zoltán Kodály Memorial Museum and Archives, the Hungarian University of Fine Arts and the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts. Other landmarks include the House of Terror and the Oktogon junction. A Budappest feature on the avenue's 150th anniversary also mentions Kodály Körönd and Liszt Ferenc Square as places along the route.

The avenue's name has changed with politics. It became Stalin Street in 1950, was briefly called the Avenue of Hungarian Youth during the 1956 uprising, was renamed People's Republic Street in 1957, and regained the name Andrássy út in 1990. The year 2026 is the 150th anniversary of its inauguration.
Good to know
Use the M1 metro to ride under the avenue, or walk the route on the surface to look at the palace facades above street level.
The avenue ends at Heroes' Square beside City Park, so it works well as a one-direction walk with the metro for the return.
Check the official sites of the Opera House, the House of Terror and the Hopp Museum for visiting details, since each has its own arrangements.

docs.historyIntro: Andrássy Avenue tells the story of how nineteenth-century Budapest designed a capital with imperial-scale ambitions and a distinctive public life.

children.text: Created during the city's great period of expansion, the avenue connected the central streets with the developing City Park. Its broad urban design supported prestigious residences, public institutions and an increasingly fashionable cultural district.

The Hungarian State Opera and later grand villas mark different stretches of the avenue. The Millennium Underground Railway, built for the 1896 festivities, runs beneath the corridor, making architecture and transport part of the same historical route.

docs.name: Váci Street
docs.description: Váci Street is the pedestrian street running south from Vörösmarty Square, long a shopping and promenading route in downtown Pest. It takes its name from the road to Vác, has a mixed German, Greek and Serbian past after 1686, and carries a mix of historic facades, souvenir shops and cafés.

children.text: Váci utca is a central pedestrian street in downtown Pest, running south from Vörösmarty Square. Wikipedia describes it as one of the city's main pedestrian thoroughfares and often called the most famous in the city, with many restaurants and shops aimed at visitors. Its name refers to the road to the town of Vác; a walking article on We Love Budapest adds that a gate stood between numbers 2 and 3 until it was demolished in 1789, when the street was lengthened and Vörösmarty Square created.

After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686, the Habsburgs shaped the street, joining land behind the Downtown Abbey with the remains of an older Ottoman street. They sold plots mainly to imperial Germans, Greeks and Serbs, with some Jewish buyers, so the street was not typically Hungarian, and most shop signs were in German until the late eighteenth century. A 1911 arrangement with the Piarists, who were rebuilding their school at number 27, required a pedestrian alley to connect through to Elisabeth Bridge.

The street rewards looking up. The We Love Budapest walk points to the Pesti Theater at number 9, the Hungarian Crown at number 14, a carved wooden gate at number 15, a half-cut Pegasus at number 20, the Harris Bazaar at number 34, the Officers' Casino at number 38, a plaque marking a Swedish king's visit at number 43, and the Serbian House at number 66. Wikipedia mentions that the shop Alter és Kiss was founded by Antal Alter in 1829 at number 10, now number 13. Some buildings were bombed in the wars and later rebuilt.

Today the street is a place for souvenirs, shopping and eating, and for a stroll south from Vörösmarty Square. Wikipedia also warns that some bars along the street are known for clip joints, where tourists are lured in and then charged heavily for drinks, so it is sensible to check a menu and its prices before you sit down.
Good to know
Start at Vörösmarty Square, where the M1 metro line has its southern terminus, and walk south along the pedestrian street.
Look above the shop windows for the older facades and house numbers mentioned in walking guides.
Check menus and prices before sitting in any bar or restaurant, and avoid anyone inviting you in off the street.
Since shop hours vary, check each shop's own page for current opening times.

docs.historyIntro: Váci Street is a busy pedestrian route, but beneath the shops lies the memory of an older commercial Pest shaped by trade and changing city life.

historySections.heading: From historic street to shopping promenade

children.text: The street belongs to Pest's long-established urban centre. As Budapest modernised, commercial façades, cafés and stores gave the route a central place in the city's public life. Architectural details from different periods survive above contemporary shopfronts.

Today the street joins squares, restaurants and side lanes rather than functioning as a single monument. Its seasonal decorations and street activity reflect the continued role of the centre as a place for promenading, trade and encounters.

docs.name: New York Café
docs.description: A Belle Époque coffeehouse on the ground floor of the former New York Life Insurance building on the Grand Boulevard. Its frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco and sixteen carved fauns draw visitors, and for decades writers and poets treated it as an informal office. Today it sits inside a hotel.

children.text: The New York Café occupies the ground floor of what was built as the Budapest office of the New York Life Insurance Company, at Erzsébet körút 9-11 on the Grand Boulevard. Wikipedia gives the opening date of the building as 23 October 1894 and names Alajos Hauszmann, Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl as its architects. The company's name explains the name of the café, and the building is now the Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel.

The café became known for its interior, which visitors describe as frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco panels, marble columns and large chandeliers. Wikipedia credits the sculptor Károly Senyei with the statues and ornaments of the facade and with the café's sixteen devilish fauns. It also describes the café as a longtime centre of Hungarian literature and poetry, and a travel guide notes that writers used it as an informal office for working, meeting colleagues and finding patrons.

The twentieth century was less kind. The building was damaged in the Second World War and later nationalised under communism. In 1954 the café was renamed the Hungaria Café, and in 1957 the sculptors Sándor Boldogfai Farkas, Ödön Metky and János Sóváry carved replicas of the damaged allegorical sculptures, among them figures of Thrift and Wealth and of America and Hungary. The café regained its New York name in 1989, after the fall of communism.

In early 2001 the Hungarian government sold the building to the Italian hotel group Boscolo, and after a complete renovation it reopened as a hotel on 5 May 2006 with the restored café. The hotel changed names several times and has been called Anantara New York Palace Budapest since November 2021. For visitors, the café is on the Grand Boulevard near Blaha Lujza tér, and because it sits inside a hotel it is worth confirming current access and any booking arrangements on the official site.
Good to know
Metro line M2 and trams 4 and 6 are listed by one guide as the way to reach the area around Blaha Lujza tér on the Grand Boulevard.
Look up at the ceilings and for the carved fauns, which Wikipedia attributes to Károly Senyei.
The café is part of a hotel, so check the official site for current opening times, access and any reservation rules.

historySections.heading: An ornate café in a growing metropolis

children.text: The café opened within the New York Palace at the end of the nineteenth century. Elaborate ceilings, gilding and large mirrors gave it the kind of theatrical interior that made Budapest's café culture famous.

Coffeehouses became social workplaces where editors and writers exchanged ideas over long afternoons. The palace's story also reflects twentieth-century changes of use and later restoration, which returned the interior to its current lavish appearance.

docs.name: Fisherman’s Bastion
docs.description: Fisherman's Bastion is a fairy-tale neo-Romanesque terrace of towers and arcades on Castle Hill, built between 1899 and 1902, with some of the best panoramic views over the Danube and Pest. Its seven towers are said to represent the seven Hungarian tribes.

children.text: Fisherman's Bastion looks like a medieval fortress but is a product of the 19th century. It was designed by Frigyes Schulek, the architect who also led the restoration of the neighbouring Matthias Church, and built in the neo-Romanesque style, with the building work dated to 1899-1902 by the Research Centre for the Humanities and other Hungarian sources. English Wikipedia and the Hungarian Wikipedia infobox give 1895-1902, but Hungarian Wikipedia's text says construction itself began only in 1899 and that the whole bastion was handed to the capital in 1905. Its white towers, stairways and arcades were conceived as a decorative lookout terrace rather than as a working defensive wall.

Its seven towers are traditionally said to represent the seven Magyar tribes that settled in the Carpathian Basin in 895. The name is most likely linked to the fishermen's quarter (Halászváros, 'Fishtown') below the hill; the popular explanation that a fishermen's guild defended this stretch of the city walls is also often repeated, but the quarter is the likelier source, so treat the name as an association rather than a precise historical record.

In front of the church stands the bronze equestrian statue of Saint Stephen, the first king of Hungary, by the sculptor Alajos Stróbl. Stróbl began it in 1896 according to English Wikipedia (Hungarian Wikipedia says 1898), and it was unveiled in 1906 on a neo-Romanesque pedestal designed by Schulek.

The views are the reason most people come: from the terraces you look over the Danube to Margaret Island, Gellért Hill and the whole of Pest, with the Parliament building prominent on the far bank. Fisherman's Bastion is part of the Buda Castle Quarter in Budapest's UNESCO World Heritage listing, inscribed in 1987.
Good to know
Visitor guides describe early morning and evening as calmer times to come; the terraces look east across the Danube towards Pest.
Check the visitor source for which terraces are open and whether a ticket is needed at the time of your visit: access arrangements have changed over the years.
Matthias Church is next door, so the two fit naturally into one visit.

docs.historyIntro: Fisherman's Bastion may look like a medieval fortress, but its fairy-tale terraces belong to the great nineteenth-century reshaping of Buda Castle. Its towers frame some of Budapest's most recognisable views.

historySections.heading: A picturesque lookout above an older wall

children.text: The present bastion was built around the turn of the twentieth century as part of the wider restoration of the Castle Hill area near Matthias Church. Rather than an active military fortress, it became a monumental terrace overlooking Pest and the Danube.
The neo-Romanesque towers and arcades recall medieval architecture, helping visitors imagine the older Castle District while enjoying a modern public viewpoint.

The name is commonly connected with the medieval fishermen's guild said to have defended this stretch of the walls. The Castle District's historical institute notes that a neighbouring area called the Town of Fishermen offers another likely origin.
Both explanations link the monument to the riverside settlement beneath Castle Hill, showing how local place names preserve older layers of the city.

stories.title: The seven towers and the Magyar tribes

children.text: The Bastion's seven towers are conventionally interpreted as symbols of the seven Magyar tribal leaders associated with the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin.
The towers are architectural symbolism rather than the remains of seven medieval guard posts.

docs.name: Shoes on the Danube Bank
docs.description: Shoes on the Danube Bank is a memorial of sixty pairs of iron shoes along the Pest embankment, unveiled on 16 April 2005. It honours people shot into the river by Arrow Cross militiamen in 1944 and 1945, and is a place for quiet respect rather than posing for photographs.

children.text: Shoes on the Danube Bank, in Hungarian Cipők a Duna-parton, is a memorial on the Pest bank of the Danube, about 300 metres south of the Hungarian Parliament, between Roosevelt Square and Kossuth Square. It consists of sixty pairs of cast-iron shoes in the styles of the 1940s, fixed to the stone embankment: men's shoes, women's heels and children's shoes, each different. Behind them is a stone bench about 40 metres long. There is no rail or barrier between the visitor and the shoes.

The memorial was conceived by the film director Can Togay and made with the sculptor Gyula Pauer. It was unveiled on 16 April 2005. Cast-iron signs in Hungarian, English and Hebrew read: To the memory of the victims shot into the Danube by Arrow Cross militiamen in 1944-1945. Erected 16 April 2005.

The memorial recalls a specific crime. In late 1944 the Arrow Cross, the Hungarian fascist movement that had come to power in a German-backed coup, took Jewish people from Budapest to the riverbank. Victims were made to take off their shoes, which were valuable and could be resold, and were then shot so that their bodies fell into the river. Most of the killings are placed around December 1944 and January 1945. Wikipedia gives a figure of about 23,500 people shot into the Danube during the Arrow Cross terror, about 20,000 of them Jews, and says Arrow Cross police took as many as 3,600 Jews from the Budapest ghetto and shot them on the riverbank.

The same article records an act of rescue. On 8 January 1945, Károly Szabó and 20 policemen with drawn bayonets rescued the occupants of a building on Vadász Street whom an Arrow Cross brigade had forced toward the river; Szabó was named Righteous Among the Nations in 2012, and Pál Szalai was similarly honoured in 2009. Soviet forces liberated Budapest in February 1945.

Visitors often leave stones, flowers, candles and notes among the shoes. The Wikipedia article notes a 2023 incident in which a tourist, apparently unaware of the meaning, stepped into the shoes for a photo. The memorial is best approached quietly, as a place of mourning and remembrance.
Good to know
Treat it as a grave site: do not step into or move the shoes, and avoid posing for photographs on the memorial.
It lies on the Danube Promenade a short walk from the Parliament building, so it fits well with a riverside walk on the Pest side.
Visitors often leave small stones, flowers or candles; follow the example of others there rather than leaving litter.

docs.historyIntro: Shoes on the Danube Bank is a Holocaust memorial. Its simple forms honour the people murdered beside the river during the Second World War.

children.text: The memorial consists of sixty pairs of iron shoes positioned beside the river. They evoke the footwear left behind by people shot into the Danube during the Arrow Cross terror in 1944–45, including Jewish victims and others persecuted by the regime.

The installation uses ordinary men's, women's and children's shoes to make individual lives visible in the landscape of the capital. It is not a decorative attraction: its meaning comes from remembrance of people whose lives were violently taken.

stories.title: Why the shoes were left at the river

children.text: Shoes were valuable possessions, and the victims were often forced to remove them before being shot. The empty pairs in the monument convey both the economic brutality and human loss of the killings.

docs.name: Gellért Hill & Citadella
docs.description: A dolomite hill rising above the Danube in Buda, topped by the Citadella fortress built in the 1850s and the Liberty Statue. Slopes hold a monument to Saint Gellért, a church inside a cave and wide views over the city, with the Citadella's access arrangements to check before you climb.

children.text: Gellért Hill is a dolomite rock rising above the Danube in Buda. Wikipedia gives its height as 235 metres, and the Citadella stands about 140 metres above the river. The hill lies in Budapest's first and eleventh districts, and since 1987 the area has been part of a World Heritage site called the Banks of the Danube. It rose along a tectonic breakline, which explains the surrounding hot springs and caves.

The hill is named after Saint Gellért, Bishop of Csanád, who according to Wikipedia died on 24 September 1046 in Buda during the Vata pagan uprising. Accounts of his death differ: one says he was stoned, pierced with a lance and thrown from the cliff into the Danube, another says he was rolled down a hill in a cart, and the barrel story is described as an unverified tale. A large bronze statue of the bishop holding a cross stands on the northeastern slope and faces Elisabeth Bridge.

The Citadella was built in 1851-1854 under the Austrian commander Julius Jacob von Haynau, after the 1848-49 Hungarian revolution, and was designed by Emmanuel Zitta and Ferenc Kasselik. Hungarian forced labourers built it. Wikipedia describes a U-shaped fortress around a central courtyard that originally held about 60 cannons. Austrian troops moved in during June 1854, and Budapest took possession in late 1899. Wikipedia says an open-air display shows five Red Army pieces, and that the Citadella reopened on 5 April 2026 after years of renovation.

The Liberty Statue stands at the east end of the Citadella. Sculpted by Zsigmond Kisfaludi Strobl, the bronze figure is 14 metres tall and holds a palm leaf. It was first erected in 1947 in remembrance of Soviet troops ending the Nazi German occupation. After 1989 the inscription was changed to honour all who sacrificed their lives for the independence, freedom and prosperity of Hungary. Two of the four statues from the base were removed and relocated to Memento Park.

Down the slope is the Cave Church, formed in a natural cave system and dedicated in 1926. One guide says the Pauline order ran it until the 1950s, when the communist authorities arrested the monks and walled up the church, and that the wall came down in 1989. English Wikipedia says the hillsides were covered with vineyards from the 18th century, although Hungarian Wikipedia points to Evliya Çelebi's 1660s account of vineyards in the surrounding Buda hills and says phylloxera destroyed them at the end of the 19th century. English Wikipedia also says a land register of 1789 records 128 hectares of vineyard on the hill, a figure it takes from a 2007 Hungarian book on the lost vineyards of Buda that could not be checked against the register itself. It adds that a cave found during private construction work in January 2007 is covered in gypsum, calcite and aragonite crystals; a Hungarian news report says the entrance was found in late December 2006.
Good to know
Check the official Citadella site for current access to the fortress and the Bastion of Freedom exhibition before you go.
One guide says the paths are steep with many steps, so they are not ideal for strollers.
The Cave Church and the Gellért Baths are at the foot of the hill by Szent Gellért tér; check their own pages for visiting arrangements.

docs.historyIntro: The Citadella crowns Gellért Hill, where military history, religious memory and sweeping views meet above Budapest.

children.text: The Habsburg authorities built the Citadella in the aftermath of the Hungarian revolution of 1848–49. Its commanding position above the river gave the fortress a strongly political presence in a city marked by struggles over autonomy.

The Liberty Statue and later public use shifted the hill's symbolism from military control towards national memory and sightseeing. Reconstruction has altered access at different times, so past descriptions of interior visits should not be treated as current opening information.
