docs.name: City Park (Városliget)
docs.description: Budapest's principal city park, a rectangle about 1.4 kilometres long and just under a kilometre wide behind Heroes' Square. It staged the 1896 millennium celebrations and holds Vajdahunyad Castle, the zoo, the Széchenyi thermal bath, a lake for boating and skating, and the museums and music venue added under the Liget Budapest project.

children.text: City Park, or Városliget, is a rectangle of parkland in Zugló, Budapest's 14th district, about 1.4 kilometres long and just under a kilometre wide. Its main entrance is at Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue, and the park is bounded by Hungária körút, Ajtósi Dürer sor, Vágány utca and Dózsa György út.

The ground was once marshy pasture known as Ökör-dűlő, the Ox Meadow; the earliest mention cited by Wikipedia is from 1241, as Ukurföld. Visit Hungary says the idea of turning the neglected woodland on the city's edge into a public park emerged in the late 18th century, that the park opened to the public in the early 19th century (some sources say 1813), and that around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries the Rákos stream marshes were drained and an artificial lake with islands was created. By the 1880s it had become a metropolitan park with illuminated promenades and fountains.

The park was the main venue of the 1896 millennium celebrations, by which time Andrássy Avenue, the Millennium Underground and the Grand Boulevard had been built. For that exhibition Ignác Alpár designed Vajdahunyad Castle as a temporary set of 21 replicas of historic buildings. Between 1904 and 1908 it was rebuilt in brick and stone, mixing Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements; its main façade copies Hunyadi Castle in Vajdahunyad, now Hunedoara in Romania. The castle houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture, which opened its exhibition there in 1907, and in its courtyard stands Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III.

Several institutions are older than the castle. Wikipedia dates the Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden to 1866, the ice rink to 1870 and Gundel Restaurant to 1894, while the first circus building in the park opened on 27 June 1889 according to Wikipedia's Capital Circus article and the circus's 125th-anniversary press coverage, although Wikipedia's City Park article gives 1891 for the first performance in the circus building; the Széchenyi thermal bath also stands in the park. The lake in front of the castle is a boating lake in summer, and in winter the ice rink operates on the drained lakebed.

The park has changed again in recent years. In 2019 the government began the Liget Budapest project to turn it into a cultural precinct; the House of Music Hungary, designed by Sou Fujimoto, opened in January 2022, and the Museum of Ethnography opened on 23 May 2022.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Hősök tere (Heroes' Square) or Széchenyi fürdő; both are named as access points by Budapest visitor guides.
You can walk in from Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue.
Zoo, bath, museums and restaurants each have their own pages; check the official site of each venue for current opening times and tickets.

docs.historyIntro: Városliget is both a public park and one of Budapest's great museum-and-entertainment landscapes, developed through centuries of urban change.

historySections.heading: From open land to metropolitan park

children.text: As Pest expanded, the area evolved into a planned green space for recreation. The 1896 millennium celebrations brought major exhibition buildings and commemorative projects, leaving a distinctive mixture of parkland and architectural landmarks.

historySections.heading: A park with many cultural lives

children.text: The park's historic zoo, Vajdahunyad Castle, bathing facilities and lakes have been joined by newer institutions such as the House of Music. Seasonal skating and boating show how the same landscape is used in different ways across the year.

docs.name: Great Market Hall
docs.description: The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér is Budapest's largest indoor market: a steel-and-brick hall opened in 1897 with a colourful tiled roof, selling produce, paprika and local food across three floors. It stands at the Pest end of Liberty Bridge.

children.text: The Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok) was designed and built by Samu Pecz and opened with a ceremony on 15 February 1897. It stands at Fővám tér, at the end of Váci utca on the Pest side of the Liberty Bridge. The steel structure covers around 10,000 square metres, behind a brick facade with a neo-Gothic entrance gate, and the roof is covered in colourful Zsolnay tiles from Pécs.

Inside, the stalls are spread over three floors. On the ground floor you find fresh produce, meat, pastries, sweets, spices and spirits, together with the food souvenirs visitors take home: paprika, Tokaji wine, Túró Rudi, kolbász sausage and salami. The upper level has eateries and souvenir stalls, and the basement holds fishmongers, pickled-vegetable stalls and some specialist butchers.

The hall was heavily damaged in World War II and then deteriorated. A thorough renovation began in 1991 when the hall was closed; Hungarian sources give 1994 for the end of the reconstruction, while English Wikipedia says the market reopened in 1997. In 1999 it received the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence.
It works both as a place for local shoppers and as a sightseeing stop. Go earlier in the day for the fresh produce and a calmer atmosphere; the upper-floor food stalls are popular at lunchtime.
Good to know
Opening days and hours vary: check the current times before you go.
Prices differ from stall to stall, especially for food souvenirs: compare before you buy.
The Liberty Bridge, Váci utca and the Gellért Thermal Bath are close by.

Today, visitors encounter market stalls and Hungarian products under one of the city's distinctive historic interiors. Trading patterns vary, so the experience can differ by day.

docs.name: Margaret Island Water Tower
docs.description: A reinforced-concrete tower in the middle of Margaret Island, completed in 1911 to supply the island with water and to serve as a lookout. Designed by engineer Szilárd Zielinski with architect Rezső Vilmos Ray, it is 57 metres high and today also hosts exhibitions and festival events.

children.text: The Margaret Island Water Tower stands in the central part of the island, next to the open-air stage. It was completed in 1911 to secure the island's growing water supply and was designed from the start to work both as a water tower and as a lookout. The engineering was entrusted to Dr. Szilárd Zielinski, a professor at the Technical University and a European pioneer of reinforced concrete who introduced the material to Hungary; he worked with the architect and designer Rezső Vilmos Ray. The official tower site calls their collaboration a major technological innovation in modern Hungarian architecture.

The official technical data give a height of 57 metres, a water tank 13 metres in diameter with a capacity of 600 cubic metres, and main columns with a free height of 13.2 metres. A concrete staircase 24 metres high and an iron staircase 20 metres high add up to 153 steps. A Hungarian tourism page names the dome hall, with its floor 27 metres up, as the highest publicly accessible level, and a Budapest article describes an Art Nouveau spiral staircase leading to a viewing room with eight balconies and views of the city, the Danube bridges and the Buda hills.

The tower was declared a monument of townscape significance in 1977. It has been operated by the island's open-air theatre since 2011, and since 2012 it has served as a lookout tower, a visual art exhibition space and a venue for the Budapest Summer Festival. The Grand Stage and the Water Tower were rebuilt in two phases, in 2013 and 2014, with funding from the Government of Hungary and the Municipality of Budapest.

The tower makes sense against the island around it. Margaret Island is about 2.5 kilometres long and 500 metres wide and lies in the Danube between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge. It takes its name from Princess Margaret, daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent there in the 13th century, and Wikipedia notes that its present form came from joining three islands at the end of the 19th century. Other sights include the Centenary Memorial, the Musical Fountain, the Japanese Garden and the Palatinus bath.
Good to know
Check the official tower site for current opening times, tickets and any closures on performance days or holidays; access to the lookout varies.
The tower stands beside the Margaret Island open-air stage in the middle of the island, so it combines easily with a walk through the parkland.
Car access to the island has been restricted since the 1980s, so plan to arrive on foot, by bicycle or by public transport.

docs.name: Liszt Ferenc Academy of Music
docs.description: A concert hall and music academy in an Art Nouveau building by Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl, completed in 1907 at Liszt Ferenc Square. Zsolnay ceramics, Miksa Róth stained glass and a Liszt statue by Alajos Stróbl mark it, and a restoration won a Europa Nostra Grand Prix in 2015.

children.text: The Liszt Ferenc Academy of Music, known in Hungarian as the Zeneakadémia, is both a working music university and a concert venue. It was founded on 14 November 1875 by Franz Liszt in his own home, and Wikipedia notes that it was named after him only in 1925. Its first purpose-built home, a three-storey neo-Renaissance building by Adolf Láng on today's Andrássy Avenue, served from 1877 to 1879 according to Wikipedia and now houses the Ferenc Liszt Memorial and Research Centre.

The Academy outgrew that building, and in 1907 it moved into its current home at the corner of Király Street and Liszt Ferenc Square. This Art Nouveau building was designed by Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl at the request of Baron Gyula Wlassics, then Minister of Culture. A statue of Liszt by Alajos Stróbl dominates the facade. Inside there are frescoes, Zsolnay ceramics and statues of Béla Bartók and Frédéric Chopin, and Miksa Róth made the original stained glass windows. Motifs related to Apollo and Dionysus appear throughout.

The Great Hall keeps some of its original character: its curtains in front of the glass windows are the originals from 1907, and the seat upholstery uses the same velvet. A Visit Hungary article says the armrests in the banquet hall are lower than expected so listeners can relax, and that the best acoustic seats are in the fifth row.

The European Heritage Awards entry says the concert halls and interiors were heavily altered in the 1950s. After more than a century of use, the building's systems were outdated, so the restoration reinforced the structure, installed modern mechanical, electrical and air conditioning systems and used archive photographs and on-site research to restore original materials, textures and colours. The project received the Grand Prix of the European Heritage Awards and Europa Nostra Awards in 2015.

Many well-known musicians taught at the Academy, including Liszt, Béla Bartók, Zoltán Kodály, Ernő Dohnányi, Jenő Hubay, Leo Weiner and György Kurtág, according to Wikipedia's selection. The Academy also keeps the Liszt Collection of books and manuscripts that Liszt left on his death, and its Franz Liszt Museum shows three restored rooms from his home.
Good to know
Check the Academy's official site for the concert calendar, guided visits and tickets, since the building is also a working university.
The facade and the Liszt statue can be seen from the street at the corner of Király Street and Liszt Ferenc Square.
The Liszt Memorial and Research Centre in the Academy's first building is a separate site on Andrássy Avenue, so check its own page before planning to visit both.

children.text: Franz Liszt helped establish the music academy tradition in Budapest during the nineteenth century. The institution developed into an internationally known conservatory and concert centre, bringing education and public performance together.

The historic academy building serves both students and visiting audiences. Its concert halls, decorative surfaces and performance programme make it a living part of Budapest's musical life, not merely a memorial to a single composer.

docs.name: Pesti Vigadó
docs.description: A Romantic-style cultural centre on the Pest embankment, designed by Frigyes Feszl and opened in 1865 on the site of an older dance hall. Liszt, Brahms and Dvořák performed there, and a restoration reopened the building in 2014 with a Danube-facing panorama terrace.

children.text: The Pesti Vigadó is a cultural centre on the Danube embankment in Pest, designed by Frigyes Feszl, who was commissioned in 1859. It was built on the site of the Redoute, a hall designed by Mihály Pollack, the architect of the Hungarian National Museum. The Redoute was completed in 1832 and opened to the public in 1833, and before 1848 it was Pest's only concert hall. It was destroyed in May 1849 by Heinrich Hentzi, commander of the Austrian-occupied Buda Castle, during the siege of Buda.

Construction of the new building began in 1860, and it opened with a grand ball on 15 January 1865. It is considered a symbol of Hungarian Romantic architecture, though Hungary Today notes it was not well received by the public or professionals at the time. Feszl wanted mosaics for the interior walls but the Pest City Council chose paintings, which made it the first public building in Pest decorated with frescoes. The hall was nicknamed Vigarda in mockery before the name Vigadó stuck.

Its history is closely tied to the country's public life. According to Hungary Today, Franz Liszt gave the first concert in the Redoute after the 1838 flood and played his Rákóczi March there for the first time, but other sources credit Ferenc Erkel with organising that charity concert and place Liszt's first visit to the Redoute in 1839, so the details are uncertain. On 11 July 1848 the first National Assembly delegates offered 200,000 recruits for the country's defence. A ball celebrated Franz Joseph I's coronation in 1867, and the unification of Pest, Buda and Óbuda into Budapest was celebrated in the building in 1873. Johann Strauss, Antonín Dvořák and the Budapest Philharmonic Orchestra made debuts here, and in 1881 Brahms was soloist in the premiere of his Piano Concerto in B-flat major.

The building was badly damaged in 1945 and listed as a historic monument in 1954. Reconstruction began in 1968, and the rebuilt hall opened to the public on 15 March 1980 according to the Vigadó's own history page; Hungary Today gives 12 March and mentions 660-seat and 200-seat halls. It closed in 2004, the Hungarian Academy of Arts acquired it in 2013, and it reopened on 14 March 2014 after restoration. A permanent exhibition on the building's history opened on 27 May 2017.

Today the Vigadó presents concerts, theatre, contemporary art and other exhibitions. Visit Hungary lists the Vigadó Galéria with five exhibition halls, a Banquet Hall, the Sinkovits Imre Chamber Theatre and a Panorama Terrace that overlooks the Danube, Buda Castle and the Citadella.
Good to know
Check the Vigadó's official site for the current programme, exhibitions, tours and tickets, as individual venues inside the building have separate schedules.
The building stands on the Pest Danube embankment, so it fits naturally into a riverside walk.
Its panorama terrace faces the river, Buda Castle and Gellért Hill's Citadella, but confirm access on the official page.

children.text: The Vigadó developed as a ceremonial and performance venue in the heart of Pest, reflecting the city's growing appetite for major cultural spaces. Its façade and richly decorated rooms were created for public occasions.

The building was badly damaged during the Second World War and remained under reconstruction for decades. It reopened in 1980, and the restored venue has since hosted music, art and other cultural programmes.

docs.name: Vörösmarty Square
docs.description: Vörösmarty Square is a central Pest square at the northern end of Váci Street, with a statue of the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, the Café Gerbeaud and the southern terminus of the M1 metro. It has carried many names since 1812 before taking the poet's in 1926.

children.text: Vörösmarty Square is a public square in central Pest at the northern end of Váci Street. At its centre stands the statue of the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, facing west, made by Eduard Telcs and Ede Kallós. Behind it is a fenced park and a fountain flanked by stone lions. Stairs at the north end lead down to the southern terminus of the M1 line of the Budapest Metro.

The square has had many names. In 1812 it was known as Theatro piatcza, after a theatre that stood on the site; in the 1830s it was Harmincad tér, then Játékszín tér, Séta tér in the 1840s, and German Theatre Square in 1846. It was Színház tér in 1850 and Old Theatre Square in 1866. In 1874 it became Gizella tér, after Archduchess Gisela of Austria; it was named Károlyi Mihály tér from 1918 to 1920, was Gizella tér again, and took its present name in 1926. A column in the square lists all its former names.

The square's metro station opened on 2 May 1896 as part of the first section of the Millennium Underground Railway, the first metro system in continental Europe. It was formerly called Gizella tér and was rebuilt in 1970. It is included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site listing for Budapest and Andrássy Avenue, which dates from 2002.

At the northern end of the square is Café Gerbeaud. According to Wikipedia, Henrik Kugler founded his confectionery in 1858 and moved it to this square, then called Gizella tér, in 1870, on the ground floor of the Pest Hungarian Commercial Bank. Emil Gerbeaud, born in Geneva, joined him as an associate in 1884 and gradually took over while keeping the original name. The shop was nationalised in 1948 and renamed Vörösmarty, regained its historical name in March 1984, and was extensively renovated after 1995.
Good to know
The M1 metro terminates under the square, so it is an easy meeting point on the Millennium line.
Váci Street, the pedestrian shopping street, starts here and runs south from the square.
Check the Café Gerbeaud website for current opening times and any seasonal events in the square.

historySections.heading: A meeting place through the seasons

docs.name: The 1956 Monument
docs.description: The 1956 Monument, put up in 2006 on the fiftieth anniversary of the uprising, is a government-commissioned memorial made of rusting steel columns that converge in a wedge. It stands on ground where a Stalin statue was pulled down in 1956, and it has stirred debate in Hungary ever since.

children.text: The 1956 Monument is a memorial to the 1956 Hungarian uprising, in Városliget, the City Park. It was dedicated in 2006, on the fiftieth anniversary of the revolution, and was commissioned by the Hungarian government. The design is by the i-ypszilon art group, which includes Tamás Emdi-Kiss, Katalin György, Csaba Horváth and Tamás Papp.

The site has its own history. The memorial stands where a large statue of Stalin was toppled by freedom fighters in 1956, leaving only its boots on the plinth. The monument itself is made of rusting steel columns. According to one description, they represent people gathering in growing numbers and merging into one strong force that breaks through the road in front of it.

The monument has not been uncontroversial. One source says it has drawn criticism on artistic grounds, and some see it as a government effort to rewrite history and claim credit that belongs to others. A 2006 Daily Telegraph report quoted by the same source says that opponents wanted a traditional heroic sculpture depicting people, and some critics read the steel posts as gallows, recalling the hangings after the revolution. The war-memorial.net database also notes that it created a heated debate in Hungary at the time.

For a visitor, it is worth reading the monument as a public argument as much as a piece of sculpture: its form, its location on a Stalin-statue site and the way people respond to it all reflect how Hungary remembers 1956.
Good to know
It is in City Park (Városliget), so it combines with other City Park sights in the same visit.
Look at the way the steel columns converge, and consider the different readings of the form described above.
Read about the 1956 uprising before you go; the monument says more once you know the events it commemorates.

children.text: The monument near City Park commemorates the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence. The work by the i-Ypszilon group was inaugurated on 23 October 2006, fifty years after the revolution began.

Many vertical steel columns, in rusted and stainless steel, rise in an increasingly dense wedge. One description reads them as people gathering in growing numbers and merging into one strong force, while the 56-degree angle of the wedge alludes to 1956.

children.text: The memorial is described as a wedge at a 56-degree angle, and a tourism source says its axis makes that angle with Dózsa György Road. The number alludes to the year of the revolution.

docs.name: Gresham Palace
docs.description: Gresham Palace is an Art Nouveau office and apartment building at the Pest end of the Chain Bridge, built in 1904-1906 for a London insurer. After decades of decline it was restored and reopened as a hotel in 2004, with Zsolnay ceramics, mosaics and peacock ironwork among its details.

children.text: Gresham Palace stands on the Danube bank beside Széchenyi Square and the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. It was built as the Budapest headquarters of the London-based Gresham Life Assurance Company, which took its name from Sir Thomas Gresham, the sixteenth-century English financier who founded the Royal Exchange. The company bought the site in 1880, where the neoclassical Nákó House of 1827 had stood. The new building was designed by the local architects Zsigmond Quittner and József Vágó, and one source also names László Vágó.

Construction began in 1904, the building was completed in 1906 and it opened in 1907. It combined shops and a café on the ground floor, company offices above and apartments for senior staff and others on the upper floors. It is a prominent example of Art Nouveau in Hungary. According to We Love Budapest, Géza Maróti made the facade reliefs, Miksa Róth the glass and mosaics, the Zsolnay factory supplied ceramics, and Gyula Jungfer made the wrought ironwork, which includes peacock motifs. The only surviving original stained-glass window, on the first-floor stairwell, depicts Lajos Kossuth.

The twentieth century was unkind to the building. In the Second World War the Red Army used it as barracks, and afterwards the shops and flats were nationalised and it lost its former prestige. It became decrepit and was used as an apartment building under the People's Republic. In 1990 the national government gave the palace to the city of Budapest, and over the following decade several hotel plans came and went because of legal disputes and changes of ownership.

Restoration finally followed a 2001 purchase, with the large staircase, stained glass, mosaics, ironwork and winter gardens brought back, and the hotel reopened in June 2004. It is now the Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace, with 179 guest rooms, including 17 suites, and the State General Reserve Fund of Oman bought it in 2011. Even if you are not a guest, the facade and the ironwork with its peacock motifs can be admired from the street, and the building sits beside the bridge approach and Széchenyi Square.
Good to know
Look up at the facade reliefs, and at the wrought ironwork with its peacock motifs, from the pavement.
The palace faces the Chain Bridge, so it pairs naturally with a bridge crossing and a walk to Adam Clark Square.
It is a hotel now; check the hotel's website for what areas and services are open to non-guests.

docs.name: Hungarian Academy of Sciences
docs.description: The Hungarian Academy of Sciences, founded in 1825 after Count István Széchenyi offered a year's income from his estates, has its seat in a Neo-Renaissance palace on the Pest bank. Designed by the Berlin architect Friedrich August Stüler and inaugurated in 1865, it is decorated with statues of scholars.

children.text: The Hungarian Academy of Sciences has its seat in a palace on the Pest bank of the Danube, between Széchenyi rakpart and Akadémia utca, facing what is today Roosevelt Square. The Academy was founded in 1825: at a debate of the Diet in Pressburg (now Bratislava) on 3 November 1825, Count István Széchenyi offered a year's income from his estates, and other delegates followed his example. Its task was to develop the Hungarian language and to study and promote the sciences and arts in Hungarian. It received its current name in 1845.

The palace was designed by Friedrich August Stüler, the Prussian king's architect, who produced the main facade and floor plan and chose many of the architectural and sculptural ornaments. The facade inscriptions give 1860 for the start and 1864 for the completion, and the building was inaugurated in 1865. The Academy describes it as an early, mature example of Hungarian neo-Renaissance architecture, blending Northern Italian Renaissance with Berlin neo-Renaissance tendencies. Its construction sparked heated debate, partly because the style could not grow from local tradition after the events of 1848.

Terracotta statues of scholars and allegorical figures were ordered from Berlin, with moulds by the sculptor Emil Wolff; the exception is the statue of Miklós Révai, made by Miklós Izsó, who also made the coat of arms above the central window. The main facade has statues of Galileo and Révai, the Danube facade Newton and Lomonosov, and the Akadémia Street facade Descartes and Leibniz. Lomonosov replaced Raphael after the Second World War.

Inside, the ceremonial hall has a coved vault whose ornamental elements were designed by Albert Schickedanz, with triptychs by Károly Lotz on its east and west walls showing St Stephen and King Matthias. In the vestibule, a marble relief by Barnabás Holló, installed in 1914 to commemorate Queen Elizabeth, glorifies the Compromise of 1867. The Second World War badly damaged the Scientists' Club rooms in the Akadémia Street wing, which were rebuilt in the 1950s. For many visitors the palace is simply a landmark on the riverside, a building that represents the nineteenth-century effort to make science and scholarship Hungarian.
Good to know
The palace is best enjoyed from outside: walk around it to find the statues on the Danube, Akadémia Street and square facades.
Check the Academy's official site for current opening times and whether any exhibition or hall is open to visitors.
The palace faces the Danube on the Pest bank; it is a good stop on a riverside walk.

children.text: The Academy's monumental headquarters was completed in 1865. The design by Friedrich August Stüler takes inspiration from Renaissance palaces, bringing a distinctive formality to the Danube embankment.

The institution has long stood for Hungarian learning and public debate. Its façade is also part of the famous riverside urban landscape, linking scientific heritage with the development of Pest as a capital.

docs.name: Pál-völgyi Cave
docs.description: A cave in the Buda hills found in 1904 and shown to visitors since 1919. Warm water rising through limestone dissolved its passages, and a guided route of about 500 metres passes dripstones, calcite crystals and sharp changes of level in a system that sources put at 12 km or more.

children.text: The Pál-völgyi Cave lies in the Buda hills at Szépvölgyi út 162. Its own site says it was found in 1904 and has been open to the public since 1919. The commonly told account of the discovery is that the ground collapsed under a grazing sheep in a quarry in July 1904 (some accounts say a goat), and that János Bagyura, the quarry owner's son, went in after it and found the cave; Telex says Bagyura then led the exploration.

The cave is a karst cave shaped by water from below. Telex reports that carbonic-acid-rich thermal water rising through fractured limestone dissolved the passages, and that rainwater later widened them once the cave stood further above the level of the Danube. Showcaves.com adds that the same process is linked to the thermal springs Budapest is known for. About eight of the 41 algae species found there date from the time when thermal water flooded the cave, and around 660 bats hibernate in it each winter.

Length figures depend on the source and the year. Showcaves.com gives about one kilometre in 1910, about four in 1980 and 12 mapped by 1998, while Telex says the cave and the nearby caves it was linked with after 2000, including the Mátyás-hegy and Harcsaszájú caves, form a system of 31 kilometres, which it calls Hungary's longest. Only about 500 metres are open to the public.

On the guided route you pass unique dripstones, glittering calcite crystals, narrow passages and dramatic level changes. Showcaves.com names areas such as the Theatre Hall, about 12 metres high, a Long Passage where ultraviolet light makes the calcite glow, and Fairyland, the most heavily decorated part. The cave was used as an air-raid shelter between 1939 and 1944. Telex adds that the former mine guardhouse was converted into a visitor centre in 2022.
Good to know
The cave's own page says to take bus 65 from Kolosy tér toward Szépvölgyi dűlő and get off at the Pál-völgyi cseppkőbarlang stop.
The route has over 400 stairs and one ladder, is not accessible for people with limited mobility, and is not suitable for children under 5 or under 115 cm tall.
The constant temperature is about 11 degrees Celsius, so bring a sweater even in summer; dogs are not allowed.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and tour languages before you go.

children.text: The cave belongs to the limestone and thermal-water landscape of the Buda Hills. Passageways and mineral formations reveal the action of water over very long periods, far removed from the familiar streets and monumental buildings above.

docs.name: Budapest Zoo & Botanical Garden
docs.description: Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden in City Park opened on 9 August 1866 and is one of the oldest zoos in the world. Its main gate, Elephant House and Palm House date from the 1909-1912 reconstruction, when Art Nouveau buildings were added, and it was rebuilt after the Second World War.

children.text: Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden lies within City Park (Városliget) and covers about 18.4 hectares. It opened to the public on 9 August 1866 and is described as the oldest zoo in Hungary and one of the oldest in the world. According to the zoo's own history, a private company set up by four founders established it; the best known of them is János Xántus, who later became director.

Most of the surviving historic buildings date from a major renovation between 1909 and 1912, during which the zoo was closed; it reopened on 20 May 1912. After the operating company went bankrupt in 1907, the City Council took over. The zoo's history credits Károly Kós, Dezső Zrumeczky, Kornél Neuschloss and Gyula Végh with designing most of the buildings from this period, including the main gate, the Elephant House, the Palm House and the artificial rock formations. The renovation also created Hungary's first public aquarium. The Palm House is now called America Tropicana and presents the flora and fauna of the tropical Americas.

The zoo was badly hit in the Second World War. Air raids from autumn 1944 damaged it, as it lay near a railway marshalling yard, and the worst destruction came in the Siege of Budapest. According to the zoo's account, only about two dozen of roughly 2,500 animals survived the winter and most buildings were in ruins; Wikipedia gives a lower figure for the survivors, so the exact number should be treated as approximate. It reopened on 1 May 1945 with fewer than a hundred animals, and the park was even ploughed to grow fodder.

Repairs and modernisation continued after the war. A comprehensive reconstruction began in the mid-1990s, restoring the monument-protected animal houses and bringing enclosures up to modern welfare standards. In 2014 land from the closed neighbouring amusement park was returned to the zoo. The result is a zoo where the historic Art Nouveau buildings still stand beside modern enclosures.
Good to know
Look at the main gate and the Elephant House as architecture as well as animal houses; they date from the 1909-1912 reconstruction.
Check the zoo's official website for current opening times, tickets and which houses are open.
The zoo is inside City Park, so it combines easily with other City Park sights.

children.text: Established in the nineteenth century, the zoo formed part of Budapest's growing interest in nature, education and leisure. Its location in City Park placed animal collections among the city's other developing public attractions.

The zoo is known not only for animals but for decorative architecture and planted spaces. Its role has changed with modern approaches to animal welfare, conservation and education; today's exhibits should be judged by current information, not historic conditions.

stories.title: Scientists and film stars among the visitors

children.text: The zoo's own history page says it has welcomed many renowned biologists, from Nobel laureate Konrad Lorenz to Joy Adamson, as well as several international film stars, among them Richard Burton.

docs.name: Hospital in the Rock
docs.description: A wartime emergency hospital built in the cave system under Castle Hill, later a secret Cold War nuclear bunker and now a museum. It treated casualties in the 1944 to 1945 siege and the 1956 uprising, and its wards and equipment can be seen on a guided tour.

children.text: The Hospital in the Rock and Nuclear Bunker Museum is housed in a natural cave system under Castle Hill, about ten kilometres long according to the museum's history page, which Budapest residents have used since the Middle Ages. The museum is at Lovas út 4/c and is run by a public benefit foundation. The first room built in the caves was the Air Raid Alarm Control Centre, which controlled the sirens in the Castle district from 1937 to 1945.

The hospital itself was built between 1941 and 1943 using existing cave tunnels, with caverns becoming wards and passages becoming corridors. It was ordered by Károly Szendy, then Budapest mayor and minister of war, and operated under St. John's Hospital. It opened on 20 February 1944 with three wards and one operating theatre. During the siege of 1944 and 1945 all 94 beds were constantly occupied and patients also lay in the cave corridors. The hospital had its own generators and could take X-rays when hospitals on the surface could not.

The history page records that eight Jewish doctors were assigned there to labour service, that Dr. Kálmán Koppány helped prevent their deportation, and that two of them were betrayed in November 1944 and one was killed. The breakout from the Castle came on 11 February 1945, after which less serious patients left and the rest were transferred. The museum's history page gives July 1945 as the closing date, while another account says June 1945. Other accounts give very different figures for how many wounded were treated at the peak of the siege.

In the 1950s the hospital became a top-secret institution with the code LOSK 0101/1, declassified in 2002. When the 1956 revolution began it reopened to treat civilians and soldiers, with Dr. András Máthé as head surgeon, and it operated until December 1956. Between 1958 and 1962 it was converted into a nuclear bunker with a ventilation system with a gas filter, a water supply connected to the Danube and two Ganz diesel engines. The plan was for medical staff to enter first and open the hospital for other survivors after 72 hours.

A caretaker family looked after the site until 2004, and the Krétakör Theatre Company staged performances there from 2004 to 2006. Renovation began in 2007, and it has been continuously open as an exhibition since 11 March 2008. Wikipedia notes that it features waxwork recreations of treatments and siege-era scenes.
Good to know
Visits are by guided tour; check the official Hospital in the Rock site for current tours, languages, tickets and booking.
A visitor guide suggests the Buda Castle Funicular from Clark Ádám Square, or bus lines 16, 16A or 116 to Dísz tér; check current routes before travelling.
The museum is a short walk from Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.
Guest reviews on the museum's site describe the tour as moving; it presents wartime suffering and the 1956 uprising.

docs.historyIntro: Deep beneath Buda Castle, a former emergency hospital traces Budapest's wartime siege, the 1956 Revolution and the anxious decades of the Cold War. The underground rooms tell a very human story of medicine, improvisation and survival.

historySections.heading: A hospital built into the Castle Hill caves

children.text: The natural limestone cave network beneath Buda Castle was adapted to shelter residents during air raids. Construction of an underground emergency hospital began in 1941, and it opened on 20 February 1944. Its facilities included three wards and an operating theatre.

During the siege of Budapest in 1944–45, its beds and connecting passages filled with wounded civilians and soldiers. Medical staff worked amid shortages and difficult conditions, while the subterranean location helped protect the hospital from bombing above.

The hospital reopened during the Hungarian Revolution of October 1956. Its doctors treated wounded people from both civilian and military backgrounds, and the space also sheltered families. The facility continued treating patients until December of that year.

historySections.heading: From hospital to nuclear bunker and museum

children.text: Between 1958 and 1962, the complex was adapted for a possible nuclear or chemical emergency. New ventilation, filtration and backup power systems reflected the anxieties of the Cold War. The facility remained a controlled civil-defence site for decades.

The underground complex was eventually opened to the public as a museum, with permanent exhibition operations from 2008. Today it offers an unusual way to understand twentieth-century Budapest through the stories of patients, volunteers and medical staff.

stories.title: The surgeon who wore a recovered bullet

children.text: The museum's historical account describes Dr András Máthé, who worked here during the 1956 Revolution. According to the museum, he wore a bullet on a necklace that he had removed from an injured patient's head. It is a striking account of the dangerous surgeries performed underground.
This is presented as an account recorded by the museum, not as a supernatural legend.

stories.sourceLabel: Hospital in the Rock — historical accounts

stories.title: A persistent myth about Soviet flamethrowers

children.text: The museum specifically disputes a story that Soviet troops burned out the Hospital in the Rock with flamethrowers in 1945. Its official history says this confusion relates to fighting elsewhere in the wider cave system, not the hospital wards.
A responsible guide should distinguish this documented correction from the dramatic version of the story.

docs.name: Ludwig Museum
docs.description: Hungary's museum of contemporary art with an international outlook grew from works donated by the collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig. It now occupies the Danube-facing wing of Müpa Budapest, where Hungarian and Eastern European art hangs alongside Western pop art, and it also runs Hungary's pavilion at the Venice Biennale.

children.text: The Ludwig Museum – Museum of Contemporary Art is housed in the Danube-facing wing of Müpa Budapest, the arts complex in Ferencváros beside the Rákóczi bridge. The museum describes itself as the only museum of contemporary art in Hungary that collects international art, and its 2005 move into the Müpa gave it around 3,300 square metres of exhibition space spread over three storeys.

The story begins with the German collector Peter Ludwig, who trained as a lawyer and art historian and ran a chocolate business. In 1983 the exhibition Universal Art since 1960 came to the Kunsthalle in Budapest from Vienna and drew more than 40,000 visitors in four months; it was then that the idea of a Ludwig museum in the city was first raised. The founding contract was signed in Budapest on 21 March 1989, with 70 works donated to the Hungarian state, and a further 91 works were placed on long-term deposit in 1991. The first permanent exhibition opened in Building A of the Buda Palace on 4 June 1991.

Katalin Néray directed the museum from 1993 until her death in 2007, and under her leadership it built up a programme of temporary exhibitions that began in the palace and counted more than 200 between 1991 and 2007. Peter Ludwig died on 22 July 1996, and Irene Ludwig then helped set up the Peter and Irene Ludwig Foundation. The decision to leave the palace was taken in 2003, and the Palace of Arts, which officially opened on 14 March 2005, became the museum's new home that year.

What makes the collection unusual is Peter Ludwig's stated aim of bringing together the art of the ideologically divided world before 1989. The museum therefore shows Hungarian and Eastern European work next to Western pieces. The museum names Warhol, Lichtenstein and Oldenburg among the American and British pop artists whose emblematic works the Ludwigs brought to Budapest, and Hungarian artists such as László Lakner, Dóra Maurer and Ilona Keserü among its holdings. Since the 1990s it has also collected systematically from the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Romania and Slovenia, including Roman Ondák, Zbigniew Libera and Dan Perjovschi.

One detail the museum itself highlights is that it holds the first NFT work acquired by a Hungarian museum, a network piece called New Songs of New Times, or Art as Data by the BarabásiLab group led by Albert-László Barabási. The museum also manages the Hungarian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, and its director serves as national commissioner.
Good to know
Müpa Budapest stands near the Rákóczi bridge, next to the National Theatre; the H6 and H7 suburban railway is listed as a rail connection to the complex.
Exhibitions change, so check the museum's official site for current shows, opening times and tickets before you go.
The museum's website lists a museum shop, a library and accessibility information, which is worth reading if you have particular needs.
Müpa Budapest also has its own concert hall and Festival Theatre in the same building, so it can be combined with an evening performance.

docs.historyIntro: The Ludwig Museum reflects Budapest's place in modern European art, particularly the exchange between Central European and international ideas.

historySections.heading: A collection looking beyond national borders

children.text: The museum is named for the Ludwig art-collecting tradition and focuses on modern and contemporary works. Hungarian and international artists are placed in conversation rather than separated into unrelated histories.

Located in the Müpa cultural complex, the museum uses exhibitions and educational programmes to explore art made in changing social and political settings. Its content evolves, which makes the building a different experience across visits.

docs.name: Kunsthalle
docs.description: Műcsarnok, also called the Kunsthalle, faces the Museum of Fine Arts across Heroes' Square. Built for the 1896 millennium celebrations, it follows the German Kunsthalle model: no permanent collection, just changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It is the largest exhibition space for contemporary visual art in Hungary.

children.text: Műcsarnok, which translates roughly as art hall, is Budapest's Kunsthalle. It stands on Heroes' Square at Dózsa György út 37, facing the Museum of Fine Arts. It follows the pattern of the German Kunsthalle: it keeps no collection of its own, is run by artists and stages temporary exhibitions, with Wikipedia calling it the largest exhibition space for contemporary visual art in Hungary. It is an institution of the Hungarian Academy of Arts.

The institution is older than the building you see today. It was founded in 1877 on the initiative of the Hungarian National Fine Arts Association and first occupied a building at 69–71 Andrássy Avenue, a site that now belongs to the Hungarian University of Fine Arts. The Heroes' Square building was erected in 1896 for the millennium celebrations, and the institution describes itself as the home of Hungarian visual art since that year. Wikipedia credits the design to Albert Schickedanz and Fülöp Herczog, while the institution's own history page names Schickedanz alone.

The architecture is Neoclassical, with a Greek Revival portico at the front. Behind it a three-bayed, semi-circular apse houses a roofed exhibition hall that receives light through skylights. The building was renovated in 1995, and since then it has hosted leading Hungarian and international contemporary artists. A bookshop, a library and a café overlooking the square are also part of the complex, and the institution runs an archive, workshops and an online time machine devoted to its past.

Because there is no permanent display, what you see depends entirely on the current programme. The institution's own site has marked its 130th anniversary with a jubilee exhibition called Műcsarnok 130. The Kunsthalle has also played a part in the story of other Budapest museums: in 1983 the exhibition Universal Art since 1960 came here from Vienna, and its success prompted talks about a contemporary art museum in Budapest.
Good to know
Heroes' Square is the stop on the Millennium Underground (the M1 line); the Műcsarnok site also lists trolleybus and bus connections.
Check the official Műcsarnok site for the current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, as the programme changes regularly.
The Museum of Fine Arts is directly opposite and the Museum of Ethnography is at Dózsa György út 35, so the area works well for a day of museums.
The building has a café overlooking the square, which is useful for a break between exhibitions.

historySections.heading: An exhibition venue facing Heroes' Square

children.text: The building is part of the monumental cultural setting created around the city's millennium-era development. Its prominent entrance faces the square and complements the Museum of Fine Arts opposite.

historySections.heading: Art that changes with the programme

children.text: Unlike a collection-based museum, Kunsthalle focuses on rotating exhibitions of contemporary Hungarian and international art. The history visitors encounter here is therefore also the history of new artistic ideas as they are presented.

docs.name: Gellért Thermal Bath
docs.description: The Gellért Thermal Bath is Budapest's Art Nouveau bath beside the Danube at the foot of Gellért Hill. Built in 1912–1918 with the Hotel Gellért, it is currently reported closed for refurbishment, so check the operator's notice before planning a visit.

children.text: The Gellért Thermal Bath belongs to the Hotel Gellért, on the Buda bank next to the Liberty Bridge. It was built between 1912 and 1918 in the Secession (Art Nouveau) style, and both the bath and the hotel opened in 1918. The main hall, with its gallery and glass roof, and the mosaic-tiled thermal pools are among the city's best-known interiors.

The site has a long bathing history. References to healing waters here go back to the 13th century, a hospital stood on the site in the Middle Ages, and baths were built under Ottoman rule. The old name, Sárosfürdő, 'muddy bath', recalls the mineral mud that settled at the bottom of the pools. The water, at about 35–40 °C, contains calcium, magnesium, hydrocarbonate and other minerals.

The complex was extended in 1927 with an outdoor artificial wave pool, and in 1934 a thermal bath under a glass dome was installed in the hotel's former winter garden. Near the end of World War II the bath's Art Nouveau women's section was bombed, destroying its pyrogranite facade and wooden dressing rooms, and the post-war repairs were plainer. All pools became mixed-gender in 2013.

Important for planning: the bath is reported to have closed in October 2025 for a long refurbishment, with reopening planned for 2028. Because dates like these can change, check the operator's official website for the current status before you build a visit around it. Budapest has other thermal baths in the meantime, including the Széchenyi, Rudas and Lukács baths.
Good to know
Check the current opening status first: the bath is reported closed for refurbishment until 2028.
The Liberty Bridge and Gellért Hill (with the Citadella) are directly beside the building.
Széchenyi, Rudas and Lukács are the nearest alternatives if you want a thermal bath meanwhile.

The operator announced a closure for major renovation beginning in October 2025. This attraction's historic significance does not mean it can currently be booked for bathing.

docs.name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath
docs.description: The Széchenyi Thermal Bath in City Park is a vast neo-Baroque bathing palace of indoor and outdoor pools fed by two thermal springs, open since 1913. It is one of the largest thermal bath complexes in Europe, set in the Városliget park.

children.text: The Széchenyi Thermal Bath opened in June 1913 and covers a total area of 6,220 square metres. It was designed by Győző Czigler, who died in 1905; construction began in 1909 under Ede Dvorák and Kálmán Gerster. The yellow neo-Baroque building, with its domes and courtyards, stands in City Park, close to Heroes' Square.

The baths are fed by two thermal springs. The first was reached by Vilmos Zsigmondy's artesian well, drilled between 1868 and 1878 in City Park, which found water at 74.5 °C at a depth of about 970 metres. A second spring, discovered in 1938 at a depth of roughly 1,240 to 1,256 metres (sources differ), supplies water at 77 °C. The bath was planned as the 'Artesian spa' and was named after István Széchenyi when it opened.

Today the complex has three outdoor and fifteen indoor pools, along with saunas and steam rooms. Outdoor pool temperatures range from 27 to 38 °C, and the indoor pools from 18 to 38 °C. The main swimming and thermal sections are open to men and women together.

The bath has been expanded over time: an extension designed by Imre Francsek Jr. was completed in 1927, a thermal section and a day hospital were added in the 1960s, and a full renovation ran from 1999 to 2009.
Good to know
Metro line 1 (the yellow Millennium Underground) stops at Széchenyi fürdő, right beside the entrance.
Ticket types, cabins and lockers, and opening hours vary: check the operator's website and book ahead in busy seasons.
Bring or hire a swimsuit, towel and flip-flops according to the ticket you choose.

docs.name: Hungarian National Gallery
docs.description: The country's largest public collection of Hungarian fine art, displayed in the royal palace on Buda Castle hill. Founded in 1957 and installed in the castle in 1975, it holds medieval wooden altars, Gothic panel paintings and works by Munkácsy and Csontváry, and the palace also contains the Habsburg Palatinal Crypt.

children.text: The Hungarian National Gallery is the largest public collection documenting Hungarian fine art. It was established to display Hungarian art and first opened on 5 October 1957 in the building that had formerly housed the Supreme Court. In 1959 the government designated Buda Palace as its future home, and in 1975 the gallery moved into Buildings B, C and D of the palace, with its exhibitions opening in provisional form that October. Building A of the castle was acquired in 2005, adding exhibition space. At its founding the collection already held about 6,000 paintings, 2,100 sculptures, 3,100 medals, 11,000 drawings and 5,000 prints.

The setting is as much a part of the visit as the art. The palace on this site dates back to the 14th century, with building work under Louis the Great, Sigismund and Matthias Corvinus. It was badly damaged during the Ottoman occupation from 1541 and the Battle of Buda in 1686, and Baroque rebuilding began in 1749 under Maria Theresa. Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann later enlarged it, and the palace was inaugurated in 1912. The siege of Budapest reduced it to ruins in 1944–45; it was rebuilt by 1966, with Lajos Hidasi's modernist dome dating from 1961, and the interiors were completed only in the 1980s.

Inside, the collection runs from the Middle Ages to the 20th century. It includes 15th-century wooden altars, Master MS's The Visitation from Selmecbánya and works by Károly Markó the Elder, Pál Szinyei Merse, József Rippl-Rónai and Tivadar Kosztka Csontváry. The museum's catalogue lists a version of Mihály Munkácsy's Christ before Pilate, dated 1881. The gallery's permanent displays were assembled step by step: medieval panel paintings, wooden sculpture and Baroque art in 1979, Late Gothic winged altarpieces in 1982, and medieval and Renaissance stone carvings in 1985.

Beneath Building C lies the Habsburg Palatinal Crypt. Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary from 1795 to 1847, was the first to convert the castle chapel crypts into a family burial place, and the marble sculpture of the palatine and the bronze angel are by György Zala. The crypt was broken into and ransacked in 1973 and then walled up; after restoration it was reconsecrated on 3 October 1987 and opened to the public in 1989. Twenty-four members of the family are now buried there. Visits are arranged by the museum, so look at its official page before planning to see it.
Good to know
The gallery is in Buda Castle; the castle hill can be reached on foot or by the funicular from Clark Ádám Square.
The same palace complex holds the Budapest History Museum in Building E and the National Széchényi Library in Building F.

Displays change, so check the official site before a visit built around the late medieval altarpieces: a tourism listing says they are to move to the Museum of Fine Arts after restoration, with no date given.
The Palatinal Crypt cannot be visited casually; the museum's official page explains how visits are arranged.

children.text: The Gallery took up its present accommodation in Buda Castle in 1975. The palace setting gives medieval religious works, nineteenth-century painting and newer art a striking historical framework.

The National Gallery and Museum of Fine Arts came under a unified institutional structure in 2012. Their collections tell complementary stories, with the Castle museum retaining its strong emphasis on Hungarian art.

docs.name: Hungarian National Museum
docs.description: Hungary's national museum occupies a Neoclassical building by Mihály Pollack, built between 1837 and 1847 and grown from Count Ferenc Széchényi's donation of 1802. The area in front of it is tied to the revolution of 15 March 1848, and its collections stretch from prehistory to the modern age, including the Medieval Hungarian Coronation Mantle.

children.text: The Hungarian National Museum is the country's main museum of history. It began on 25 November 1802, when Count Ferenc Széchényi decided to donate his collections to the nation; the gift included 11,884 printed volumes, 1,156 manuscripts, maps and engravings, thousands of gold coins and some antiquities and paintings. Act VIII of 1808 then formally established the museum. In 1813 the state bought the plot of the Batthyány family on which the present building stands, and Act XXXVII of 1836 funded a new building after János László Pyrker donated his picture gallery in 1836.

Mihály Pollack designed the Neoclassical building, which was constructed between 1837 and 1847 on Múzeum körút. Wikipedia names Raffael Monti of Milan as the maker of the statues in the portico, among them an allegorical figure of Hungary flanked by Science and Art. The staircase and ceiling were painted by Károly Lotz and Mór Than, whose work has been in place since 1875. The garden has hosted concerts, including performances by Ferenc Liszt.

The building holds a special place in Hungarian memory because of 15 March 1848. The square in front of the museum was one of the key sites of the revolution, and according to the museum, Sándor Petőfi addressed the crowd there; the museum adds that, contrary to later tradition, he did not recite the Nemzeti dal there, although popular tradition (repeated by Wikipedia) places its reading on the front steps. Ágoston Kubinyi, who directed the museum from 1843, was entrusted that morning by Petőfi and Jókai with two freshly printed leaflets, the Nemzeti dal and the Twelve Points, and in 1849 he obtained a safe-conduct for the museum from the imperial commander to protect its collections. The Ceremonial Hall hosted sessions of the Upper House of the first National Assembly in 1848, and the central state commemoration of the national holiday is held in front of the museum each year.

The permanent displays are arranged chronologically. Prehistory up to the Avar period, which ends in 804 AD, is on the ground floor, while the history of Hungary from 804 onwards is on the first floor, where the Medieval Hungarian Coronation Mantle is also kept. Medieval and early modern stone inscriptions are on the ground floor, and a Roman lapidary is in the basement. Objects mentioned in the museum's description include the 11th-century Byzantine enamel plaques of the Monomachus Crown, Scythian golden deer ornaments from the 6th century BC and the chainmail of the 15th-century commander Pál Kinizsi.

The museum once held far broader collections. A law of 1949 separated the ethnographic and natural-history collections, which became the Museum of Ethnography and the Hungarian Natural History Museum, and the National Széchényi Library became independent. The Castle Museum in Esztergom joined in 1985, and the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History became a department in 2017.
Good to know
The museum is at Múzeum körút 14–16 in District VIII.
The Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library's Wenckheim Palace is a short walk from the museum, so the two can be visited together.
Exhibitions change, so check the museum's official site for current opening times, tickets and which displays are on view.
The museum's garden has long been used for concerts and festivals; check its programme for outdoor events.

children.text: The museum originated in the nineteenth-century movement to preserve the country's historical and artistic heritage. Its monumental classical-style building and garden became a landmark in the changing urban landscape of Pest.

The area in front of the museum is strongly associated with the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 and public gatherings linked to its demands. The setting remains a place where museum collections and civic memory overlap.

docs.name: City Park Boating Lake
docs.description: The lake in front of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park, where pedal boats, rowing boats and stand-up paddleboards are rented in the warmer months. In winter the same drained lakebed becomes the City Park Ice Rink, so the setting changes completely with the season.

children.text: The City Park lake lies in front of Vajdahunyad Castle, and the castle forms the backdrop for boaters. Visit Hungary notes that when the Rákos stream marshes were drained around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries, an artificial lake with islands was created.

In summer it works as a boating lake. The lakeside operator rents pedal boats and, depending on the water level, rowboats and stand-up paddleboards in season, and the shore hosts summer events such as paddleboard yoga; check the operator for current boats and dates. The same announcement describes the water as a lake of 60,000 square metres, but the article does not say who operates it, so check the boating lake's own site for details.

In winter the lakebed is drained and the City Park Ice Rink takes its place. Wikipedia explains the cycle from the rink's side: in summer the rink area is flooded to form a pond used for boating. A guide to Budapest City Park similarly says that, depending on the season, visitors can skate or rent a rowing boat.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the lake is a short walk from either, or you can walk along Andrássy Avenue.
Confirm the operating season and what is available on the day on the boating lake's own site, since boats are seasonal.
The ice rink uses the same space in winter, so the lake looks very different from one month to the next.

docs.name: City Park Ice Rink
docs.description: A skating rink in City Park with a history going back to 1870, a neo-baroque main building and a surface of about 12,000 square metres. It has hosted European and world skating championships, and in warmer months the same space is flooded to form the boating lake.

children.text: The City Park rink grew out of the Skating Association of Pest, founded at the end of 1869 under Géza Kresz. According to Wikipedia the rink officially opened on 29 January 1870 in the presence of Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria, and the first race was held on 2 February. On 6 January 1871 Jackson Haines gave a figure skating show there, and floodlights for night skating were installed in 1879.

The buildings changed as the rink grew. A wooden pavilion burned down in 1874 and was replaced by a skating hall designed by Ödön Lechner. The present neo-baroque main building, designed by Imre Francsek, followed in 1895 according to the rink's own history, Hungarian Wikipedia and Budapest heritage pages, although some sources give 1893. Championships followed: according to Hungarian Wikipedia the rink hosted the European Figure Skating Championships in 1895 and 1909 and world figure skating championships in 1929, 1935 and 1939.

Artificial ice was introduced on 26 November 1926, and the season grew to 105 days. Bombing in 1944 caused serious damage, though by autumn 1945 a larger part of the rink was serviceable again. In the 1960s the skating area was enlarged and standard 400-metre speed skating tracks were added.

A renovation between 2009 and 2011 gave the listed main building a full heritage restoration, and a 2011 business-press report says its entrance hall was returned to its original 1926 state, with gilded columns and railings. The rink reopened on 16 December 2011. Wikipedia gives the skating and bandy surface as 180 by 67 metres, the ice hockey rink as 60 by 30 metres and the total skating area as about 12,000 square metres. It describes the rink as the only bandy ice surface in Hungary. In summer the area is flooded to form a pond used for boating.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the rink is in the lakebed in front of Vajdahunyad Castle.
The rink operates on a separate seasonal calendar, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and skate hire.
Skating can be combined with a walk to Heroes' Square and Andrássy Avenue.

docs.name: The Tomb of Gül Baba
docs.description: The Tomb of Gül Baba is an octagonal Ottoman tomb on Rózsadomb, built between 1543 and 1548 for a Bektashi dervish who died in 1541. It later served as a Jesuit chapel, was restored several times, and is described as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

children.text: The Tomb of Gül Baba is an octagonal Ottoman tomb on Mecset Street in the Rózsadomb district of Buda, a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge. It was built between 1543 and 1548 on the orders of the Ottoman pasha of Buda, and has a shallow dome covered with lead plates and wooden tiles. Wikipedia describes it as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

Gül Baba was a Bektashi dervish and poet, and a companion of Sultan Suleiman I. He is thought to have died in 1541 around the time of the Ottoman capture of Buda; accounts differ on whether he died during the first Muslim religious ceremony in the city after the victory or was killed fighting beneath the city walls. Suleiman is said to have declared him patron saint of the city. In Hungary he is known as the Father of Roses, which Wikipedia calls a probable misunderstanding of the mystical meaning of his name, noting that roses were already in Hungary before the Ottoman conquest.

The tomb survived the Habsburg capture of the area in 1686, after which the Jesuits turned it into a Roman Catholic chapel dedicated to St Joseph. Later, János Wagner owned the land, maintained the site and allowed Muslim pilgrims from the Ottoman Empire to visit. In 1885 the Ottoman government commissioned a Hungarian engineer to restore it; the work was completed in 1914, and the tomb was declared a national monument.

The tomb was restored again in the 1960s and the 1990s. A large renovation was completed in October 2018, and the site was inaugurated by Viktor Orbán and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. A 1987 plan by the Hungarian and Turkish governments to build an Islamic centre and mosque there was halted by the political changes of 1989 and nothing was built.
Good to know
Mecset Street, where the tomb stands, is a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge, so wear comfortable shoes.
Check the official site or Budapest Info for current visiting arrangements, as access to the tomb and its grounds may be limited.
It is a religious and pilgrimage site for some visitors, so dress and behave respectfully.

docs.historyIntro: The tomb of Gül Baba is a small domed Ottoman shrine on Rózsadomb, described as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

children.text: Gül Baba was a member of the Bektashi dervish order who died in Ottoman Buda in 1541. His tomb (türbe) was built between 1543 and 1548 by Mehmed Paşa, the beylerbeyi of Buda; it is octagonal with a shallow dome. The tomb became an important pilgrimage site, and the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi reported that more than 200,000 Muslims attended his funeral prayer.

historySections.heading: A chapel, then a national monument

children.text: The tomb was not damaged when Habsburg armies took Buda in 1686, and the Jesuits later converted it into a Roman Catholic chapel dedicated to St Joseph. In 1885 the Ottoman government commissioned a Hungarian engineer to restore it; the work was completed in 1914 and the site was declared a national monument. It was restored again in the 1960s and, according to the cited article, in 2018. The tomb stands on Mecset (Mosque) Street in the Rózsadomb district, a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge.

stories.title: The Father of Roses and the name Rose Hill

children.text: Gül Baba's name is often rendered as 'Father of Roses'. A local tradition connects him with extensive rose gardens on the hillside and says that Rózsadomb, or Rose Hill, received its name from him.
The picturesque story is part of the site's traditional identity; the direct origin of the district name should not be treated as an independently proven fact.

stories.title: A funeral attended by a sultan?

children.text: A story associated with Gül Baba says that Sultan Suleiman I personally attended a magnificent funeral following the taking of Buda in 1541.
The account is presented as a legend in descriptions of the monument, not as a confirmed historical detail.

docs.name: Café Gerbeaud
docs.description: A confectionery founded in 1858 that moved to Vörösmarty Square in 1870 and took its name from the Swiss-born confectioner Emil Gerbeaud. Marble, exotic woods and Rococo-style stucco shaped the interior, and the café survived nationalisation under another name before the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984.

children.text: Café Gerbeaud stands on Vörösmarty Square in downtown Pest and is one of the best-known coffeehouses in Budapest. Gerbeaud's own timeline says the confectioner Henrik Kugler opened a café-confectionery on 14 October 1858 at what is now József nádor Square, and that he moved to today's Vörösmarty Square in 1870. Wikipedia says the new premises were on the ground floor of the head office of the Hungarian Commercial Bank of Pest, when the square was still called Gizella Square.

The name comes from Emil Gerbeaud, a Swiss confectioner who gained experience in Germany, France and England. Kugler had no successor and met Gerbeaud in Paris in 1882. Gerbeaud came to Budapest as a partner, gradually took over the shop and kept the original name. He introduced products such as butter creams, Parisian creams and many tea pastries. Wikipedia reports that by the end of 1899 he employed about 150 people, and Gerbeaud's own timeline notes that he served on the juries of world fairs in Brussels and Paris and received the French Legion of Honour.

The interior owes much to a 1910 design with advice from Henrik Darilek, who mainly used marble, exotic woods and bronze, according to Wikipedia. The ceiling stucco is in the Rococo style of Louis XV, the chandeliers were inspired by Empress Maria Theresa, and the café had French and Secessionist tables bought at the Paris world fair. Wikipedia lists Ferenc Deák, Franz Liszt and Empress Elisabeth among its guests.

Emil Gerbeaud died on 8 November 1919 and his wife ran the business until 1940. The shop was nationalised in 1948 and renamed Vörösmarty after the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, and the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984. In 1995 a German businessman, Erwin Müller, bought the building, according to the café's timeline, and the interior and offer have been renewed since, most recently in 2025. Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, begins at the square, and the Vörösmarty tér station of the M1 metro lies beneath it.
Good to know
The M1 metro runs under Vörösmarty Square, and Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, starts at the square.
Sources disagree on small details, such as whether Gerbeaud arrived in 1884 or a year after meeting Kugler in 1882, so treat exact early dates with care.
Check the official site for current opening times and the seasonal terrace arrangements before you go.

docs.historyIntro: Café Gerbeaud is one of the places where Budapest's tradition of elaborate confectionery meets the social history of its grand city-centre cafés.

historySections.heading: From Henrik Kugler to Emil Gerbeaud

children.text: Confectioner Henrik Kugler opened a café in Pest in 1858, moving to the square now known as Vörösmarty Square in 1870. The Swiss-born Emil Gerbeaud joined the business in the 1880s and helped turn it into an internationally known name in cakes and chocolates.

The business survived war and changes in ownership. After post-war nationalisation, the café operated under the name Vörösmarty before the historic Gerbeaud name returned in 1984. Its continued presence on the square makes it a living part of Budapest's pastry history.

stories.title: From paper cake trays to chocolate classics

children.text: The confectionery's own chronology credits Kugler with popularising cakes sold on paper trays and Gerbeaud with developing an expansive range of sweets. Its history also describes the introduction of cat's-tongue chocolates and cognac sour cherries to the local confectionery tradition.

docs.name: Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library
docs.description: The central building of Budapest's public library network is housed in the Wenckheim Palace, a neo-Baroque palace completed in 1889. Its ceremonial rooms, including a glass-roofed Imperial Staircase, the Golden and Silver Salons and two ballrooms, are preserved within a working library of more than 1.1 million volumes.

children.text: The Fővárosi Szabó Ervin Könyvtár, the Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library, is the largest library network in Budapest. Its central library is in the Wenckheim Palace, and the library's own page counts this among the most beautiful palaces of its time. The building is also a working library: it has about 13,000 square metres of floor area, seats 1,000 readers and holds more than 1.1 million volumes, which Wikipedia calls the largest public book collection in the city.

The palace was built when the district behind the National Museum was being laid out in the 1860s and later. Count Frigyes Wenckheim commissioned it, and the Saxon architect Artúr Meinig designed it in a mainly neo-Baroque style with some neo-Renaissance elements; it was completed in 1889. According to the library, the family kept the palace for only about 15 years after the count's death. In 1919 it was expropriated, first for a joiners' craft association and then for the Proletarian Museum, and it was briefly occupied by the Romanian army that year. Political parties and a journalists' and artists' club used it afterwards.

The library itself was founded in 1904 and was first housed in the Central Town Hall. The capital bought the Wenckheim Palace in 1927, converted it over four years, and the library opened there on 21 April 1931. Because of its architecture the palace could only partly function as a library and could no longer house the growing collection, so the municipal assembly approved an extension and reconstruction in 1997. Work began in 1998 to the design of Péter Hegedűs, and the complex reopened to readers on 12 September 2001. In 2003 it received the Prix d'Excellence of the International Real Estate Federation.

The ceremonial rooms are the reason many visitors come. A wrought-iron triumphal arch at the Szabó Ervin tér entrance leads to the Imperial Staircase, which has stucco ornament and marble and is lit through a glass roof. From the oval Reception Hall, which has fireplaces on both sides, the Golden Salon and the Silver Salon open off, and a Small and a Big Ballroom are separated by a glass door, with an orchestral gallery above and large mirrors facing the windows. The Mirrors' Corridor was originally a resting place for dancers. The former Baroque courtyard is now a glass-roofed atrium, and the former stable houses a coffee shop.
Good to know
The library is at Szabó Ervin tér, with the Reception Hall windows facing Kálvin tér, close to the Hungarian National Museum.
It is first of all a working library, so confirm on the official fszek.hu site which areas visitors can enter and when.
The ceremonial halls are used for events, so access to them can vary from day to day.
If you only want to see the interiors, check the library's pages for any guided tours or events before you go.

children.text: The Central Library moved into the historic building in 1931. docs.name: Museum of Ethnography
docs.description: Hungary's museum of ethnography moved in 2022 into a new building at the edge of City Park, designed by Marcel Ferencz of NAPUR Architect. It has a planted roof garden and a facade that carries almost half a million pixels, and below ground there are nearly 7,000 square metres of exhibition space.

children.text: The Museum of Ethnography began in 1872 as the Ethnographic Department of the Hungarian National Museum, and its first director was John Xantus de Vesey. According to the museum's own history page, it became independent of the Hungarian National Museum in 1947. For most of its history it lacked a purpose-built home. Wikipedia lists a series of moves, starting with the Várkert Bazár in 1892 and a building on Csillag utca in 1893, where the first permanent exhibition opened in 1898. In 1906 the collection moved to the empty Hall of Industry from the Millennial Exhibition, and in 1929 it reopened on Könyves Kálmán körút after storm damage. In 1975 it moved to the Palace of Justice opposite the Parliament.

The new building is in City Park at Dózsa György út 35, as part of the Liget Budapest project. Marcel Ferencz of NAPUR Architect designed it, and the inauguration ceremony was held on 22 May 2022, with visitors admitted from the afternoon of 23 May. The museum's director said the opening paid off a debt of 150 years.

The building curves with two wings that carry a roof garden planted with shrubs and perennials, rising to the height of the surrounding trees. The glass facade is covered by a metal grid holding almost half a million pixels that display selected motifs from the collections. Below ground there is almost 7,000 square metres of space for temporary and permanent exhibitions, including a ceramics space where almost 4,000 objects line both sides of a 40-metre staircase. Above ground are a bookshop, a restaurant, a library, a documentation centre and an interactive museum for children.

The collections are among the largest of their kind in Hungary. Wikipedia lists approximate figures including around 50,000 textile and costume items, almost 30,000 ceramic objects, 340,000 photographs, 30,000 manuscripts and 4,500 phonograph cylinders, among them sound recordings contributed by Béla Bartók and László Lajtha. Holdings cover Africa, Asia, Oceania, Indonesia, Europe and the Americas.
Good to know
The museum is at the entrance to City Park, at Dózsa György út 35, close to Heroes' Square and the Kunsthalle at number 37.
Check the museum's official site for current opening times, tickets and which permanent and temporary exhibitions are on.
Much of the exhibition space is below ground, so look at the site's accessibility information if you need step-free routes.
The roof garden is part of the architecture; check the official site for any access arrangements.

docs.name: House of Terror Museum
docs.description: The House of Terror at Andrássy út 60 is a museum and memorial to the victims of the fascist and communist regimes in 20th-century Hungary, in the building used by both the Arrow Cross and the ÁVH.

children.text: The House of Terror stands at Andrássy Avenue 60. In the 20th century the building was used by two oppressive regimes: the Arrow Cross Party, the Hungarian fascists, and the ÁVH, the communist state security police. It opened as a museum on 24 February 2002, after a foundation bought the building in December 2000 and carried out a year-long renovation.

The interior, the exhibition halls and the facade were designed by Attila Ferenczfy-Kovács. The black structure framing the building, with its blade-like walls, is intentionally stark among the pale facades of Andrássy Avenue, and photographs of victims are displayed on the outside.

The permanent exhibition covers Hungary's relations with Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union and the Arrow Cross and ÁVH years, and it serves as a memorial to the people who were detained, interrogated, tortured or killed in the building. In the basement you can see reconstructed cells like those the ÁVH used for prisoners. A T-55 tank is also displayed, carrying photographs of victims of Hungarian communism.

The museum's presentation has been discussed by historians; some critics argue that it presents Hungary mainly as a victim of foreign occupiers and gives too little attention to Hungarians' own roles in those regimes. It is a good idea to read other sources on the period and treat the museum as one perspective on a contested history.
The subject matter is serious and some displays are disturbing, so allow time and consider whether the visit is suitable for young children.
Good to know
Check the current opening days, ticket types and exhibition status on the museum's official website before your visit.
Some displays are disturbing: consider whether the visit suits younger children.
