docs.name: House of Unicum
docs.description: A visitor centre in the old Zwack distillery at Dandár utca 1, telling the story of Unicum, the Hungarian herbal liqueur. It combines period bottles, documents and family photographs with a 270-degree film, and visitors can see the old distillery and the cellar where the drink matures in oak barrels.

children.text: The House of Unicum is at Dandár utca 1 in District IX and tells the story of Unicum and the Zwack family. The exhibition shows period bottles, documents, family photographs and relics, with QR codes that link to descriptions, videos or extra images. A 270-degree film interpreted by the Zwack family tells the brand's story, and the old distillery building shows the production technology and the medicinal herbs and spices used in the drink.

Unicum is a herbal liqueur with a recipe based on more than 40 herbs and spices, aged in oak barrels. According to a legend that Wikipedia and other sources repeat, the drink dates from 1790, when the court physician Dr Zwack offered it to Emperor Joseph II, who exclaimed 'Das ist ein Unikum!' (this is unique). It is a story told about the origin of the name, and Wikipedia presents it as legend rather than verified history. The documented firm is dated to 1840, when József Zwack founded the company; the first factory was on Váci utca in Budapest, and in 1892 the company moved to its headquarters on the Danube in Ferencváros. The name Unicum was officially registered on 22 May 1883, together with the round bottle with a red cross that is still used.

The 20th century was turbulent for the family. The distillery was bombed four times in 1944, according to a McDaniel College account of a visit, and after the war the Communist state confiscated the factory. The Zwack family went into exile, while a state-run version was produced from a false recipe. Family members rebuilt production in Italy, and Péter Zwack returned to Hungary in the late 1980s; in 1992 he established the Zwack Unicum company and restored production to the original family recipe.

The visit includes the old distillery, which shows how the drink is made, and the cellar. According to the McDaniel account, Unicum ages for six months in oak barrels, and visitors can taste it on draught. A sample shop sells the full range of products and Unicum souvenirs. Today the range also includes variants such as Unicum Plum, which was introduced in 2012.
Good to know
The visitor centre is at Dandár utca 1 in Ferencváros; check the museum's official page for directions and the nearest public transport.
Visits are built around a guided tour and tasting, so check the official site for current tour times, languages and booking arrangements.
Because the tasting involves a strong alcoholic drink, plan the rest of your day accordingly.
Sources describing the legend and the family history differ in some dates, so treat the exhibition itself as the authority on the story.

docs.name: Underground Railway Museum
docs.description: A museum inside a disused stretch of the original 1896 tunnel beneath Deák Ferenc tér. Three historic carriages from the M1 line stand on the old tracks, alongside plans, maps and models, and a Zsolnay-tiled 'Gizella tér' sign in the entrance hall recalls the line's first city-centre terminus.

children.text: The Underground Railway Museum, also known as the Millennium Underground Museum, sits under Deák Ferenc tér in central Budapest and is reached through the pedestrian subway that links the square to Deák Ferenc tér metro station. It occupies a tunnel that once carried the tracks of Line M1, which opened on 2 May 1896 in Hungary's millennium year and which the operator BKV describes as the first underground railway on the continent.

The line was built from 1894 to 1896 using the cut-and-cover method, with the Hungarian subsidiary of Siemens & Halske commissioned to construct it. It was meant to bring passengers to City Park along Andrássy Avenue without surface traffic spoiling the street. The original line was 3.7 kilometres long with 11 stations. According to Wikipedia, the original station under Deák Ferenc tér lay only about 2.7 metres below the surface and sat on a sharp curve, so in the 1950s the route was diverted, leaving a stretch of the old tunnel (put at about 60 metres by Hungarian Wikipedia and an industrial-heritage listing, and at 80 metres by English Wikipedia) empty and walled off. The same source says that in the 1960s plans to fill it in gave way to a proposal for a metro exhibition.

The museum opened in 1975, on 26 October according to Wikipedia although one tourism site says 28 October, with three historic carriages lowered into the tunnel by crane, and it was renewed in 1996 for the line's centenary. The vehicles are No. 1, a metal-clad motor car from 1896 shown as it was when withdrawn in 1973; No. 19, a wooden-clad motor car from 1896 restored to its original condition; and No. 81, a driving trailer from 1960. On the platform opposite are relics, plans, maps, photographs and models that trace the history of the line, with a final section on the later metro lines.

Details in the entrance hall repay a look. The name Gizella tér, in Zsolnay glazed tile, comes from the line's original city-centre terminus, which is now Vörösmarty tér station, and panels list people who helped build the railway. A marble plaque records that Emperor Franz Joseph rode the line in 1896 and approved naming it after him. The line you can ride today runs between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út.
Good to know
Enter through the pedestrian subway between Deák Ferenc tér and the metro station on that square.
After the museum, ride Line M1 itself between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út to see the line the museum celebrates.
Check the operator BKV's official page for current opening times and tickets, and for temporary exhibitions.
The museum's site lists a children's corner and a shop, which may help if you are visiting with a family.

docs.historyIntro: Budapest's underground railway museum tells the story of an urban transport innovation created for a rapidly modernising capital.

children.text: The first line of the Budapest underground opened in 1896, serving the boulevard and celebrations of the Hungarian millennium. It was a landmark in continental European electric rapid transit and remains integral to the identity of Andrássy Avenue.

historySections.heading: A museum inside the old tunnel

children.text: A reconstruction of Deák Ferenc Square station in 1955 left a section of the earlier tunnel unused. The museum opened there in 1975, preserving transport equipment and original historical context below today's busy interchange.

docs.name: Szamos Chocolate Museum
docs.description: A small private museum above a Szamos café-shop on Kossuth Lajos tér, across from Parliament. Assembled by the Szamos family over about thirty years, it follows chocolate from cocoa to bar through moulds, pots, tins and marzipan sculptures. The official Szamos site lists it with guided tours booked online, but check current details before visiting.

children.text: The Szamos Chocolate Museum in Budapest is a private museum on the upper floor of a Szamos shop and café at Kossuth Lajos tér, on the corner across from the Parliament building. The venue described here is the one at Kossuth tér; Szamos has other shops and workshops elsewhere, which are separate venues. The Budapest Times reports that the museum was assembled over about 30 years and opened in 2016, and the official Szamos site lists it as a visitor attraction with online-booked guided tours; a visitor guide updated in October 2026 also describes it as operating, but check the official site for current details before planning a visit.

The collection was built up by Gabriella Szamos and her husband Gyula Kelényi, and the exhibition was compiled by the cocoa expert Anikó S. Nagy. According to a 2017 description and a visitor guide updated in October 2026, a guided tour runs through six rooms and follows chocolate from cocoa cultivation to moulding. There is a Biedermeier-style Sweet Salon about chocolate habits in the 18th and 19th centuries, with chocolate pots, cups and porcelain, and a workshop with working historical machines such as a milk separator and a chocolate mixer. According to the official Szamos site, visitors can also try making a chocolate product and take it home.

The objects on display include moulds for chocolate figures, coffee and chocolate sets, promotional items and a gallery of decorated metal chocolate boxes. Marzipan features prominently, including a large marzipan replica of Jean-Étienne Liotard's painting The Chocolate Girl, about 78 kilograms according to the Szamos site. The Budapest Times also mentions marzipan models of the Parliament building and the Hungarian crown jewels.

The museum is also a window into a family business. Mátyás Szamos (1918–2002) was born Mladen Szavits and grew up in the Serbian community of Szentendre. He began an apprenticeship in 1935 at the József Auguszt confectionery, and a visiting Danish confectioner taught him to make marzipan roses, which became his trademark. The first Szamos shop in downtown Pest opened in 1987, he received the Order of Merit of the Republic of Hungary in 1999, and the company's main base is in Pilisvörösvár. The business is now run by the third generation of the family.
Good to know
The museum is at Kossuth Lajos tér, in front of the Parliament building, so it fits easily with a visit to Parliament.
Guided tours are booked online through the official Szamos site. The museum's page offers guided tours with online time-slot booking; check it for tour languages and group arrangements.
Do not confuse it with other Szamos shops or sites in the region; this entry covers only the Budapest museum at Kossuth tér.
The tour is described as including tastings of chocolate, so check the official site for details of what is included.

docs.historyIntro: The Szamos Chocolate Museum places Budapest's love of confectionery in the setting of an exhibition devoted to chocolate and traditional sweetmaking.

children.text: The museum near Kossuth Square introduces chocolate as a craft and cultural product rather than simply a dessert. Its displays draw on the traditions of Hungarian confectioners and the changing objects associated with making and enjoying sweets.

A visit is a reminder that family businesses, recipes, shop design and packaging can be part of a city's story. Exhibition formats and any tastings can change, so contemporary programme information should be checked separately.

docs.name: Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center
docs.description: A photography centre at Nagymező utca 8, established in 2013, the centenary year of Robert Capa's birth and set in an Art Nouveau house of 1912. It holds a large collection of Capa prints, shows permanent displays on Capa and André Kertész, and runs temporary exhibitions, workshops and the annual Capa Grand Prize.

children.text: The Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center at Nagymező utca 8 in Terézváros was established by the Hungarian State on 12 July 2013 and opened on 3 December 2013, in the centenary year of Robert Capa's birth. Capa was a Hungarian-American photographer, and the state acquired his legacy in 2008 and brought it back to Hungary. That led to the plan for a photography institution. A selection of about 30 images was first shown at the Hungarian National Museum in March 2009, and the collection was later shown at the Ludwig Museum.

The centre holds more than 900 prints of Capa's photographs, together with 48 vintage prints that cover his career. Cornell Capa and the writer Richard Whelan selected the prints from the negatives and three sets were made; the other two are at the International Center of Photography in New York and the Fuji Art Museum in Tokyo. The centre's site lists two permanent exhibitions, Robert Capa – The Photojournalist and André Kertész – The Sentimentalist. It also organises temporary exhibitions, workshops and the annual Robert Capa Photography Grand Prize.

The house itself is part of the interest. It is an Art Nouveau building from 1912 commissioned by the art collector Lajos Ernst; Wikipedia credits it to the architect Gyula Fodor. The staircase has a large glass window by Miksa Róth, based on designs by the painter József Rippl-Rónai, and the stone benches were designed by Ödön Lechner. The Ernst Museum, which showed Ernst's private collection, occupied the building until August 2013. After Ernst's death in 1937 the cultural institution here changed names several times, and for decades the house served as a branch of the Kunsthalle.

Nagymező utca is also home to the Mai Manó House at number 20, so the centre pairs naturally with that house of photography on the same street. The Capa Center's site lists an event hall, the 8F Gallery and the Robert Capa Café on the premises.
Good to know
The centre is at Nagymező utca 8 in District VI, on the same street as the Mai Manó House at number 20.
Exhibitions change, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and which temporary shows are on.
The centre's site lists a separate exhibition in the 8F Gallery; check the official site for what is on view on which days.
The permanent exhibition on Capa shows 140 prints according to Wikipedia; check the official site for the current display.

docs.historyIntro: The Robert Capa Centre celebrates the contribution of Hungarian photographers to international visual storytelling, especially documentary images.

historySections.heading: A centre named for a Budapest-born photographer

children.text: Robert Capa, born in Budapest in 1913, became one of the most influential war photographers of the twentieth century. The photography centre opened during the centenary year of his birth to recognise photographers and the power of their work.

The centre presents contemporary exhibitions, often including press and documentary photography. In these images, history is not only a collection of dates but the records of how individuals witnessed moments of conflict, change and ordinary life.

docs.name: Mai Manó House
docs.description: Built in 1894 at Nagymező utca 20 as the multi-storey studio of the court photographer Manó Mai, this neo-Renaissance house keeps its decorated facade, glass-roofed studio and Zsolnay details. Since 1999 the House of Hungarian Photography has used it for exhibitions and a photography library.

children.text: Mai Manó House at Nagymező utca 20 was built as a purpose-designed photographic studio. Manó Mai (1855–1917), known for his child portraits, received the title of imperial and royal court photographer in 1885 and became an independent photographer in Budapest in 1878. He photographed the funeral procession of Lajos Kossuth in 1894 and Béla Bartók in 1903, and won a gold medal at the 1900 Paris World Exhibition. In 1906 he launched the periodical A Fény (The Light), which was edited from the same house.

Mai and his wife bought a one-storey house on the site in January 1892, and in January 1893 he applied for a permit to demolish it and build a new studio house. The plans were drawn by Rezső Nay and Muki Strausz, József Mann was the master builder, and the residence permit was granted on 31 July 1894. The building has eight levels that appear as three storeys from outside. The neo-Renaissance facade has statues, reliefs, ornaments and frescoes on terracotta tiles, with allegorical figures representing painting and photography. Inside are a carved oak staircase, stained glass by Miksa Róth and a Sunlight Studio with a glass balcony and slanted glass roof, whose street-side niches use Zsolnay pyrogranite.

After Mai's death, Hugó Weisz of Arad took over running the house. In 1931 Sándor Rozsnyai and his wife Mici, known as Miss Arizona, bought it from the photographer's son and built the Arizona Club in the courtyard, which operated until 1944. The Manó Mai Gallery opened on the mezzanine in 1995, and the Foundation of Hungarian Photography began buying lease rights from tenants in 1996. On 18 March 1999 the House of Hungarian Photography opened on the first and second floors.

Today the building holds exhibition halls, the József Pécsi Photography Library and offices, and the Library network page notes that parts of it still need restoration. Its official site lists current, future and past exhibitions, a bookshop and a library, and it is operated as part of the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.
Good to know
The house is at Nagymező utca 20 in District VI, on the same street as the Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center at number 8.
Look at the facade before you go in: the statues, reliefs and allegorical figures of painting and photography are part of the 1894 design.
Check the official Mai Manó House site for current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, because the programme changes.
Parts of the building are still awaiting restoration, so not every historic room is necessarily accessible; ask or check before visiting.

docs.historyIntro: Mai Manó House is itself a historic photographic artefact: an elaborate nineteenth-century studio created for a professional portrait photographer.

children.text: Hungarian photographer Mai Manó commissioned the building in 1894 on Nagymező Street. Its richly decorated staircases, stained glass and monogrammed ironwork reflect the social standing of studio portrait photography in that era.
The house is now used for photography exhibitions, books and research. Its survival allows visitors to see how the profession once presented itself architecturally as well as through photographs.

stories.title: The studio owner's initials in the stairs

children.text: The visitor account points out the 'MM' monogram on the ornamental staircase railings. It is a small detail that connects today's exhibition visitor with the photographer who had the building made.

docs.name: Vasarely Museum Budapest
docs.description: Set in an outbuilding of Óbuda's baroque Zichy Mansion, this museum is devoted to Victor Vasarely, the Hungarian-born artist often called the grandfather of Op art. Its rooms follow him from early advertising graphics to the geometric and kinetic works of the 1960s and 1970s, with temporary shows alongside.

children.text: The Vasarely Museum stands on Szentlélek tér in Óbuda, in a wing of the Zichy Mansion complex beside the Danube. The mansion itself is an 18th-century baroque building, and the museum occupies the former storage building of the palace rather than the main house, which today holds the Kassák Museum. Next door in the other outbuildings is the Óbuda Museum, so one walk can cover three quite different collections.

Victor Vasarely was born Győző Vásárhelyi in Pécs in 1906 and left Hungary for Paris in 1930. Before that he studied in Sándor Bortnyik's workshop in Budapest, a school shaped by Bauhaus ideas of visual education. In France he met the gallerist Denise René in 1944 and, from 1947, focused on the geometric and optical abstraction that made him famous. His 1937 painting Zebra is regarded by some as one of the earliest examples of Op art.

The Budapest museum grew out of gifts that Vasarely made to Hungarian institutions. One guide notes that Vasarely gave works to the Museum of Fine Arts several times after 1959. The museum opened in 1987. The collection is usually described as numbering more than 400 works, a figure that includes both original pieces and reproduced editions.

Inside, the display traces his path from academic drawings and advertising graphics of his early years to the Op art and kinetic pieces of the 1960s and 1970s. Look for the way flat patterns appear to swell, tilt or vibrate as you move past them; that effect is the point of the work, and it is why the museum rewards slow walking. The building also hosts temporary exhibitions, including solo and group shows with Hungarian and international artists.

Vasarely is honoured elsewhere too. A museum in his birthplace Pécs was established in 1976, and the Fondation Vasarely in Aix-en-Provence also opened in 1976 in a building he designed. Seeing the Óbuda collection gives a Hungarian view of an artist who spent most of his life in France.
Good to know
Check the official Vasarely Museum site for current opening times, tickets and temporary exhibitions before you go.
The Kassák Museum and the Óbuda Museum share the Zichy Mansion complex, so they combine easily into one visit.
The museum is on Szentlélek tér in Óbuda; use the BudapestGo journey planner to find the best public transport route from your hotel.

historySections.heading: A Hungarian-born pioneer of optical art

children.text: Victor Vasarely helped shape the twentieth-century movement known as Op Art. His experiments with patterned shapes and colour relationships challenged the viewer's perception without relying on conventional illusionistic painting.

The Budapest museum introduces his work in Óbuda and explains his ambition to make modern visual art approachable. The collection forms part of a wider story connecting Hungarian artists with the international avant-garde.

docs.name: Madame Tussauds Budapest
docs.description: Madame Tussauds Budapest fills the Palazzo Dorottya in downtown Pest, between Vörösmarty Square and the Danube promenade. It presents wax figures of Hungarian and international personalities in themed settings, including a recreated Buda Castle tunnel, and Hungarian craftspeople built many of the surrounding sets.

children.text: Madame Tussauds Budapest is in downtown Pest, not in the Castle District. It occupies the Palazzo Dorottya at Dorottya utca 6, in a building that stands between Vörösmarty Square and the Danube riverside promenade. The attraction opened on 25 May 2023 and covers about 2,000 square metres according to a report in the Budapest Times.

The route is built around themed zones with around fifty figures. Hungarian history and culture are represented by figures such as Lajos Kossuth, Empress Sissi, King Stephen I, Sándor Petőfi, Mihály Munkácsy and Ferenc Liszt. Sport and entertainment bring in Ferenc Puskás, László Papp, Béla Lugosi, Katinka Hosszú and Harry Houdini, while international singers, film actors, politicians and royal figures fill other rooms. The figures were chosen after market research and negotiations over the rights to use them.

Several settings are Budapest scenes recreated indoors. Press coverage of the opening names a Buda Castle Tunnel, a meeting with stars on the Danube embankment, a helicopter filming scene on Fisherman's Bastion and a themed world of spas. Interactive screens, light and sound effects and selfie points are part of the design.

According to We Love Budapest, each figure was made by about twenty artists at a workshop near London, taking three to four months, and the hair alone took six weeks. The sets around them were made in Hungary by stained-glass artists, architectural sculptors, woodcarvers, ornamental tinsmiths, gilders and theatre and film set designers.

The brand goes back to Anna Marie Tussaud (1761-1850), a French artist who specialised in life-size figures of famous people. Her first permanent exhibition opened on Baker Street in London in 1835. The Budapest venue is a recent addition to that tradition, and its 17 Hungarian figures, out of 51 in total according to We Love Budapest, give it a local character.
Good to know
Check the official Madame Tussauds Budapest site for current opening times and tickets; popular periods can fill up.
The entrance is on Dorottya utca, a short walk from Vörösmarty Square, so it fits easily into a downtown Pest walk.
Figure line-ups change over time; confirm on the official site which personalities are on display before you go.

docs.historyIntro: Madame Tussauds Budapest is a recent attraction in an older building: a wax-figure exhibition that opened in 2023 inside the Palazzo Dorottya, a Pest house that stood empty for almost a decade before its renovation.

historySections.heading: From London waxworks to a global brand

children.text: The name comes from Anna Marie Tussaud (1761-1850), a French artist who specialised in life-size figures of famous people. According to Wikipedia, she opened her first permanent exhibition on Baker Street in London in 1835, after decades of touring. That idea, a gallery of recognisable personalities modelled in wax, is the one the Budapest attraction continues, with figures chosen after market research and negotiations over the right to portray each person.

The exhibition is in the Palazzo Dorottya at Dorottya utca 6, in Pest beside Vörösmarty Square. Hungarian architectural press knows the building as the former Wurm House and refers to it as the Pollack-Hauszmann building. Before its renovation it was unoccupied for almost a decade. The project was commissioned by RDM, a group of Italian investors, and led by the Zoboki Demeter and Partners architectural office, with a facade refresh and restoration of the building's original look. Afterwards the lower storeys held a garage and commercial spaces and the upper floors offices and residential units.

Madame Tussauds Budapest opened on 25 May 2023, filling about 2,000 square metres of the palazzo. Reports on the opening describe a red carpet route past around fifty figures. We Love Budapest reported that each figure was made by about twenty artists at a workshop near London, taking three to four months, and that Hungarian craftspeople, including stained-glass artists, architectural sculptors, woodcarvers and set designers, made the settings. Press coverage also noted that organisers asked the public which personalities they most wanted to see.

docs.name: Light Art Museum (LAM)
docs.description: The Light Art Museum, known as LAM, occupies the 1890s Hold Street Market Hall designed by Győző Czigler. It is built around light as an art form, with works by pioneers such as László Moholy-Nagy and contemporary artists. A June 2026 report announced a temporary closure, but the museum's site now lists a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026; check it for current status.

children.text: The Light Art Museum, or LAM, is at Hold utca 13 in Budapest's fifth district, inside a former market hall. The hall was built between 1892 and 1896 to plans by Győző Czigler as Market Hall No. 5, one of six large market halls built in Budapest in that era. Its eclectic structure covers about 2,107 square metres, and the museum keeps the hall's industrial character rather than hiding it.

The museum presents itself as a space dedicated to light as an independent art form, and one local article called it the world's first light art museum. Coverage from its first season lists around thirty-five works, including holograms, laser installations, animations, shadow and light objects and interactive pieces that visitors can approach closely.

The reviews and previews name some of the historic anchors. These include László Moholy-Nagy's 1931 light-space modulator, a kinetic sculpture that light projections were cast onto, and works by György Kepes and Victor Vasarely. Alongside them are contemporary pieces, such as Kiégő Izzók's Re-Fracture, an installation of sixty high-power tubes synchronised to music.

The best-known sight is a huge inflatable zeppelin hanging in the main hall, with animations and projections on its interior. A sponsored article about the first exhibition describes a balloon about forty metres long and roughly 2,000 square metres of textile surface, so treat those numbers as promotional.

Status needs care. A June 2026 article reported that the museum was temporarily closing at the end of June 2026 as its exhibition More than Human ended, with no date for a full reopening; the museum's own website and an October 2026 We Love Budapest article later described a new exhibition, EGO, running from October 2026. A March 2026 guide still described it as operating. Check the museum's own website for the current situation before planning a visit, and if you are sensitive to flashing lights or loud sound, ask the staff about the exhibits before you go in.
Good to know
Check the official LAM site (lightartmuseum.hu) first: a June 2026 report announced a temporary closure, but the site now lists a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026.
Arany János utca on the M3 metro line is the nearest metro station named by one visitor guide.

A March 2026 Xpatloop guide advises that visitors with light sensitivity should check with staff for a safe route through the exhibits, because some installations involve strobe lights and loud audio; the museum's own site does not mention this.
Flash photography is not allowed according to visitor guidance; read the rules on the official site.

docs.historyIntro: The Light Art Museum occupies a market hall from the 1890s. Its story runs from a working food market through a renovation, a pandemic closure and a 2022 conversion to a museum of light, with a temporary closure announced for mid-2026.

historySections.heading: A market hall for central Pest

children.text: The hall at Hold utca 13 was built between 1892 and 1896 to plans by the architect Győző Czigler as Market Hall No. 5, one of six large market halls built in Budapest in the Austro-Hungarian era. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as eclectic, covering 2,107 square metres, with 190 permanent and 80 temporary stalls, plus police and ambulance rooms, a coffee-measuring point and a market supervision office. A restaurant and a meat-inspection building were attached.

The hall was renovated in 2014 and renamed Belvárosi Piac, the Inner City Market, and gradually became a producers' market. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, declining tourism during the COVID-19 pandemic led to a temporary closure from 1 January 2021. A local article on the museum recalls that the hall had once been a place where people bought produce, fish and meat, and that this activity had ended.

historySections.heading: From market to museum of light

children.text: The building reopened to visitors in September 2022 as the Light Art Museum Budapest, according to We Love Budapest and a sponsored report; Hungarian Wikipedia gives both summer 2022 and November 2022, so the exact start is unclear. An opening show, The Revolution of Light, featured work by György Kepes, László Moholy-Nagy and Victor Vasarely alongside contemporary Hungarian-origin artists, and was extended to 15 August 2023. A June 2026 article reported that the museum would temporarily close at the end of June 2026 and gave no reopening date; the museum's website and an October 2026 article later described a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026, so check the official site for its current status.

docs.name: Cinema Mystica Budapest
docs.description: Cinema Mystica is an immersive audiovisual art space in the historic Párisi Udvar, at Ferenciek tere. Created by the digital artists of Global Illumination, it fills grand halls with projections, sound and interactive installations; its current show, Form in Flux, features works by 26 Hungarian and international artists.

children.text: Cinema Mystica is an immersive audiovisual art venue at Ferenciek tere 10, inside the historic Párisi Udvar. It was created by the digital artists of Global Illumination, and visitors are meant to interact with installations and projections rather than only watch them. A 2026 article puts the venue at over 1,200 square metres, spread through the building's grand halls.

The story began elsewhere. A May 2022 article describes an earlier Cinema Mystica show at Kristály Színtér on Margaret Island, with sixteen new-media installations. In July 2023 We Love Budapest reported the move into the Párisi Udvar as the country's first permanent immersive digital exhibition space, with 21 installations in ten rooms, 85 projectors and five kilometres of cable. An article in July 2026 marked the third anniversary and said more than 500,000 visitors had come.

The current main show is Form in Flux, Patterns of Consciousness, open since early summer 2025 with works by 26 Hungarian and international artists. Pieces named in coverage include The Visitors, four monumental human-shaped figures that respond to light and sound; All Eyes on You, a floor of eyes in a Flower of Life pattern that reacts to movement; and The Oracle, an LED chamber that generates an astrological reading from a visitor's birth date.

Other spaces include the Solfeggio Room, where sound-responsive visuals made in real time with TouchDesigner are projected onto four walls and the floor, and Futurama Budapest, an installation made for MVM Future Talks that takes visitors through the Budapest skyline up to the 27th century.

The setting is part of the appeal. The Párisi Udvar was restored over several years and reopened in 2019 as a hotel building, and Cinema Mystica uses its grand halls. Shows change over time, so what you see depends on the current programme.
Good to know
Booking online in advance is recommended because capacity is limited and the exhibition can sell out; check the official Cinema Mystica site for tickets and opening times.
The venue is accessed from Ferenciek tere in downtown Pest.
Exhibitions are renewed periodically, so check what is currently on before you go.
The Párisi Udvar arcade itself is worth a few minutes if you have time before or after your session.

heroImage.alt: The glass-roofed Art Nouveau arcade of the Párisi Udvar, where Cinema Mystica is located

docs.historyIntro: Cinema Mystica began as a 2022 exhibition on Margaret Island and moved in 2023 to its present home in the Párisi Udvar, a Pest arcade that was restored and reopened as a hotel building in 2019.

historySections.heading: A first showing on Margaret Island

children.text: A May 2022 We Love Budapest article describes the first Cinema Mystica exhibition at Kristály Színtér, a cultural centre on Margaret Island, in a Bauhaus-style building that the article says was formerly a mineral water-bottling plant. It showed sixteen new-media installations that combined art and technology, including Let There Be Life, a room with video projected on the walls, ceiling and floor showing the origin of life. The article names the visual artist and musician Dávid Vígh (Takkra) and the visual group Glowing Bulbs among those involved, and does not identify the founders of Cinema Mystica.

The permanent home is in the Párisi Udvar at Ferenciek tere 10. According to We Love Budapest, the Downtown Savings Bank commissioned the architect Henry Schmahl, who conceived the building in 1912-1913, and it was one of Budapest's earliest reinforced concrete buildings. According to Hungarian Wikipedia it became a listed monument in 1976 (a 2018 We Love Budapest article gives 1967 for heritage protection), and the arcade stood largely empty for years; the Jégbüfé ice-cream parlour and a hologram shop were among its well-known tenants. Restoration began in 2014, and the building reopened as a hotel in The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, with the passage open to the public.

In July 2023 We Love Budapest reported that Cinema Mystica had moved into the Párisi Udvar as the country's first permanent immersive digital exhibition space, with 21 installations in ten rooms, 85 projectors and five kilometres of cable. By July 2026, the venue marked its third anniversary, reporting more than 500,000 visitors and four exhibitions so far. The current show, Form in Flux, has run since early summer 2025 with works by 26 Hungarian and international artists.

docs.name: IKONO Budapest
docs.description: IKONO Budapest is an immersive, interactive art experience at Váci utca 27, in the heart of the downtown shopping street. Its rooms include a ball pit, a mirror maze and a light-painting space, created with artists such as Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and it is part of a European IKONO network.

children.text: IKONO Budapest is an immersive art museum at Váci utca 27, on the main pedestrian shopping street of downtown Pest. It has been open since September 2023, and the idea is that visitors step into the art instead of only looking at it: touching, listening, moving and interacting are encouraged. The official site describes it as suitable for people of all ages.

The Budapest venue belongs to the IKONO Xperience network. According to We Love Budapest, the brand first opened in Madrid in 2020 and has since expanded to Rome, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. The official Budapest page lists Madrid, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin among the network's cities, so this is a format tried elsewhere rather than something designed only for Budapest.

Room counts depend on the source: the opening-week article spoke of ten fantasy worlds, while the official site now speaks of twelve rooms. Named experiences include the Lantern Sanctuary, where light and shadow create dreamlike scenes; a light-painting room inspired by Picasso's experiments with light; and The Love Within, an immersive work by the artist Koketit about self-love. Reviewers and press mention a large ball pit, a mirror maze and a Super Mario-themed room.

Rooms were created with international artists. The opening-week article names Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and the venue page for Budapest credits the American visual artist Heather Bellino with installations that invite visitors to look for hidden meanings, patterns and symbols. A walk through takes about an hour according to the same article.
Being on Váci utca, IKONO is easy to combine with a downtown walk. Sources give no details about the building itself, so treat this as an experience venue rather than a historic site.
Good to know
Check the official IKONO Budapest site for current opening times, tickets and booking conditions.
Wear comfortable clothes if you plan to try the ball pit, and check the official site for rules on bags and photography.
Váci utca is a pedestrian street in downtown Pest, so IKONO fits easily into a walk through the centre.

docs.historyIntro: IKONO Budapest is the Hungarian branch of a young European network of immersive art museums. Its short history runs from a first venue in Madrid in 2020 to a Váci utca opening in September 2023.

historySections.heading: From Madrid to a European network

children.text: According to We Love Budapest, the IKONO brand first opened in Madrid in 2020 and then expanded to Rome, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. A September 2023 article said the first IKONO exhibit had opened in Madrid about three years earlier, with Rome and Barcelona following before Budapest. The official IKONO site presents Budapest as part of the IKONO Xperience network, which also has locations in Madrid, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. The sources consulted do not name the founders.

The Budapest venue is at Váci utca 27, on the pedestrian shopping street of downtown Pest, and has been open since September 2023. A We Love Budapest article published on 5 September 2023 described it as recently opened, with ten fantasy worlds including a colourful jungle, a large ball pool, a UV-painted sea installation, a light-painting room inspired by Picasso's experiments with light and a quiet room. Sources give no details about the building's earlier history.

The rooms were created with international artists. The opening article names Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and the venue profile says the Budapest venue was created with the American visual artist Heather Bellino. The official site now describes twelve rooms, naming experiences such as the Lantern Sanctuary, light painting and The Love Within, an immersive work by Koketit about self-love, so the programme has been extended since opening or is counted differently.

docs.name: Tropicarium – The “Shark Zoo”
docs.description: Tropicarium, known as the Shark Zoo, is a marine and tropical aquarium inside the Campona Shopping Center in Budapest's 22nd district. Opened in May 2000, it has eight halls, sand tiger and brown reef sharks seen from a 12-metre tunnel, a ray pool and a rainforest section with alligators.

children.text: Tropicarium is an aquarium and animal exhibition inside the Campona Shopping Center, at Nagytétényi út 37-43 in Budapest's 22nd district. It opened on 26 May 2000. The official site calls it one of the largest marine aquariums in Central Europe, and a history page for the attraction gives its size as almost 3,000 square metres. It is a different venue from the zoo in City Park and from the similarly named Tropicarium in Kolmården, Sweden.

The concept goes back to Károly Farkasdi, a Hungarian businessman living in Sweden, who with his family created a first establishment of this kind in Kolmården in 1990. The Budapest project followed: construction began in September 1999 and took eight months. A visitor guide says the build used hundreds of tons of concrete and iron, with filtration and purification systems, and that most of the decoration was handcrafted by Tropicarium staff.

The exhibition is arranged in eight halls with hundreds of species. They include a Hungarian fauna section, freshwater and saltwater tanks, a coral reef, a reptile and insect house and a rainforest with alligators and dwarf caimans, where a tropical rain shower falls above the alligator enclosure every 15 minutes. Monkeys and snakes are also kept.

The headline attraction is the shark aquarium, with sand tiger and brown reef sharks, which visitors can watch from a 12-metre viewing tunnel running beneath it. A ray pool lets visitors touch and feed rays under staff guidance. Feeding days are set by animal group in the official schedule, so check the site if you want to see a particular feeding.

The operators have said they add one or two new aquariums or terrariums at a time so that returning visitors find something new, and a page last updated in 2010 reported nearly four million visitors in about eight years. The attraction is described as wheelchair and stroller accessible, and a cloakroom is available because the indoor air is warm.
Good to know
Check the official Tropicarium site for current opening times and tickets, and for holiday arrangements.
Tropicarium is inside the Campona Shopping Center in the 22nd district, outside the centre; plan the journey with a public transport planner or check the shopping centre's directions.
Flash photography is not allowed, and visitors cannot re-enter the exhibition once they leave it according to the site.
Guided tours in Hungarian and English must be booked in advance by email.

docs.historyIntro: Tropicarium grew out of a concept first built in Sweden in 1990 and opened in Budapest on 26 May 2000, inside the Campona Shopping Center, after eight months of construction.

children.text: A history page for the attraction credits the concept to Károly Farkasdi, a Hungarian businessman who lived in Sweden between 1963 and 1998. In 1990 he and his family created the first such establishment in Kolmården, Sweden. The Budapest aquarium is a separate venue from the Swedish one.

Intensive construction began in Budapest in September 1999 and took eight months. A visitor guide says the work involved hundreds of tons of concrete and iron, filtration, purification and IT systems, and that most of the decoration was handcrafted by Tropicarium staff. The facility opened on 26 May 2000 in the Campona Shopping Center, on the outskirts of the city, and was described as the largest sea aquarium in Central Europe at almost 3,000 square metres, arranged in eight rooms.

The history page says the operators add one or two new aquariums or terrariums at a time to give returning visitors something new. About eight years after the opening, they reported nearly four million visitors. That page was last updated in 2010, so later developments are not covered there. Check the official site for the present exhibits, which include sand tiger and brown reef sharks and a 12-metre viewing tunnel.

docs.name: Óbuda Museum
docs.description: The Óbuda Museum sits in an outbuilding of the baroque Zichy Mansion on Fő tér. Its permanent exhibition, Óbuda - Three Faces of a Town, follows the district from its medieval royal days to the 1970s, with period scenes such as a manor salon, a cooper's workshop and a small inn.

children.text: The Óbuda Museum is at Fő tér 1 in Óbuda, the old town on the Buda side of the Danube that was once a royal centre. It is part of the Zichy Mansion complex, a one-storey baroque building built for Count Miklós Zichy between 1746 and 1752 according to the Kassák Museum, which occupies the main house. Renovation of the complex began in 2008, and the museum's own description says the building's design was matched to the design of the square.

The permanent exhibition, Óbuda - Three Faces of a Town, covers the district from the Middle Ages to the 1970s in three units. The first presents medieval Óbuda when it was a royal centre. The second covers the village-like small town from the Zichy era to the early 20th century. The third shows the demolition of older buildings, the rebuilding of the area and the social changes that came with it.

The exhibition includes hands-on activities, tasks and recreated scenes. According to the museum, visitors walk in over cobblestones that link past and present, and rooms include a manor-house salon with Miklós Zichy, the workshop of the cooper Simon Tóbiás and a small inn. An English-language audio guide is available.

An older museum helps explain the name. The first local and settlement museum of Budapest opened in Óbuda in 1927 in an old boys' school as the Árpád Museum of Óbuda, but its collection was lost in the Second World War. The current museum is not its successor and regards itself only as its spiritual heir.

The surrounding complex is useful context. The outbuildings also contain the Vasarely Museum, and the Térszínház and Hello Wood workshops, while the Kassák Museum is in the mansion. The Óbuda Museum also runs other sites in the district, including the Goldberger Textile Collection on Lajos utca.
Good to know
Check the official Óbuda Museum site for current opening times, tickets and any temporary exhibitions.
The Vasarely Museum and the Kassák Museum are in the same Zichy Mansion complex.
An English audio guide for the permanent exhibition is mentioned on the museum's profile; confirm availability on the official site.

docs.historyIntro: Óbuda Museum explores the layered past of the northern Buda district, from its medieval royal days to the 1970s.

historySections.heading: A district older than modern Budapest

children.text: Óbuda incorporates traces of the Roman world alongside later village, town and industrial development. The museum helps explain how separate places came together in the capital formed in 1873.

historySections.heading: Everyday life as a historical source

children.text: Its displays include urban history and collections of objects from ordinary households. The 'Toys in the City' (Játék a városban) exhibition, which the museum calls Budapest's only permanent toy-history exhibition, presents Hungarian toys through the theme of the city.

docs.name: Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives
docs.description: Beside the Dohány Street Synagogue, this museum and archive presents Hungarian Jewish history, ritual objects and the Holocaust. It holds Judaica and what the museum describes as Europe's most comprehensive Jewish community archives, in a 1930s building by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó on the site of Theodor Herzl's birthplace.

children.text: The Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives is at Dohány utca 2, within the complex of the Dohány Street Synagogue in Pest's former Jewish quarter. The synagogue was built in 1854-1859 to plans by Ludwig Förster, with an interior by Frigyes Feszl, and consecrated on 6 September 1859. The museum is attached to it, so a visit puts the building, the memorials and the collections in one place.

The Association of European Jewish Museums says the idea of a separate Jewish exhibition arose during the 1896 millennial celebrations, when Judaism was recognised as one of Hungary's historic religions. The first collection of about 1,500 objects was kept in a downtown apartment. The museum's own building was designed by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó in a style matching the synagogue; sources give 1931 or 1932 for its construction and move-in.

The building stands on the site of Theodor Herzl's birthplace according to Wikipedia. Its collections combine Judaica, everyday and ritual objects and archives. Notable items include a pair of copper rimonim (Torah finials) dated 1602, and a Roman-era gravestone regarded as the oldest trace of the Hungarian Jewish community. According to Wikipedia, the silver trowel used to lay the synagogue's keystone is kept at the museum.

A history of loss runs through the displays. The museum records that in 1942 two employees of the Hungarian National Museum hid the valuable artefacts in a cellar, which is credited with preserving the collection. The collection includes a Holocaust room, and the synagogue complex includes the Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park, where Imre Varga's Tree of Life memorial carries victims' names on its leaves.

The museum and archives were reunited as one institution at the end of 2014. The archives are described as the most comprehensive Jewish community archives in Europe. Because the site is a place of worship, a memorial and a museum, visitors should follow the guidance on dress and behaviour given on the official site.
Good to know
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets, security checks and any dress or head-covering requirements.
The Dohány Street Synagogue, Heroes' Temple and Raoul Wallenberg Memorial Park are in the same complex, so plan enough time for the whole site.
Treat the museum, courtyard and cemetery as places of remembrance: keep voices low and follow staff instructions.

docs.historyIntro: The Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives preserve objects and records that reveal centuries of Jewish life in Hungary.

historySections.heading: A collection bound to the Jewish Quarter

children.text: The museum is located close to the Dohány Street Synagogue, in an area central to Budapest's Jewish religious and cultural history. Its holdings include objects associated with ritual life, communities, art and documentary memory.

The archival role is especially significant in understanding the Holocaust and the complex continuity of Hungarian Jewish communities before and after it. The institution invites consideration of living traditions as well as loss and remembrance.

docs.name: Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism
docs.description: Founded in 1966 in Buda Castle's former Fortuna Inn, this museum now stands on Korona tér in Óbuda. It follows Hungarian shops, brands, hotels and restaurants from the late 19th century to the Second World War, with recreated interiors and two rooms linked to the writer Gyula Krúdy.

children.text: The Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism is at Korona tér 1 in Óbuda. It was established in 1966 and first worked in the former Fortuna Inn in the Buda Castle district until 2005; the museum has since moved to its present Óbuda address. A profile describes it as the only museum of its kind in the world, with exhibits drawn from across Hungary.

One permanent display, Hosting guests, to be guests, opened on 11 December 2014. It traces Hungarian civilian hospitality from the late 19th century to the Second World War, mainly through room interiors. The title is taken from a 1933 etiquette book by Károly Gundel and Frigyes Karinthy. A separate part of the museum is devoted to trade, with measuring and fairs, and recreated shops such as a sweetshop, an ironmonger's and a stationer's.

Visitors will also find displays on department stores such as the Great Parisian Store and Corvin, and on old brands such as Kajla, Százszorszép and Bambi. An Advertisement Board room shows glazed objects from the trade collection with boards about smoking, drinks and insurance. Touchable objects, drawers to open and touchscreen quizzes make the displays practical for children.

A section titled I have never had a home presents two rooms linked to the writer Gyula Krúdy, who spent his last three years and died in Óbuda. One is furnished as a cheap hotel, and Krúdy's habit of eating in restaurants is reflected in a room furnished as one.

The museum also runs workshops where visitors learn the history of foods such as ice cream or chocolate and then make them, and the building includes the Kultea Theatre, which hosts concerts, book launches, tastings and lectures. Guided tours are available, mostly in English.
Good to know
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and workshop bookings.
Korona tér 1 is in Óbuda (1036); use the BudapestGo planner to find the best way there from your hotel.
Guided tours should be arranged in advance on the official site; most are offered in English.
Combine with the Óbuda Museum, Goldberger Textile Collection and Fő tér, all in the same district.

docs.historyIntro: This museum explores how Hungarian shops, hospitality businesses and visitor culture have shaped everyday life and city streets.

children.text: Trade and hospitality history includes objects easily overlooked elsewhere: shop fittings, signs, menus, packaging, photographs and documents. Together they reveal the changing experiences of customers, staff and travelling visitors.

Budapest's cafés, markets and restaurants are tied to wider changes in urban work and leisure. The museum interprets this world through collections and exhibitions, with themes that may change from one visit to another.

docs.name: Goldberger Textile Collection
docs.description: On Lajos utca in Óbuda, the Goldberger Textile Collection occupies the former main building of the Goldberger company, a textile printing firm whose roots go back to the 1780s. The permanent exhibition follows the family and the factory from the 1784 blue-dyeing workshop to the winding-up of the factory, with interactive elements that explain textile printing.

children.text: The Goldberger Textile Collection is part of the Óbuda Museum's network, at Lajos utca 138 in Óbuda. It occupies the former main building of the Goldberger company, which the museum's own profile says was founded in 1784. The building is over 200 years old according to the museum's profile, and the museum says the family's first workshop opened in the present building at the end of the 18th century.

Sources disagree slightly on the start of the firm. The museum gives 1784, while Wikipedia says that Ferenc Goldberg founded a dyeing factory on today's Lajos utca in 1785 with a Czech bluemaker named Stibrall. The firm modernised under later generations. Wikipedia records a perrotine printing machine bought in 1845, a visit by Emperor Franz Joseph I in 1857 and the family's ennoblement with the prefix Buday in 1867.

Leó Goldberger became chairman and chief executive in 1920, and the company set up a weaving mill in Kelenföld in 1923 and a spinning mill in 1927. It reached its peak in 1938-1939. Leó Goldberger was arrested by the Gestapo on 19 March 1944 and died at Mauthausen concentration camp on 5 May 1945. The factory was nationalised in 1948, later became part of BUDAPRINT, which went bankrupt in 1989, when liquidation proceedings were opened against it.

According to the museum's own site, the permanent exhibition has five units. They follow the Goldberger family from its settlement in Óbuda and the founding of the blue-dyeing workshop in 1784, through the growth into a factory, mechanisation and international success under Leó Goldberger, to the years under the planned economy and the winding-up of the factory, and the display uses interactive elements to explain textile printing. Older listings mention a display about a Tamási slipper workshop, but the museum's current exhibition page does not, and a 2014 Infostart report says the workshop's machines were shown in Óbuda until 2012 and then went back to Tamási.
Sewing machines, scale models and authentic copies of equipment give a physical idea of how patterned cloth was produced.
Good to know
Check the official Óbuda Museum site for current opening times and tickets for the Textile Museum.
The collection is at Lajos utca 138, away from Fő tér; check the route before you go.
According to the museum's visitor page, the nearest stops are Tímár utca and Szentlélek tér on the H5 suburban railway, and the museum has no public parking.

historySections.heading: A factory woven into the district

children.text: The Goldberger company became a well-known name in Hungarian textile manufacturing. The museum collection stands in the former factory premises on Lajos Street, connecting industrial history with the architecture of the workplace.

historySections.heading: Fabric as a record of social change

children.text: Textile production reveals changing tastes, technology, labour and everyday consumption. The Óbuda Museum collection preserves those stories through manufacturing objects and examples of the fabrics associated with the enterprise.

docs.name: Aquincum Museum
docs.description: The Aquincum Museum and its archaeological park in Óbuda preserve part of the Roman civil town of Aquincum. A neoclassical museum building opened in 1894, ruins of streets, houses and a Mithras temple stand outdoors, and the best-known find is a Roman water organ dated to AD 228.

children.text: The Aquincum Museum is in the Óbuda district, on the site of the Roman town of Aquincum. Aquincum began as a military base on the frontier of the Roman Empire, and Legio II Adiutrix was stationed there by AD 89. After Pannonia was reorganised in AD 103 it became capital of Pannonia Inferior, and it later received municipal status and then the rank of colonia. By the end of the 2nd century the town had at least 30,000 inhabitants according to Wikipedia.

Roman remains first came to light in 1778, when a vine-grower found part of an underfloor heating system. One source says Maria Theresa ordered the baths left open under protective cover, making them Hungary's first protected historic monument. Professional excavations began in the later 19th century, and the museum's neoclassical exhibition building opened on 10 May 1894.

Outdoors, the archaeological park contains part of the civil town. Visitors see excavated houses, shops and a market along two streets, a civilian amphitheatre, a reconstructed Roman house known as the House of the Painter and a reconstructed Mithras temple. Indoors, the collections include finds from the local mithraeum and a very large body of archaeological material. Wikipedia says the Budapest History Museum, to which Aquincum belongs, holds more than a million objects.

The best-known object is the Aquincum water organ. Remains were found in 1931 when the archaeologist Lajos Nagy excavated the civil town's fire brigade building, and bronze plates indicate that the instrument was given to the fire brigade in AD 228. Wikipedia calls it the only Roman water organ known to survive. In 2007 a former transformer house on the grounds became the museum's new main building, with the exhibition Rome in Aquincum, which displays the organ.

The Second World War did serious damage. Bombing of the nearby Óbuda gas factory damaged the museum building by about 40 percent, the ruin area was hit by twelve bombs and almost half the finds were destroyed. The permanent exhibition reopened in 1948. The wider Budapest History Museum network also includes Roman sites in Óbuda such as a Baths Museum and a Military Town Museum.
Good to know
Check the official Aquincum Museum and Budapest History Museum sites for current opening times, tickets and which exhibitions are running.
The outdoor archaeological park is a large site, so allow time for a walk between the museum and the ruins; wear comfortable shoes.
The Baths Museum and Military Town Museum are separate Roman sites in Óbuda; check the official sites for how to visit them.

docs.historyIntro: Aquincum is where Budapest's Roman history becomes tangible, through the surviving streets, baths and public spaces of an ancient settlement.

children.text: Aquincum developed as an important Roman centre in the region of present-day Óbuda. Its archaeological remains include residential buildings, spaces for trade and bathing, and traces of the public life of a provincial settlement.
The museum's ruin garden brings visitors close to the surviving walls of the civilian town. Exhibited finds help interpret how Romans lived, worked, gathered and adopted customs far from Rome itself.

stories.title: Why some call Aquincum the Hungarian Pompeii

children.text: Travel guides such as We Love Budapest describe the open-air archaeological site as 'the Hungarian Pompeii', a nickname rather than an official title. The comparison is a modern description of the extensive ruins, not a claim that Aquincum was buried by the eruption at Vesuvius.

docs.name: Budapest History Museum — Castle Museum
docs.description: The Castle Museum occupies Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, and tells the story of Budapest from prehistory to the late twentieth century. Its most distinctive rooms are the restored medieval palace spaces in the basement and a hall of Gothic sculpture found buried in 1974.

children.text: The Castle Museum is the part of the Budapest History Museum housed in Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, with its main entrance from the Lion Courtyard. Its displays cover roughly two thousand years of the city's past, arranged from the medieval palace in the basement up to prehistory on the top floor.

The basement is the reason many people come. After the damage of the Second World War, archaeologists uncovered the remains of the medieval royal palace beneath the later buildings. The Gothic Hall, built by King Sigismund in the early fifteenth century, is an irregular rectangle of 20.2 by 11.55 metres divided into two naves with rib vaults. Its ribs, pillars, arches and window niches were restored by the sculptor Ernő Szakál in 1961 and 1962, and the architect László Gerő planned the wider reconstruction. Nearby are the palace chapel, stretches of castle wall and a room devoted to the Corvina library.

On the ground floor are the Gothic sculptures from the royal palace. In 1974 a sealed cellar of a townhouse in front of the palace yielded more than sixty sculptural torsos and thousands of fragments from the court of King Sigismund of Luxembourg, who reigned from 1387 to 1437. Some pieces still carry traces of paint, and many were never finished; one guide says the workshop broke up before the work was done, though the reasons remain unclear.

Upstairs, Budapest, Light and Shadow follows about a thousand years of the city's history, while a second exhibition follows the Royal Palace itself from 1686 to today. The top floor, In Pursuit of Lost Times, begins with stone tools about fifty thousand years old and runs to the Hungarian conquest.

The museum has older roots than the castle. Budapest's city assembly decided to found a municipal museum in 1887, and the medieval department and the directorate moved into the restored castle in 1967, after which the whole institution became known as the Budapest History Museum. It also runs the Kiscelli Museum, the Budapest Gallery and the Medieval Jewish Prayer House.
Good to know
The entrance is in the Lion Courtyard of Building E on the Buda Castle hill; a second entrance leads to the King's Cellar. Check the official site for current opening times and tickets.
The Hungarian National Gallery and the National Széchényi Library are in the same palace complex, so the museum fits easily into a longer castle visit.
One visitor guide notes that the basement level with the medieval rooms cannot be reached by wheelchair; confirm access arrangements on the official page.

docs.historyIntro: The Castle Museum uses the layers of Buda's Royal Palace to tell the story of the city from antiquity to the modern era.

children.text: The museum is housed inside Buda Castle, itself a structure transformed by medieval royal life, Ottoman-era conflict and later rebuilding. Rooms and surviving fragments link physical architecture to the city's changing political role.

historySections.heading: From separate towns to a capital

children.text: The permanent exhibitions explore Roman Aquincum, the medieval royal palace, the Ottoman wars, the fusion of Buda, Pest and Óbuda and the city's rapid growth around 1900. Visitors can see how the modern metropolis emerged from communities with distinct histories.

docs.name: Kiscelli Museum
docs.description: Set in a Baroque Trinitarian monastery on a plateau above Óbuda, the Kiscelli Museum shows Budapest's urban history from the eighteenth century on and houses the Budapest Municipal Gallery. Its bare-brick former church, now an exhibition and concert space, is the building's most unusual interior.

children.text: The Kiscelli Museum stands at Kiscelli utca 108 in Óbuda, on a plateau above Bécsi út, and is a branch of the Budapest History Museum. It presents the history of Budapest from the eighteenth century onward and is also the home of the Budapest Municipal Gallery, the Fővárosi Képtár.

The building began as a Trinitarian monastery. The Baroque complex was built from 1745 to 1758 to designs by the Viennese architect Johann Entzenhoffer, with a church beside the north wing of the two-storey friary. A copy of the Mariazell cult statue was placed there, and the site became a place of pilgrimage known as Kiscell, from the German Klein Zell. One visitor guide gives 1760 as the year the church was consecrated.

In the 1780s, under Joseph II, the order was dissolved; sources give 1783 or 1784. It served as a military hospital, barracks and storage space. Around 1911 (sources give 1910 or 1911) the Viennese furniture manufacturer and collector Miksa Schmidt bought the property and converted it into a mansion, and for a long time it was called the Schmidt Castle. When he died, his will of 1935 left the complex to the capital city for use as a museum.

The Second World War did great damage, and the fighting of November 1956 caused more. A visitor guide reports that the roof was destroyed and that a new one was built between 1976 and 1983, with the church interior deliberately left as bare brick. The former church, with its raw brick nave and empty niches, now hosts large temporary exhibitions and concerts, and the Municipal Gallery held its first exhibition in the ruin in 1988.

The permanent rooms hold some distinctive objects: the original 1712 figures from the Holy Trinity column that stands in front of Matthias Church, a collection of old Pest and Buda shop signs, the complete fittings of the Golden Lion pharmacy and a printing room with a Columbia press. Around the museum lies the Kiscelli park forest, about fifteen hectares of woodland that Schmidt laid out as the mansion's grounds.
Good to know
A visitor guide lists tram 17 from Széll Kálmán tér, or trams 19 and 41 from Batthyány tér to Szent Margit Kórház, then a steep walk up Kiscelli utca. Bus 165 from Kolosy tér avoids the climb.
One visitor guide says there is no lift and the upper floor cannot be reached by wheelchair, and that some permanent-room labels are in Hungarian only. Check the official site for access details.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the programme of exhibitions and concerts in the church space.
Allow time for a walk in the Kiscelli park forest around the museum.

docs.historyIntro: Kiscelli Museum occupies an evocative historic complex in Óbuda, where the history of the building adds another layer to its collections.

children.text: The complex's past includes religious use, later military and residential functions and wartime shelter. Its architecture preserves traces of the changing roles that historic buildings can acquire across centuries.

historySections.heading: A home for urban history and art

children.text: As part of the Budapest History Museum, Kiscelli holds collections about the modern city's social and material culture alongside fine art. The museum grounds connect indoor exhibits to the building's complicated past.

docs.name: Budapest Gallery
docs.description: The Budapest Gallery is the contemporary-art arm of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition house at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda occupies an old dwelling house whose recorded history goes back to the early eighteenth century, and it presents Hungarian and international art across painting, photography, design and architecture.

children.text: The Budapest Gallery shows contemporary Hungarian and international art, and its exhibition house stands at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda. The gallery aims to present contemporary art to the public and to introduce Hungarian artists to audiences abroad, and its programme reaches beyond painting to architecture, photography, media art, applied arts and design.

The institution has had several names and homes. It was founded in 1979 as the Budapest Fine Arts Directorate, with one department for public art and one for fine art, and was renamed Budapest Gallery in 1983. In 2011 the city assembly made it a main department of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition department first worked from the Klotild Palace building in Szabadsajtó utca and moved in 2013 to the Bálna building on the Danube, where it ran the New Budapest Gallery until 2019.

The Lajos utca house itself has a long and modest history. A museum page records the building as a Bear House at the beginning of the eighteenth century, says it was rebuilt as a dwelling house toward the end of that century, and notes that further extensions were added in the nineteenth century. It is now the gallery's exhibition house.

Besides changing exhibitions of living artists, the house holds a permanent display of works by the sculptor Pál Pátzay, who lived from 1896 to 1976. The small statues in that exhibition, which opened in 1982, come from the Budapest History Museum's own collection. The gallery also looks after the Imre Varga Collection, devoted to another sculptor, which has its own address on Laktanya utca in the same district.
Good to know
The gallery is in Óbuda at Lajos utca 158; check the official site for the current exhibition programme, opening times and tickets.
Exhibitions change often, so look at the gallery's programme before you travel and see what is on.
The Imre Varga Collection on Laktanya utca is a separate site run by the same gallery, so confirm which venue a given exhibition uses.

docs.historyIntro: Budapest Gallery connects the city's historic cultural spaces with new visual ideas and contemporary artistic debate.

historySections.heading: Exhibiting art within the city's history

children.text: The Gallery forms part of Budapest's city-museum network and has presented work by Hungarian and international contemporary artists. Rather than offering one fixed narrative, its temporary programmes track the changing questions explored by artists.

The museum's Óbuda location ties the modern exhibitions to a district with a long Roman, town and industrial heritage. That setting can be part of the experience even when the art on the walls is explicitly contemporary.

docs.name: Hungarian Railway History Park
docs.description: A railway museum in a former locomotive depot in Budapest's 14th district, with a 34-stall roundhouse, a turntable and more than a hundred vehicles from steam locomotives to rare railcars. Visitors can also try a locomotive simulator and see a small railway running through the grounds.

children.text: The Hungarian Railway History Park, Magyar Vasúttörténeti Park, stands at Tatai út 95 in Budapest's 14th district, on the site of the former Northern depot of the Hungarian State Railways. It covers more than 70,000 square metres and displays over a hundred vehicles and pieces of equipment, mostly railway vehicles.

The site has its own history. The depot was built in 1911 as a twin: a 22-stall building and a 34-stall building. Only the larger one survives, because the smaller was destroyed during the Second World War. The surviving roundhouse and turntable now display locomotives, which is why the park is full of engines standing in their old stalls. From 1951 to 1990 the depot carried the name Hámán Kató Fűtőház.

The museum's roots go back further than the park. A small railway open-air museum had operated at Ópaks station in Paks from 1985 to 2000, and the Hungarian Railway Museum Foundation was founded on 22 November 1999. The park itself opened on 14 July 2000.

The fleet runs from steam to electric traction, and some of it still works and is used for nostalgic trips in Hungary and abroad. Named exhibits include a teak dining car built for the Orient Express in 1912, the Árpád railcar of 1934, the steam locomotive MÁV 411.118 of the USATC S160 class and a Soviet GAZ-13 Chaika that served Prime Minister Jenő Fock and was later converted to run on rails.
Visitors can also ride the garden railway in the grounds, which the park's ticket information lists; check the park for its other hands-on attractions.
Good to know
Nearby bus stops are served by routes 30 and 30A, among others; Angyalföld station is about a 15-minute walk away. Check current routes before you set off.
A halt called Vasútmúzeum on the Budapest to Esztergom line is reported to be served only at weekends and on holidays, so confirm train times if you plan to arrive by rail.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the dates of special events and train rides.

docs.historyIntro: The Railway History Park preserves the machines and practices that helped connect Hungarian cities, industries and travellers in the age of steam.

children.text: Rail transport transformed the movement of people and goods through Hungary during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Engines, carriages and railway infrastructure reflect the engineering ambition that made those connections possible.

historySections.heading: A museum built for large machines

children.text: The Budapest park gathers historic railway equipment in an open-air setting. The vehicles reveal how technology, passenger comfort and industrial design changed, while operational demonstrations and visitor activities depend on the current programme.

docs.name: Medieval Jewish Prayer House
docs.description: A small vaulted prayer hall on the ground floor of a house in the Castle District's old Jewish quarter, with Hebrew wall paintings from the Ottoman period and tombstones in a side room off the gateway. Sources differ on how old the hall is, and it is again used for worship.

children.text: The Medieval Jewish Prayer House is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 on the Buda Castle hill, in what was once the Jewish quarter of Buda. The Castle District heritage site describes the building as a single-storey, unpretentious burgher's house that preserves the remains of a medieval Jewish worship hall. It is run by the Budapest History Museum, whose exhibition there is called The Jewish population of Buda in the Middle Ages.

Visitors pass through a barrel-vaulted gateway. In a room to the left stand tombstones from the medieval and Ottoman periods; turning right leads to the worship hall, whose roof is supported by pillars. On the vault is a painting from the Ottoman era showing a drawn bow with a line from Hannah's prayer, The bows of warriors are shattered, and nearby fields with Stars of David carry a priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers.

Sources disagree on the building's dating. Museum and tourism pages say the prayer house was built at the end of the fourteenth century and uncovered in 1964 during monument-protection research, which also revealed seventeenth-century Jewish inscriptions. A 2018 article instead links the hall to the Ottoman period and says it was found in 1968 during postwar reconstruction, starting from two fresco fragments in the gateway. The scholar Sándor Scheiber decoded the lettering and attributed it to Jews of the Sephardic rite rather than the Ashkenazi rite first suspected.

The hall is not the only synagogue site on the street. A far larger Great Synagogue is recorded at number 23, built in 1461 and destroyed in the siege of 1686. Its ruins were found in 1964 by the archaeologist László Zolnay, who reburied them under a concrete slab, and they still lie beneath the courtyard of a Baroque palace.

After years as an exhibition space, the hall was renovated at the initiative of the Unified Hungarian Jewish Congregation and regained its religious function in the autumn of 2018. It holds about seventy people, was designed inside by Tibor Somlai and still serves as an exhibition space on weekdays.
Good to know
The house is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 in the Castle District, a short walk from the other Buda Castle sights.
Because the hall is again used for worship, check the official site for current visiting arrangements, opening times and tickets before you go.
It is a small room, so a visit is short; combine it with the Castle Museum, which belongs to the same museum group.

children.text: The surviving building is linked to Jewish religious life in the medieval and Ottoman periods. Architectural details and painted inscriptions help reveal a community whose history is not always visible in the district's grander royal buildings.

historySections.heading: A small site with lasting significance

children.text: The Budapest History Museum's interpretation includes historic symbols, writing and related finds. As with other sites of religious heritage, its history should be approached with respect for the people and traditions represented.
