docs.name: Petőfi Museum of Literature
docs.description: Hungary's national literary museum fills the Károlyi Palace, a classicist building where a prime minister was arrested in 1849 and the Hungarian National Council was formed in 1918. Its collections include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song and a complete Vizsoly Bible, and it reopened in 2023.

children.text: The Petőfi Museum of Literature, Petőfi Irodalmi Múzeum, is housed in the Károlyi Palace at Károlyi utca 16, on the corner of Károlyi Mihály utca and Ferenczy István utca. It was founded in 1954 and took over the legacy of the Petőfi–Jókai House, which dated from 1909. Its first two years of exhibitions were held at the Hungarian National Museum, it received a palace at József nádor tér in 1955, and it moved into the Károlyi Palace in the spring of 1957.

The palace is described as one of Budapest's most important classicist monuments. It was rebuilt from 1832 to designs by the Viennese architect Anton Pius Riegl, with József Hofrichter leading the construction, and the new palace was inaugurated in 1841. In the Reform Era it housed the literary salon of László Bártfay, where Franz Liszt played. In January 1849 Lajos Batthyány, prime minister of the first responsible Hungarian government, was arrested there, and in October 1918 the Hungarian National Council was formed in the building.

Count Mihály Károlyi was its last private owner. After he emigrated in 1919 the state confiscated the palace (a heritage register dates this to 1920), and the capital took over the building in the late 1920s, in 1928 or 1929 depending on the source. The capital's picture gallery was based there until 1953, and the Petőfi Museum moved in four years later. Hungarian Wikipedia records auctions of the family's art in 1932 and of a library in 1937. Renovations took place in 1996 to 2000 and again in 2022, and the building reopened in January 2023 with a new permanent Petőfi exhibition.

The collections centre on Hungarian literature. They include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song, the manuscript of József Attila's poem At the Danube, and a complete copy of the Vizsoly Bible, known as the Károlyi Bible. The museum also holds the literary estates of writers such as Mór Jókai, Zsigmond Móricz, Ferenc Karinthy, Tibor Déry and Antal Szerb, and exhibits a printing press of the Landerer and Heckenast firm.
Good to know
The palace is at Károlyi utca 16 in central Pest, near the inner-city walking routes; check the official site for opening times and tickets.
Check the official English pages for what is available to non-Hungarian readers, as well as the current exhibitions.

historySections.heading: A palace for the written word

children.text: The museum is housed in one of Budapest's notable classicist buildings. It collects and interprets writings and objects associated with Hungarian authors, allowing manuscripts and personal possessions to become historical evidence.

Sándor Petőfi remains strongly associated with the Hungarian national awakening and 1848 Revolution. A museum named after him also explores a wider range of literary voices, revealing how the country's changing identity has been expressed through literature.

docs.name: Hungarian Agricultural Museum and Library
docs.description: Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park is a Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque ensemble designed by Ignác Alpár and built for the 1896 Millennium celebrations. The museum was founded in the same year and holds the national collection on agriculture, hunting, fishing and related food-industry material.

children.text: The Hungarian Agricultural Museum occupies the Baroque wing of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park. The castle was designed by Ignác Alpár and built in 1896 for the Millennium celebrations marking a thousand years since the Hungarian conquest. It was first a set of copies of historical buildings, made mainly of wood and cardboard, and its main façade copies Hunyad Castle in Vajdahunyad, today Hunedoara in Romania, which gave it its name.

The museum itself was founded in 1896. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the founding decree was signed on 20 June 1896 by the agriculture minister Ignác Darányi, and the museum opened in the castle on 12 September 1897 under its first director, Árpád Balás. The temporary structure was not built to last. It was closed in July 1899 and demolished, and the museum moved to a rented house on Kerepesi út until the castle was rebuilt.

The rebuilding in brick and stone was approved in 1900 and followed Alpár's plans, with the Gothic and Renaissance-Baroque wings finished in 1904 and the Romanesque section in 1908. The museum moved back in 1904, and Franz Joseph I reopened it on 9 June 1907. English Wikipedia gives 1907 for the opening of the exhibition, so the dates in the sources differ slightly. The castle was declared a monument in 1991.

Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the museum has 39 collections and that in 2016 it was estimated to hold more than 400,000 objects. Notable holdings include the first steam locomotive to arrive in Hungary in 1852, a trophy collection and a collection of wheat varieties. In 2015 the Gate Tower and the Apostles' Tower were opened to visitors, and the same year original plans by Alpár were found in a walled-up room.

The courtyard holds Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III, and the Ják Chapel stands in the castle grounds but is not run by the museum. The museum's library has been merged with the national agricultural library, and its holdings in the castle were moved to Attila út in 2019 and 2020.
Good to know
The castle is in City Park, so it combines easily with a walk around the lake and the other buildings of the park.
Relocation of the museum has been discussed in recent years; check the official site for the current status, opening times and tickets before you go.
The statue of Anonymus stands in the castle courtyard, and the Ják Chapel is in the castle grounds.

docs.historyIntro: The Agricultural Museum is housed in Vajdahunyad Castle, a building born from the celebrations of Hungary's millennium in 1896.

historySections.heading: A romantic castle made for a public exhibition

children.text: The story begins with the 1896 celebrations marking a thousand years of Hungarian statehood. Vajdahunyad Castle gathered architectural references from different periods to present the country's past in a single picturesque setting.

historySections.heading: Farming history in the city park

children.text: The Agricultural Museum and Library use the castle to explore Hungary's agricultural heritage, tools, crops and rural life. The contrast between romantic architecture and practical subjects is part of what makes the visit distinctive.

docs.name: Hungarian Natural History Museum
docs.description: Hungary's national natural history museum grew out of collections given to the National Museum in the early nineteenth century. Its exhibition building stands in the Ludovika complex in Pest's eighth district, and its collections cover anthropology, zoology, minerals and fossils.

children.text: The Hungarian Natural History Museum, Magyar Természettudományi Múzeum, grew out of the Hungarian National Museum. In 1802 Count Ferenc Széchényi gave his library and coin collection to the nation, and his wife Julianna Festetics later donated a mineral collection that became the root of the natural science collections. Archduke Rainer gave the first palaeontological collection in 1811, and in 1818 the botanical department began with the plant collection of Pál Kitaibel.

Separate departments for zoology, botany and mineralogy were created within the National Museum in 1870. The zoological department moved to a building at Baross utca 13 in 1928, partly because of the 1927 International Zoological Congress in Budapest, and a partly independent natural history museum was set up in 1933. An anthropology department was created soon after 1945, and the museum became independent in 1949.

The 1956 revolution caused heavy losses. The National Museum building was hit on 24 October, destroying parts of the Africa exhibition and mineral and palaeontological material, and on 5 November an incendiary bomb struck the Baross utca building, destroying tens of thousands of specimens and about a hundred thousand books and offprints.

In 1994 the government decided to place the museum in the Ludovika Academy complex, a historic site originally built as a military academy. Collections began moving in from 1995, and the exhibition building opened in 1996. The museum's own history page describes the exhibition building as the rebuilt Ludovika riding hall, the former Alfa cinema building that burned down in 1992. Other Hungarian sources add that the Alfa cinema opened there in 1958 and closed in 1990, and that a fire in May 1992 destroyed the roof structure. The Ludovika site now houses mineralogy, geology and palaeontology, anthropology, parts of zoology and the library.

The anthropology collection is described as one of the ten largest in Europe. Since 1 July 2024 the museum has been a branch institution of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Centre. Moving the museum out of Ludovika has been discussed since 2010 without a move taking place, so its exhibitions are best checked before a visit.
Good to know
The exhibition site is at Ludovika tér 2 to 6 in the eighth district; the nearest metro stops on line M3 are Semmelweis Klinikák and Nagyvárad tér.
Check the official site for current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, since the museum's future location has been under discussion.
The botanical collection is housed in an Art Nouveau palace on Könyves Kálmán körút that a source says is not open to visitors.

docs.historyIntro: Budapest's Natural History Museum opens a window into the country's scientific collecting tradition and the diversity of life and geology.

children.text: The museum's origins lie in the historic study and preservation of the natural world. Over generations, scientists assembled animal, plant, mineral and fossil collections that support both public understanding and research.

Exhibitions use specimens and explanations to show how habitats, species and geological landscapes change. Scientific collections hold evidence far older than Budapest itself and remind visitors that the region's natural history is part of a much larger world.

docs.name: Franz Liszt Memorial Museum and Research Centre
docs.description: On the first floor of the Old Academy of Music on Vörösmarty utca, the museum preserves the apartment where Franz Liszt stayed whenever he was in Budapest from 1881 until his death in 1886. His pianos, desk, library and furniture are displayed in the rooms where he lived.

children.text: The Liszt Ferenc Memorial Museum and Research Centre is in the Old Academy of Music at Vörösmarty utca 35, just off Andrássy út. It opened in September 1986 and occupies the building in which the Academy of Music taught from 1879 to mid-1907, after its first four years in a building on Hal tér. The Academy had been founded with Liszt as its founding president and a professor, and he took no salary for his teaching.

Liszt was given a service apartment on the first floor and lived there, whenever he stayed in Budapest, from January 1881 until his death in 1886. The apartment is now the memorial museum, furnished with his instruments, furniture, library and personal belongings. A visitor article notes that the rooms look little changed and that the furniture in the two larger rooms stands where it did in his time.

Look for the walnut writing desk in the corner of the study-bedroom, made for him by his friend the piano maker Ludwig Bösendorfer, with a pull-out three-octave keyboard in place of the middle drawer, which Liszt could use to try out passages. The core collection is Liszt's donation to the Academy and includes a Bösendorfer and two Chickering pianos, a Mason & Hamlin cabinet organ, a combined piano and organ by Erard and Alexandre, and a piano-harmonica by Bachmann. His Budapest library of books and scores is also here.

After the Academy moved to its new palace on Liszt Ferenc tér on 12 May 1907, the building was used by a music school, a coffee shop, associations and a foreign trade company. The Ministry of Culture and Education bought it in 1980 and gave it to the Academy of Music. A first Liszt memorial room had opened in the new Academy building in 1925, and the research centre was founded together with the museum in 1986.

Some key exhibits are on loan from the Hungarian National Museum, which Liszt himself had given important relics from his career. Documents and memorabilia from relatives and pupils, among them Eduard Liszt, Jenő Hubay and István Thomán, have also been added over the decades, together with later purchases and bequests.
Good to know
The museum is at Vörösmarty utca 35, in front of the Vörösmarty utca stop of the Millennium Underground on Andrássy út.
The concert hall next to the apartment hosts concerts, so check the official site for the current programme, opening times and tickets.
The former dining room and ground-floor foyer are used for temporary exhibitions, so what you see may vary.

docs.historyIntro: The Franz Liszt Memorial Museum keeps the pianist and composer's life close to the city where he helped establish a lasting musical institution.

children.text: Franz Liszt was central to the establishment of the academy of music that carries his name. His connections with Budapest made the city an important centre for his later work, teaching and musical advocacy.

The memorial museum is linked to the Liszt Academy and its research centre. Its permanent exhibition fills the entrance room, Liszt's study-bedroom and the drawing room, while the former dining room and the ground-floor foyer host temporary Liszt exhibitions.

docs.name: Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts
docs.description: A museum of Asian art in the villa on Andrássy út where the optician and collector Ferenc Hopp lived. It grew from his bequest to the state and now holds Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Tibetan and other collections, with a garden that still contains the statues and pagodas he installed.

children.text: The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts is at Andrássy út 103, in the villa and garden that its founder left to the state. Ferenc Hopp, an optician and photographer who took over the Calderoni optical firm in 1864, was born in Fulnek in Moravia in 1833 and died in Budapest on 9 September 1919.

Hopp made five journeys around the world, with a focus on East Asia, especially China and Japan, and he lectured on his travels to the Hungarian Geographical Society. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914 and that his Japanese collection numbered nearly 2,000 items at his death. His collection also drew on Africa, America and Australia, but East Asian art was the standout.

In 1919 he left the villa, the garden and several thousand objects to the state. Sources give the number as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 items. His will required that the building be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum always bear his name. It opened in 1923, and its collection has grown through gifts, purchases and transfers from other museums, including the Zichy North Asian collections and the Indian collection of Imre Schwaiger.

The collection now covers China, Japan, India, Southeast Asia, Nepal, Tibet, Mongolia, Korea and the Middle East. Japanese medieval art and Chinese bronzes and porcelain are especially significant. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, while a 2021 article says about 30,000, so the figure depends on the source. After 1945 the museum also received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea.

The villa garden still holds the Asian statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp erected. The museum is part of the Budapest World Heritage site and is a specialist museum of the Museum of Fine Arts.
Good to know
The museum is on Andrássy út at number 103, a stretch of the avenue with several other museums and villas near the City Park end.
Temporary exhibitions focus on individual Asian countries and peoples; check the official site for what is on, plus opening times and tickets.
Allow a few minutes to walk around the garden, which is part of what Hopp left to the state.

docs.historyIntro: The museum exists because of one man's will. Ferenc Hopp, a Budapest optician who travelled widely in Asia, left his villa, garden and collection to the state in 1919 on condition that they become a museum bearing his name.

children.text: Ferenc Hopp was born in Fulnek in Moravia on 28 April 1833. Hungarian Wikipedia says he began as an optician's apprentice at the age of thirteen under István Calderoni, was sent to Vienna in 1853 and then to New York, returned in 1861 and took over the firm in 1864 while keeping its name. The firm made optical instruments and cameras and introduced the manufacture of school teaching aids to Hungary. Once he could afford to travel, he made five journeys around the world; sources date them slightly differently, but all place them between the early 1880s and the 1910s. East Asia, above all China and Japan, drew him most. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914, and his Japanese collection reached nearly 2,000 items by his death.

Hopp died in Budapest on 9 September 1919. In his will he left his villa and garden at Andrássy út 103 and his collection to the Hungarian state. Sources give the size of the collection as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 objects. He had first thought of dividing the collection among the Museum of Fine Arts, the Museum of Applied Arts and the Ethnographic Museum, but he decided instead on a single museum. His will required that the villa be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum should always carry his name. It also required that other state-owned Eastern collections be added to his own.

The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts opened in 1923, and Zoltán Felvinczi Takács, who described Hopp in 1914, became its first director. Objects were transferred from the Museum of Applied Arts, the Museum of Fine Arts, the Ethnographic Museum and the Hungarian National Museum, and private collections such as Vince Wartha's, Jenő Zichy's North Asian material and Imre Schwaiger's Indian collection were added. After 1945 the museum received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, and a 2021 article gives about 30,000. The villa garden still holds the statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp put there.

docs.name: BudaTower – Mary Magdalene Tower
docs.description: The Mary Magdalene Tower is the surviving part of a Gothic parish church on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District. The church was used by Hungarians in medieval Buda, became a mosque under the Ottomans, and was demolished after the 1945 siege. The tower reopened to visitors in July 2025 under district council management, so check its current status.

children.text: The Mary Magdalene Tower stands on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District, close to Matthias Church. It is all that remains of the Church of Mary Magdalene, one of two large churches of medieval Castle Hill. The Matthias Church served the German community, while the Magdalene church was the parish church of Buda's Hungarians.

The Castle District heritage site says the parish was formed in the mid-thirteenth century as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church, with a small single-nave first church. By the end of the fifteenth century the late Gothic church had six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower, built by the town's Hungarian community. During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants, until the Fifteen Years War, when it became a mosque.

After the siege of 1686 only the tower remained usable. The Franciscans cleared the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, and the tower was repaired in Baroque style. Francis I was crowned Hungarian king in the church in 1792, in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison, and in 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.

The siege of 1944 and 1945 brought down the vaults of the nave and sanctuary. Repairs began but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, at the same time as the church building was demolished. A porch built for the coronation of Francis I survives, as does a late Gothic gate leading to a star-vaulted lower storey.

The former churchyard is now an archaeological park, sealed off by a glass wall, and the site of the church is a garden of ruins with a reconstructed sanctuary window. A news report says the tower opened to tourists in 2017, that the district council withdrew the previous operator's concession in early 2025 and the tower closed in February 2025, and that it reopened on 15 July 2025 under the council's own management. Its present status should be checked.
Good to know

The tower closed in February 2025 and, according to a July 2025 news report, reopened on 15 July 2025 under the first district council. Check the official site or the district's pages for its current status before you plan around a climb.
One visitor guide mentions buses 16, 16A and 116 and the Castle District funicular as ways to reach the area.
Even when the tower itself is closed, the ruins garden and the surrounding square are close to Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.

docs.historyIntro: The tower is the only part of the Church of Mary Magdalene still standing. The church served Buda's Hungarian community for centuries, passed through Ottoman, Franciscan and military hands, and was demolished after damage in the siege of 1944 to 1945.

historySections.heading: A parish church for the Hungarians of Buda

children.text: According to the Castle District heritage site, the parish was formed in the middle of the thirteenth century, soon after the town's founding, as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church. Excavations show that the first church was small, with a single nave. By the end of the fifteenth century a late Gothic church had been completed with six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower on its western front, built by the town's Hungarian community. A news article gives 1247 and King Béla IV as the origin, so the sources differ on the earliest date. Both agree that the church was the Hungarian counterpart of the Matthias Church, which served the German population.

historySections.heading: Ottoman rule, Franciscans and the garrison

children.text: During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants. In the Fifteen Years War, from 1591 to 1606, the Christians lost the building and it became a Muslim place of worship. The siege of 1686 left the church badly damaged, and only the tower could still be used. The Franciscans then removed the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, repairing the medieval tower in Baroque style. Joseph II closed the monastery. In 1792 Francis I was crowned king of Hungary in the church, and in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison. In the late nineteenth century, while the Matthias Church was being rebuilt, the parish moved here. In 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.

historySections.heading: Destruction in 1945 and the surviving tower

children.text: In the siege of 1944 and 1945 the vaults of the nave and sanctuary collapsed. Repairs began straight after the fighting, but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, and the church building was demolished at the same time. The former churchyard is now an archaeological park behind a glass wall, and the site of the nave is a garden of ruins. The tower was reported to have opened to tourists in 2017. A news article from March 2025 says the district council took back the operator's concession and closed the tower while it developed a new concept, so the tower's present status should be checked.

docs.name: Museum of Illusions
docs.description: A compact walk-through attraction near Deák Square where visitors step into tilted rooms, a swirling Vortex Tunnel and forced-perspective set-ups. It belongs to a franchise that began in Zagreb in 2015, and 2026 reports describe a closure and renovation, so confirm its current status first.

children.text: The Museum of Illusions in Budapest is a compact exhibition space at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út 3, a short distance from Deák Ferenc tér. Rather than displaying objects behind glass, it asks visitors to step inside optical puzzles and see how easily the brain can be misled. One city guide groups the exhibits into illusion rooms, installations and flat images.

Rooms named by that guide include the Tilted Room, the Vortex Tunnel, the Reversed Room, the Ames Room and the Infinity Room. Among the installations it lists the Beuchet Chair and an oversized-chair set-up that plays with forced perspective, an anti-gravity corner, a Clone Table, a True Mirror, holographic displays and puzzle tables. The flat illusions include Rubin's Vase. The Vortex Tunnel, a walk-through installation that plays with balance and perception, is the exhibit most reports single out. Taking photographs in the set-ups is a large part of the experience, and a report from the opening period noted that some attractions require flat-soled shoes.

The Budapest museum is one branch of a franchise. According to Wikipedia, founders Tomislav Pamuković and Roko Živković opened the first Museum of Illusions in Zagreb, Croatia, in 2015, and franchising began in 2016 with museums in Zadar and Ljubljana. The Budapest branch was reported as newly opened in December 2021.

Reports about its current state differ. A short news item dated 28 July 2026 said the museum would close in its current form on 24 August 2026 and return later in a brand-new, more modern version, without giving a reopening date. A visitor guide with an update date of 20 October 2026 describes the museum as reopened after a renovation. Because the sources do not agree on a clear timeline, treat the exhibit list above as what has been documented and confirm what is on show before building a day around it.
Good to know
Check the official site for the current status, opening times and tickets, because 2026 reports describe a closure followed by a renovated version.
The museum is close to Deák Ferenc tér, so it is easy to combine with a walk through central Pest.
An opening-period report advised wearing flat-soled shoes, since some attractions require them.

docs.historyIntro: The Budapest Museum of Illusions is a branch of a franchise that began in Croatia in 2015. The Budapest venue near Deák Square was reported as newly opened in December 2021, and 2026 reports describe a closure and a renovated version.

historySections.heading: A Croatian idea becomes a franchise

children.text: According to Wikipedia, the Museum of Illusions was founded by Tomislav Pamuković and Roko Živković. The founders say the idea came from contemplating how to escape the corporate environment, and the article says it was inspired by the National Geographic show Brain Games. The first museum opened in 2015 in Zagreb, Croatia, after two years between idea and realisation. Franchising began in 2016 with museums in Zadar, Croatia, and Ljubljana, Slovenia. As of May 2023, the franchise had 43 museums in 25 countries, according to the same article.

A We Love Budapest article published on 9 December 2021 described the Budapest museum as newly opened, at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út 3, near Deák tér in downtown Budapest. It reported optical illusion rooms that make visitors look huge or tiny, or appear upside down, and a main attraction in the form of a tunnel that creates the impression the whole world is moving. The same report said the franchise had operations in Zadar and Zagreb and, in the writer's words, more than 50 major cities, and noted that the article may contain outdated information.

historySections.heading: Reports of a closure and a renovated museum

children.text: A Budappest news item dated 28 July 2026 said the museum would close in its current form on 24 August 2026 and return later in a brand-new, more modern version, giving no reopening date and no reason. A Hungary Unlocked guide with an update date of 20 October 2026 describes the museum as reopened after a renovation. The two sources do not give a shared timeline, so the current status should be confirmed on the museum's official channels.

docs.name: Fradi Museum
docs.description: The club museum of Ferencvárosi TC, housed in the club's stadium in Budapest's ninth district. Exhibits include a reconstructed dressing room and wooden stand, shirts, trophies and Flórián Albert's Ballon d'Or, and a visit can be paired with a tour of the arena itself.

children.text: The Fradi Museum is the museum of Ferencvárosi Torna Club, the football club known as Fradi, and it sits inside the club's arena in Budapest's ninth district. The club was founded on 3 May 1899 by Ferenc Springer and a group of residents of the Ferencváros district. Its green and white colours and the nine-stripe badge point back to that district, and the nickname Fradi comes from Franzstadt, the German name for the area.

A visitor review describes the route through the museum. It begins with a timeline of milestones that covers football but also the club's other sports and their Olympic and world championship successes. A reconstructed dressing room holds shirts and boots from different decades, and the review notes that early teams wore pyjama-like kits and played on a field on Soroksári Road. A 1950s room features a 1956 radio recording announcing the club's re-founding after the communist regime had renamed it, changed its colours and taken its best players. Another room has a reconstructed wooden stand from the old Üllői út ground, where archive match footage can be watched.

The trophy rooms centre on the 1965 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, won by beating Juventus 1-0 in Turin. Wikipedia also notes the 1937 Mitropa Cup among the displays. The review mentions shirts and coaching diaries of former players and managers, Imre Schlosser's contract, and Tibor Nyilasi's Silver Boot. The last room, which the review calls a sanctuary, holds Flórián Albert's Ballon d'Or, which Wikipedia dates to 1967.

The museum belongs to the stadium that opened in 2014. The new arena was built in 2013 and 2014 on the site of the older Albert Flórián stadium and was designed by Ágnes Streit and Szabolcs Kormos. Its first match, on 10 August 2014, was against Chelsea. Sources differ on the museum's date: Wikipedia says it opened on 7 August 2014, while a 2015 review says it received official museum status in 2015 when it moved into the arena. The club's page says a museum entry also admits visitors to a stadium tour that takes in the home dressing room and the pitch-side benches, and that the combined visit takes about 50 minutes.
Good to know
Check the official Fradi site for current opening times, tickets and the stadium tour, because match days can change what is available.
The arena is in the ninth district near Népliget, and Wikipedia gives the metro line 3 station at Népliget as about a two-minute walk away.
A review says experienced supporters guide some tours and that an app offers an audio guide in several languages, but confirm this is still offered.

docs.historyIntro: The Fradi Museum tells the story of Ferencvárosi Torna Club, founded in 1899 in Budapest's ninth district. It now sits inside the club's arena, which replaced the older Albert Flórián stadium in 2014.

children.text: Wikipedia says Ferencvárosi Torna Club was founded on 3 May 1899 by Ferenc Springer and a group of residents of Budapest's ninth district, Ferencváros. The club's colours are green and white, and the nine stripes on the badge, five green and four white, represent the district. The nickname Fradi comes from Franzstadt, the German name for the area. The club's earlier home was the Üllői út stadium, where it had played since 1911; it was later known as Stadion Albert Flórián and was demolished in 2013.

historySections.heading: Re-founding, European finals and the Fairs Cup

children.text: A review of the museum says its 1950s room features a 1956 radio recording announcing the club's re-founding, after the communist regime had renamed the club, changed its colours and recruited its best players. Wikipedia records the club's 1964-65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup win, in which it beat Juventus 1-0 in Turin in the final. It lost the 1968 Fairs Cup final to Leeds United and the 1975 European Cup Winners' Cup final to Dynamo Kyiv. In 1995-96 it was the first Hungarian club to qualify for the renewed Champions League.

historySections.heading: A new arena and a museum of its own

children.text: Wikipedia says the old stadium was demolished in 2013 and the new one was built on its site, with construction in 2013 and 2014. It was designed by Ágnes Streit and Szabolcs Kormos and opened on 10 August 2014 with a match against Chelsea. The Fradi Museum is inside the stadium. Wikipedia says it opened on 7 August 2014, while a 2015 review says it existed for decades but received official museum status in 2015 when it moved into the new arena. Sources therefore differ on the exact year.

docs.name: Lukács Thermal Bath
docs.description: A thermal bath in Buda's Felhévíz district whose springs have been used for centuries. Wikipedia traces bathing on the site to at least the 12th century, and the present complex developed from the 1880s onward. Over time it became a favourite of Hungarian writers, composers and filmmakers, and it still has a medical side.

children.text: The Lukács Bath (Szent Lukács gyógyfürdő) lies on the Buda side in the 2nd district, in an area the Middle Ages called Felhévíz, a name that refers to its thermal springs. Wikipedia says thermal baths have been used on the site since at least the 12th century, by the Knights Hospitaller. During the Ottoman period the spring water powered a mill, and a wall inside the bath is described as a remnant of the Ottoman Császár powder mill.

The present bath grew from development that began in the mid-1880s. A Hungarian cultural article says Palotay bought the area from the treasury in 1884 and named it Szent Lukács, Saint Luke, after which the bath became a public limited company in 1893, with a mud bath, spa hotel and public steam bath. Rezső Ray the elder designed the hotel, and Rezső Hikisch unified the facade in a Classicist-Biedermeier style in the 1920s. A drinking-cure hall was built in 1937, during the First International Congress of Bathing.

Lukács was well known across the Monarchy and Europe, and until the Széchenyi and Gellért baths were completed it was Budapest's most significant thermal bath. Budappest, a travel site, names the composer Zoltán Kodály as a regular guest and the writers Gyula Illyés and Tibor Déry and the filmmakers Károly Makk and Péter Bacsó as notable patrons. In the courtyard and walls are gratitude plaques left by visitors who felt healed. Many were lost in the Second World War, and the surviving ones were built into the walls during renovation.

After the war a hospital moved into the former hotel, and the rheumatology institute based there from 1951 has since been reorganised, while Lukács still combines medical treatment with bathing. Wikipedia lists thermal pools of different temperatures, swimming pools, a wellness section, sauna facilities and a gallery. A restoration completed in 2013 is reported to have received an ICOMOS award. Across Frankel Leó út is the Malom Lake area, where a building known as the Turkish bath was never Turkish at all, but a people's steam bath built by Palotay.
Good to know

The bath's official site lists trams 4, 6, 17 and 19, buses 9 and 109 and the HÉV suburban railway (Margit híd stop) as ways to reach it; check BKK's journey planner for the best route to Frankel Leó út 25-29.
Facilities, sauna rules and which pools are available differ by section, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules.
Look for the gratitude plaques in the walls and the drinking-cure hall from 1937.

docs.historyIntro: The Lukács Baths sit on springs that have been used for bathing for centuries, and the complex still carries traces of its Ottoman past inside its walls.

children.text: According to the bath's own history, thermal baths have been used on this site since at least the twelfth century, reportedly by the Knights Hospitallers. A wall inside the complex is a remnant of a former Ottoman powder mill, the Császár mill, which used the hot spring water as a source of power. The neighbouring Császár Thermal Bath is described as the oldest continuously operating thermal bath in Budapest: it was originally built by Szokoli Mustafa and redesigned in 1844 by József Hild.

The first spa hotel on the site was completed in the 1880s and named after Saint Luke. A drinking-water hall followed in 1937 and a health clinic in 1979. The water is rich in calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates and contains a substantial amount of fluoride. Part of the complex belongs to the National Institute of Rheumatology and Physiotherapy. Much of this history rests on the bath's own account, so treat individual dates as the operator's, not as independently verified.

docs.name: Rudas Thermal Bath
docs.description: A Buda bath beside Erzsébet Bridge whose Ottoman core, an octagonal pool under a dome on eight columns, dates from the 16th century. Later wings add a swimming pool and a modern wellness area. Its gender-separated apron bathing was added to Hungary's national intangible heritage list in October 2026.

children.text: The Rudas Baths stand at Döbrentei tér 9 on the Buda bank, at the foot of Gellért Hill beside Erzsébet Bridge. Wikipedia describes it as founded in 1571 or 1572 under Ottoman rule, when Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, the governor of Buda, commissioned it. Other sources give a work period of 1566 to 1572 for converting the earlier building, so the exact dates vary by source. A guide from We Love Budapest adds that Hospitaller knights had built a hospital and a bath on the site under King Béla IV.

The Ottoman core is the main thing to see. An octagonal pool lies under a hemispherical dome supported by eight columns, with small windows letting in light. A 2012 article gives the dome a diameter of about ten metres. The Ottoman-period name, Jesil Direkli ilidzsa, is translated as green-columned bath, though We Love Budapest notes that archaeologists have never found the green column, and offers one theory that the later name Rudas comes from a Serbian and Bosnian shortening meaning mineral-water bath.

The complex grew in stages. Xpatloop reports that the swimming pool was built in 1896 and that from 1936 the thermal bath was visited exclusively by men. A 19th-century classicist wing houses an indoor pool, and the Juventus wing, on the site of a former mineral-water bottling plant, opened in 2014 as a modern wellness area with a facade of girih patterns. Wikipedia notes a comprehensive interior renovation that ended with a reopening at the beginning of 2006.

Rudas also carries a social tradition. A Time Out report dated 20 October 2026 says that the gender-separated bathing in cotton aprons was added to the National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage, and that the listing protects the practice, not the building. Visitors should check the official site for which days are single-sex and which are mixed, because those arrangements have changed over time. Wikipedia also records that the opening scene of the 1988 film Red Heat was filmed here.
Good to know
The bath's official site lists trams 19, 41, 56 and 56A and several bus lines as ways to reach Döbrentei tér; check BKK's journey planner for the best route.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the schedule of men's, women's and mixed days, which have changed over time.
The baths stand at the foot of Gellért Hill, so the hill is close by for a walk before or after your visit.

docs.historyIntro: The Rudas Baths are one of the few places in Budapest where you can still bathe in an Ottoman hammam: an octagonal pool under a dome, beside the Danube, that is more than four hundred years old.

historySections.heading: An Ottoman bath on the Danube

children.text: The baths were founded in 1571 or 1572 during Ottoman rule, commissioned by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, who was governor (beylerbey) of Buda from 1566 to 1578. They keep many elements of a hammam, including an Ottoman dome and an octagonal pool, and are described as echoing the monumental Ottoman bath buildings of Istanbul. They stand at Döbrentei tér, on the Buda side of Erzsébet Bridge, at the foot of Gellért Hill.

historySections.heading: Thermal water and a new opening

children.text: The thermal water is slightly radioactive and contains sulphate, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate and a significant amount of fluoride. The complex has six therapy pools and one swimming pool, with temperatures between 10 and 42 degrees Celsius. After a comprehensive interior renovation the baths reopened at the beginning of 2006.

docs.name: Palatinus Bath
docs.description: Budapest's first outdoor beach on Margaret Island, opened in 1919 and expanded in the 1930s with a modernist changing building and a wave pool. Its thermal-well water, historic mosaics and year-round indoor wellness section, added in a 2017 reconstruction, make it one of the city's most layered bathing complexes.

children.text: The Palatinus Strandfürdő is a bathing complex on Margaret Island, fed by the island's thermal wells. According to We Love Budapest it opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, and Hungarian Wikipedia places the first opening in the era of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, before the Danube embankment had walls. It closed after a year for construction, and the new bath opened permanently in August 1921 with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools.

The best-known building was added in 1937, when the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed a modernist reception and changing block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with a wave pool. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the architectural style as Bauhaus, and the Budapest Info page for the bath carries the same label in its title. We Love Budapest records that the plan caused public debate and that the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma.

Art and sculpture have always been part of the site. At the entrance stood a sculpture by Géza Csorba and, in the ticket hall, a wall painting by István Pekáry referring to an Ady poem, both damaged or destroyed in the war. The painting was restored in the 2017 reconstruction, and Csorba's work was recarved in the 1960s. The wave pool carries a surrealist mosaic by Endre Bálint, whose style is compared to Miró's. Before the Second World War, the bath's continuous water surface made it Europe's largest outdoor bath, according to We Love Budapest.

The reconstruction of 2016-17, carried out by Archikon, winterised the building and added indoor thermal pools, a sauna section and therapy rooms, so the complex now runs outdoor and indoor sections that are not necessarily available at the same times. A 2025 news report states that the indoor section stays open year-round while the outdoor pools work only in the warm season. The wave machine, a piston-driven one, was renovated in 2026, and only a few such machines remain in Hungary, with Budapest having two, at Palatinus and Gellért.
Good to know
Outdoor pools and slides are seasonal, while the indoor wellness and thermal section is described as available through the year, so check which parts are running on your date.
Look for the mosaic by Endre Bálint at the wave pool and the Pekáry wall painting in the ticket hall.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and house rules before travelling to Margaret Island.

docs.historyIntro: Palatinus opened in 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach and grew into one of the largest open-air baths in Europe. A 1937 expansion, postwar changes and a 2017 reconstruction shaped what visitors see today.

children.text: We Love Budapest records that the bath opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, with water from the island's thermal wells, which 19th-century drilling by Vilmos Zsigmondy had made possible. Károly Arvé and Márton Nagy designed the first beach, which had no reception building yet. Hungarian Wikipedia says it closed after a year so that construction could begin and that the new bath opened permanently in August 1921, with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools. Before the Second World War its continuous water surface of about five thousand square metres made it the largest outdoor bath in Europe, according to We Love Budapest.

In 1937 the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed the central changing building, a modernist block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with the wave pool. The plan was debated in public, and the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma against critics who wanted the park setting left intact. Wave pools were then still new in Budapest: We Love Budapest notes that the first in the city was at Csillaghegy in 1927 and that Palatinus was the third. The war later destroyed sculpture and a wall painting at the entrance.

After the war the bath was restored. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a ten-thousand-square-metre sunbathing lawn added in 1958, a new restaurant in 1965, an additional area with playgrounds and a football pitch in 1975, and a five-lane slide in the 1980s. A mosaic by Endre Bálint was added at the wave pool in the 1960s. In 2002 the pools received modern filtration, and in 2016-17 the monument-protected reconstruction by Archikon winterised the main building and added a covered section with thermal and wellness facilities, so the bath could work throughout the year. The destroyed Ady-poem wall painting was restored at the same time.

docs.name: Veli Bej Bath
docs.description: A small Ottoman bath of the 1570s, set inside the grounds of a hospital in Buda's 2nd district. A central dome sits over an octagonal pool, the Hospitaller order restored it in the early 2010s, and archaeological finds from the work are on display. It is among the few Ottoman baths in Budapest still in use.

children.text: The Veli Bej Bath is a historic Ottoman thermal bath in Budapest's 2nd district, in the Felhévíz area below Rózsadomb. According to Budapest by Locals it was built in 1574-75 by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, a builder and year the Hospitaller order's own history page also gives, while another Hungarian local-history page says it was completed between 1570 and 1572. Budapest by Locals adds that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The same source calls it the oldest and most beautiful Ottoman bath in Budapest, a superlative that sits uneasily with the Rudas Bath, which Wikipedia dates to 1571 or 1572. A commemorative plaque from its construction is said to remain on a wall.

The building has been changed more than once. In 1806 István Marczibányi handed the bath to the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order that runs the neighbouring hospital; the order's own history page speaks of a gift, while another local-history page says he bought it and passed on the right to run it. A reconstruction led by József Hild in the early 1840s enlarged it and renamed it Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő; the Hospitaller order's history page says only early 1840s, while other sources give 1841-44, 1841-45, 1841-48 or 1842. In the 1970s a modern hospital wing was built around the small bath, which is why it is hard to see from the street.

The order later restored the bath with the help of archaeologists and art historians. Sources give 2011 as the completion of the work, while an article from 2018 says it reopened in 2012. Four smaller domed buildings surround a central cupola, and the main pool is octagonal under a traditional Ottoman dome, with four smaller pools around it. Original Ottoman clay pipes found during the work were preserved and can be seen between the pools and the saunas, and a small display holds finds from the excavation.

Modern wellness areas, including saunas and a jacuzzi, were added to the historic core. The bath is run with the hospital, and the sources say admission is regulated, including a limited capacity and an age limit, so check directly before travelling. Its address is Árpád fejedelem útja 7, close to the Margaret Bridge's Buda end, and it sits in the same area as the Lukács and Császár-Komjádi baths.
Good to know
Budapest by Locals gives trams 4 or 6 to Margit híd Budai hídfő, or trams 17, 19 and 41 to Komjádi Béla utca, as ways to get there.
Admission is regulated, including capacity and age limits, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules before going.
Look for the preserved Ottoman clay pipes and the small display of archaeological finds.

docs.historyIntro: The Veli Bej Bath is an Ottoman bath of the 1570s that survived the end of Ottoman rule, passed to a Hospitaller order and was restored in the early 2010s. It now sits inside a hospital complex.

children.text: Budapest by Locals states that the oldest part of the Császár spa, the Turkish bath, was built by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha in 1574-75, and that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The Hospitaller order's own history page gives the same builder and the deciphered year 1574-75, while another Hungarian local-history page dates the work to 1570-1572. The page notes that Buda had roughly seven to nine baths during the 150 years of Ottoman rule and that several of the smaller ones did not survive. Another article reports that a commemorative plaque from the building of the bath remains on a wall.

In 1806 István Marczibányi handed the bath complex to the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order, which expanded the original Ottoman buildings. A reconstruction led by József Hild in the early 1840s enlarged the complex considerably and renamed it Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő; sources date it variously between 1841 and 1848. A 2018 article dates the Hild reconstruction to 1842 and describes the result as classicist. That article adds that in the 1970s the neighbouring hospital was extended with a modern wing that now encloses the small bath, which makes it hard to see from outside.

The Hospitaller order decided to restore the complex fully and to rebuild the original Ottoman bath, working with archaeologists and art historians. Budapest by Locals says the renovation was finished in 2011, while an article published in 2018 says the bath reopened in 2012, so the sources differ by a year. Original clay pipes laid by the Ottomans were found during the work, and archaeologists had them preserved so that they can be seen between the pools and the saunas. A small display of finds, including floor coverings, dishes and grindstones, was also assembled.

docs.name: Aquaworld Resort Budapest
docs.description: A large indoor water park and hotel complex in northern Budapest that opened in December 2008 under a Ramada name. A glass dome 73 metres wide covers the leisure area, which has eleven slides, a wave pool and a surf pool. Check its current name and operator before travelling.

children.text: Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a water park and hotel resort in northern Budapest, built around a leisure area under a glass dome. A trade news item from the waterpark supplier Polin says the complex opened in December 2008 as the Ramada Resort - Aquaworld Budapest and calls it Central Europe's largest indoor water theme park. The dome is described as 73 metres wide and 21 metres high.

The same report says the complex included a 261-room hotel and a separate building with 48 apartments. The water park's attractions include a wave pool, a surf pool, a 180-metre mountain river and eleven water slides that together are almost one kilometre long. Six giant slides start from a slide tower next to the dome, reached by a glass lift or stairs, and the highest rides begin from 17 metres up, and a conveyor-type lift returns the tubes to the start. A children's wing has pools of different depths, slides and a playhouse.

A later travel guide describes the resort as one of Europe's largest indoor water theme parks, with a four-star superior hotel, an Oriental Spa and a separate Sauna World. It notes that some outdoor pools are seasonal. The guides disagree on the number of pools: the opening report counts 21, while the later guide gives 17 in one place and 15 in another, so treat any single figure with caution.

The resort lies far from the city centre. The travel guide says public transport is possible but can be tricky, naming buses 30 and 230 from Keleti Railway Station or Heroes' Square, and also mentions a shuttle from Heroes' Square. Because names, operators and arrangements can change, check the official site for the current operating details.
Good to know

Slides have height and equipment rules, and some areas such as Sauna World are sold separately, so read the official rules before booking.

docs.name: Lupa Beach
docs.description: A sandy beach resort on Lupa Lake, a former quarry in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. It was developed by Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai, who opened it in 2016. The lakeside setting includes watersports and play areas and is seasonal.

children.text: Lupa Beach lies on Lake Lupa, in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. Just Budapest describes the lake as a former quarry transformed into a recreational site, and XpatLoop, writing in 2016, called it a former quarry on the city's northern outskirts where swimming had previously been banned. It is a seasonal destination, so check when it is operating before planning a trip.

The developer was Károly Gerendai, founder of the Sziget Festival. XpatLoop reported that the resort was due to open officially on the evening of 14 July 2016, and that Gerendai described that first summer as a test period to gain experience for the next year. He is reported to have signed a 20-year lease with an option to buy, and as at Sziget the catering and other services were contracted out.

In 2017 the beach was reopened on a larger scale. We Love Budapest reported that the swimmable shoreline had been quadrupled, making the beach about 2.5 kilometres long, and Just Budapest credits Gerendai with the 2017 development. The facilities listed by Just Budapest include a wakeboard centre, kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding, diving, beach volleyball, football, a street-workout park, a children's pool, playgrounds, an inflatable water park and a promenade of food stalls, with accessible pathways.

To get there, Just Budapest suggests the HÉV suburban railway from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász, followed by a walk of about twenty minutes, and says an electric minibus runs from the station to the beach. We Love Budapest names the Budakalász-Lenfonó stop and a summer beach bus. Driving is possible via road 11 toward Szentendre.
Good to know
Take the HÉV from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász and walk about twenty minutes, or look for the shuttle that Just Budapest says serves the beach.
Lupa Beach is seasonal and outside central Budapest, so check the official site for operating dates, opening times and tickets.
Sources name different HÉV stops (Budakalász and Budakalász-Lenfonó), so confirm your stop before travelling.

docs.name: Római Open-Air Bath
docs.description: A summer-season open-air bath in Óbuda's Rómaifürdő district, on ground that once belonged to Roman Aquincum. The present layout dates from 1964 and was modernised around 2000, with a swimming pool, an adventure pool and several slides. The nearby Danube riverbank is a separate, newer public beach.

children.text: The Római Strandfürdő is an open-air bath at Rozgonyi Piroska utca 2 in Óbuda, in Budapest's 3rd district. It is a seasonal summer bath. The BKK listing for the bath describes a large green area in the former Aquincum territory, with a children's pool, a swimming pool and an adventure pool, and the operator's own site is named there for current information.

The bath's name and setting come from the area's past. The BKK listing says the Romans already regarded the local springs as sacred and that chronicles from the time of King Matthias mention a hospital here. These are statements from a listing page, not a full history, so they are best read as local tradition. Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part adds that the neighbourhood of Rómaifürdő sits beside springs where mills once operated in the early 19th century.

The layout seen today dates from a renovation. Programturizmus says the renewed bath opened in 1964 and has kept its layout since, and that in 2000 the three pools were modernised with filtered circulation. The main pool became an adventure pool with a slide, neck showers and bubble jets, and the children's pool became a playground. The slides described include a rafting slide, a steep straight slide, a combined fast-and-winding slide and a family slide that several people can use together.

Do not confuse the bath with the Danube riverbank. According to Telex, a free public Danube beach at Római-part opened in 2021, the first legal one since 1973, but swimming was not allowed there at the time and only wading was; check the posted rules for the current season. Hungarian Wikipedia says the riverside area was once dominated by boathouses and company holiday resorts. The H5 HÉV line has a stop at Rómaifürdő, the closest rail link named in the sources, though they do not give the walking route.
Good to know
The H5 Szentendre HÉV stops at Rómaifürdő and Aquincum, according to Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part; check the walking route before you go.
The bath is seasonal, so check the operator's site for current dates, opening times and tickets.
The Danube riverside beach at Római-part is a separate, seasonal site run by the Óbuda district with its own rules on bathing, so check the notices on site before going in.

docs.name: Millenáris Park
docs.description: A park of nearly six hectares in Buda's 2nd district, built around the former Ganz electrical works. Preserved factory halls now serve as event spaces and the National Dance Theatre, while the newer Széllkapu Park adds walkways, solar-topped pavilions and a suspended garden that, according to the official site, looks towards Margit körút and the Castle District.

children.text: Millenáris sits on the site of the Ganz electrical works in Buda's 2nd district. Ábrahám Ganz founded the Ganz foundry in Buda in 1844, and after his death András Mechwart developed the firm and set up its electricity department in 1878. The Lövőház Street building, completed in 1897, employed over 2,000 people, and a large assembly line was built in 1911 and 1912. The firm declined in the later 20th century, and from 2000 it operated as Ganz Transelektro.

The park was created from the former central factory. Demolition of two high-rise buildings began on 12 August 2000, and the park opened in 2001. Two of the old halls, the Great Hall (Building B) and Building D, were kept; together with a new entrance building and an underground car park they form one of the country's largest exhibition halls. Machinery from the old works is still on display. In 2002 the design received the Europa Nostra Award for the way it revived the historic factory halls.

Millenáris has hosted well-known exhibitions, among them Dreamers of Dreams in 2001 and 2002, House of the Future from 2005 to 2007 and the Palace of Wonders series, which ran on the site from 2005 to 2012. The former factory assembly hall, Building E, is now the National Dance Theatre, designed by ZDA - Zoboki Építésziroda, with two theatre halls, a chamber hall and rehearsal rooms.

Széllkapu Park is the newer part. Its walkways lead to three mushroom-shaped buildings topped with solar panels that generate energy and provide shade, and a suspended garden, reached by a panoramic lift, offers views towards Margit körút, the Castle District and the Buda Hills, according to the official Millenáris site. The official site describes the area as barrier-free; pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals. The address is Kis Rókus utca 16-20.
Good to know
Millenáris is on Kis Rókus utca, close to Margit körút, so it combines easily with the Buda side of the Danube.
Check the official Millenáris site for current opening times, events and tickets, because hours differ between the park areas and the venues.
Pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals, according to the official site.

docs.historyIntro: Millenáris occupies the site of the Ganz electrical works in Buda, one of Hungary's best-known industrial firms. After the factory declined, its central works were converted into a park and cultural centre that opened in 2001.

children.text: Ábrahám Ganz founded an iron foundry in Buda in 1844, on the site where the Foundry Museum stands today. After his death András Mechwart developed the firm and set up its electricity department in 1878. The works moved first to Kacsa Street and then to the former Király-malom main street building, and the Lövőház Street building, completed in 1897, employed over 2,000 people. In 1906 the electrical business became independent as Ganz Electricity Co., and a large assembly line was built in 1911 and 1912.

The company suffered from international competition after 1929 but led domestic electrification from the 1920s, until the Second World War cut its renewed success short. After the war it became independent again in 1949 as Ganz Electricity Factory, renamed Ganz Electricity Works in 1963. The firm then declined, and a 1991 joint venture with foreign capital, Ganz Ansaldo, did not stop production from falling. The Budapest factory was relocated to the countryside, and from 2000 the firm operated as Ganz Transelektro.

The Millenáris Foundation was established in 1996, and the former industrial site at Lövőház Street was turned into a cultural and educational centre linked to the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian state. Demolition of two high-rise buildings began on 12 August 2000 and removed about 120,000 cubic metres of debris, including 2,500 to 3,000 tonnes of steel structures. Building B, the Great Hall, and Building D were kept, and the assembly hall, Building E, was preserved. The park opened in 2001, and in 2002 the design won the Europa Nostra Award for reviving the historic factory halls.

The site soon became known for large exhibitions: Dreamers of Dreams in 2001 and 2002, House of the Future from 2005 to 2007, and the Palace of Wonders series, which ran there from 2005 to 2012. Building E, the former assembly hall, is now the National Dance Theatre, designed by ZDA - Zoboki Építésziroda. The newer Széllkapu Park, with its solar-topped pavilions and suspended garden, later received awards from the Hungarian Urban Planning Association and in the landscape architecture category of the Hungarian Real Estate Development Excellence Awards.

docs.name: Kopaszi-gát
docs.description: A long Danube embankment in south Buda, created as a regulation dam between 1870 and 1876 to reduce ice floods. After decades of industry and landfill it was redeveloped from 2006 as a landscaped park with cafés, a playground and views across Lágymányos Bay towards the BudaPart quarter.

children.text: Kopaszi-gát takes its name from the Kopaszi sandbank that once lay in this stretch of the Danube; the name can be translated as the bare bank. Ice floes jammed against sandbars here in the 18th and 19th centuries and caused icy floods. After the Pest flood of 1838, a law in 1870 ordered river regulation and a parallel dam, and the long, sandy dam was completed in 1876. Because its southern end did not reach the bank, Lágymányos Bay formed.

The water behind the dam later divided into a bay and Lágymányos Lake. In May 1896 the Orfeum owner Károly Somossy opened Konstantinápoly Budapesten, a Turkish-style entertainment quarter, here; it lost its appeal quickly because of mosquitoes and closed about six months later. In the early 20th century parts of the lake were filled in while the Budapest University of Technology was built, and the rest was used for fish farming, boating and swimming; Alfréd Hajós often trained there. After the Second World War about 1.5 million cubic metres of soil and rubble filled nearly the whole lakebed and factories took over.

After industry closed following the political change, the area deteriorated until around 2000. From 2006 restaurants, bistros and cafés opened, a playground was built and the dam was redeveloped as a green leisure park; one visitor guide says that by 2007 the embankment had become a landscaped public park, with architecture using concrete, metal, wood and glass.

The surroundings keep changing. In 2015 the district sold the bay's embankment and undeveloped land, 57 hectares in all, and the area, now called BudaPart, was planned by the firm ADEPT, which won the 2016 planning competition. The MOL Campus tower, designed by Foster + Partners, is 143 metres tall and employees moved in during December 2022, giving south Buda a new point of orientation.
Good to know
One visitor guide suggests tram 1 to Rákóczi Bridge, then about a 10-minute walk to the entrance; check current routes before you travel.
The Budapest University of Technology and Economics and Rákóczi Bridge are close by, so the park fits a walk along the Danube in south Buda.
Restaurants and cafés have their own times, so check them individually before planning a meal.

docs.historyIntro: Kopaszi-gát began as an engineering response to the ice floods that struck Pest, and over almost 150 years it has been a regulation dam, a lakeshore, an industrial zone and finally a park.

historySections.heading: Ice floods and the regulation dam

children.text: Before the river was regulated, two sandbars, the Nyúlfutási-zátony and the Kopaszi-zátony, narrowed the Danube south of Pest, and ice floes jammed against them in the 18th and 19th centuries. The Kopaszi sandbank was named for its barren appearance. The Pest ice flood of 1838 killed 153 people, destroyed over 10,000 buildings and left at least 50,000 people homeless. The water engineer Pál Vásárhelyi proposed a solution, but Pest's city leaders thought its cost of nearly nine million forints too high and shelved it. In 1870 a law ordered river regulation and a parallel dam, and the long, sandy, treeless dam was completed in 1876.

Because the dam's southern end did not reach the bank, Lágymányos Bay formed. A railway bridge connecting Ferencváros and Kelenföld split the water: the southern half was planned as a winter harbour, and the northern part became Lágymányos Lake. Factories soon followed, making the area one of the capital's industrial centres. In the early 20th century parts of the lake were filled in during the construction of the Budapest University of Technology, and the remaining water was used for fish farming, boating and swimming, with clubs, restaurants, a water polo pitch and an open-air pool. After the Second World War about 1.5 million cubic metres of soil and rubble filled nearly the whole lakebed to support industrialisation, and the recreational area disappeared.

After the regime change local industry closed and the area deteriorated until around 2000. The Aranyhal restaurant, which had operated since the 1970s, closed in 2005. From 2006 restaurants, bistros and cafés opened, a playground was built and the dam was redeveloped as a green leisure park. In 2015 the district sold the bay's embankment and undeveloped land, 57 hectares in all, and the new quarter called BudaPart was planned by ADEPT, which won the planning competition in 2016. The 143-metre MOL Campus, designed by Foster + Partners, received its first employees in December 2022.

stories.title: Konstantinápoly Budapesten, 1896

children.text: In May 1896, the year of the Hungarian millennium celebrations, the Orfeum owner Károly Somossy launched Konstantinápoly Budapesten, a Turkish-style entertainment quarter on the Lágymányos shore. It was designed by Lipót Kellner and Kálmán Gerster.
Its appeal faded quickly because of mosquitoes, and it closed about six months after opening. Somossy went bankrupt.

docs.name: Zugliget Chairlift
docs.description: Hungary's first passenger ropeway, opened on 20 August 1970, carrying double chairs for 1,040 metres from Zugliget up János Hill, a rise of 262 metres. Its nickname Libegő, meaning floater, won a public naming contest, and the top station is a short walk from the Erzsébet lookout.

children.text: The Zugliget Chairlift, known as the Libegő, runs from Zugliget in Budapest's 12th district up János Hill, the highest peak in Budapest. BKK describes it as Hungary's first passenger ropeway and gives its opening as 20 August 1970. The track is 1,040 metres long with a height difference of 262 metres between the stations, and the ride takes 12 to 15 minutes depending on the source. BKK counts 102 double chairs.

The idea is older than the line. In 1933 the engineer István Hantos Jr. proposed a suspension railway from Zugliget to János Hill, but only preparatory work was done, and the plans were revived in the early 1940s before the Second World War halted construction. The 12th District Council decided to build the line in 1967, construction started on 24 March 1969, and it opened in 1970. The official name was Jánoshegyi Légpálya, János Hill Air Lane, but a public naming contest produced the nickname Libegő, which means floater.

At the top, the Erzsébet lookout tower is a few minutes' walk away; Visit Hungary calls it the highest spot in Budapest, and the surrounding hill is covered with forests, gardens and hiking trails. BKK notes that the upper station has a wheelchair-accessible lookout on the terrace of a former restaurant.

The chairlift also links with other Buda hills attractions. BKK says the upper station can be reached on foot from the János-hegy or Virágvölgy stops of the Children's Railway, and by bus 21 or 211 from Széll Kálmán tér to Normafa followed by a walk of 20 to 30 minutes.
Good to know
BKK gives the lower station as Zugligeti út 97, at the terminus of bus 291, which runs from Nyugati pályaudvar.
Passengers with severely limited mobility are not permitted to ride, and children under 10 may ride only with an accompanying adult.
Service can be suspended in severe storms and for maintenance on set dates, so check the BKK page for the current operating service and closure days before you go.
The Erzsébet lookout tower and the Children's Railway stops at János-hegy and Virágvölgy are nearby.

docs.historyIntro: The Zugliget chairlift took almost four decades to move from a proposal to a working line. When it opened in 1970 it was Hungary's first passenger ropeway.

children.text: In 1933 the engineer István Hantos Jr. proposed a suspension railway from Zugliget to János Hill, but only preparatory work was done. In the early 1940s the Metropolitan Tramways Company revived the plans, and the Second World War halted construction. In spring 1945 the idea of a whole rope-railway network resurfaced and an Óbuda to Hármashatárhegy line was planned, but it was not built. In 1967 the 12th District City Council decided to build the János Hill line, with UVATERV providing the professional work.

Construction started on 24 March 1969 under László Pataki, who became the first service manager, with the National Mining Machinery Manufacturer Company as main contractor. The steel pillars were made in Tatabánya, two buildings were demolished to clear the route and the hanging chairs were imported from Austria. BKK gives the opening date as 20 August 1970. The line is 1,040 metres long with a level difference of 262 metres, and BKV reports about 4.5 million passengers in its first ten years.

A new wire rope was installed in 1979. A 1985 action plan proposed an alpine-style catering building at the upper station that was never built, and a reconstruction took place in 1991, with the rope replaced by an Austrian-made one in 1992. A plan in 1997 and 1998 proposed restoring the former János Hill restaurant. BKV's account does not clearly explain how the 1979 rope and the 1991 reconstruction relate, so the sequence of work on the line should be taken from the operator's current information.

stories.title: How the Libegő got its name

children.text: Visit Hungary says the name János Hill Cableway was judged unappealing, so a naming contest followed. Suggestions included Hillicopter, János Hill Hummer, Space Bus and To-and-Fro. The winning name, Libegő, means floater. BKV likewise says the name was chosen in a public naming contest and that the official name is Jánoshegyi Légpálya, János Hill Air Lane.

docs.name: Children’s Railway
docs.description: A 760 mm narrow-gauge line of about 11 km through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy, opened in stages from 1948 to 1950. Children aged roughly 10 to 14 perform most station and train duties under adult supervision, a practice recognised by Guinness World Records in 2015.

children.text: The Children's Railway, in Hungarian Gyermekvasút, runs through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy. Wikipedia gives the length as 11.2 km (its history text says 11.7 km), the gauge as 760 mm, the maximum speed as 20 km/h and the journey time as about 40 to 45 minutes. The two termini are about 235 metres apart in elevation. It is single-track and not electrified.

Children aged 10 to 14 operate all posts except the train driver, under adult supervision. We Love Budapest describes the roles as ticket inspectors, brakemen, cashiers, announcers and platform attendants. In 2015 Guinness World Records recognised it as the longest railway on which commercial traffic services are run by children.

The railway was started in 1948. MÁV decided in 1947 to build a children's railway, and Wikipedia says construction began on 11 April 1948 and the first section, from Széchenyi-hegy to Előre, now Virágvölgy, opened on 31 July 1948. The line reached Szépjuhászné about a year later and Hűvösvölgy on 20 August 1950. It was originally called the Pioneer Railway, Úttörővasút, and it closed during the 1956 revolution without damage and reopened on 3 February 1957.

The stops make a useful route through the hills. Counting the termini, the line stops at Hűvösvölgy, Hárs-hegy, Szépjuhászné, János-hegy, Virágvölgy, Csillebérc, Normafa and Széchenyi-hegy. A 198-metre tunnel lies just before Hárs-hegy. The station building at Hűvösvölgy houses a Children's Railway Museum, and at Széchenyi-hegy you can change to the Cogwheel Railway. Several stops are near other Buda hills sights, including the chairlift at János-hegy and the Normafa meadow.
Good to know
Timetables and tickets are on the official site, gyermekvasut.hu, which We Love Budapest says has English pages; check it for current opening times and the season.
At Széchenyi-hegy you can transfer to the Cogwheel Railway, and the Zugliget chairlift is near the János-hegy and Virágvölgy stops.
Vadaspark is a timetabled stop for the Wildlife Park, but We Love Budapest says it is served only for groups that request it in advance.

It was originally called the Úttörővasút, the Pioneer Railway, a name tied to the communist-era youth organisation. Today its official designation is MÁV Zrt. Széchenyi-hegy Gyermekvasút, the Children's Railway.

docs.name: Normafa
docs.description: A meadow and plateau in the Buda hills, named after a beech tree struck by lightning in 1927, with a view over the city. It has been used for walking and winter sport for well over a century, and a phased renovation since the mid-2010s has added paths, a playground and visitor facilities.

children.text: Normafa is a recreation area in the Buda hills, in Svábhegy in Budapest's 12th district, and Wikipedia gives its summit as 477 metres. A long, narrow plateau connects Svábhegy and János Hill. The site is known for panoramic views, and the open meadow looks out over the capital.

The name comes from a beech tree. Older Swabian residents called it Viharbükk, the storm beech, and according to legend it sprouted when King Matthias was born, and some believe the king napped in its shade. The hegyvidek.hu page says that in 1840 the actress Róza Schodelné Klein sang an aria from Bellini's Norma under the tree because its appearance recalled a scene from the opera, and the name then spread to the meadow. Lightning felled the tree in 1927, and a plaque commemorating it was put up in 1967.

Svábhegy has attracted hikers since the 17th century. The cogwheel railway opened in 1874 and was extended to Széchenyi-hegy in 1890. Skiing is recorded from 1895, a toboggan run was built before the First World War, and two ski jumps, one small and one large, were built in the 1920s; both are now gone. The first electric ski lift opened on Kis-Normafa in 1971 and has also been demolished.

A multi-year improvement project began to renew the area. By November 2015 its first phase had repaved the main path to János Hill, added benches and rubbish bins and upgraded the playground on Anna Meadow. A February 2020 article described a further redevelopment with a new car park and visitor centre, and reported that kiosks selling strudel and snacks were set to move. Plans may have progressed since then, so treat current facilities as something to check locally.
Good to know
We Love Budapest says bus 21 from Széll Kálmán tér goes to the Normafa stop; BKK also names bus 21 or 211 for the walk to the Zugliget chairlift's upper station.
The Children's Railway has a Normafa stop, and the Zugliget chairlift's upper station is a 20 to 30 minute walk away through the forest.
The area is used for walking, running, cycling, sledging in winter and cross-country skiing; check the district's site for current conditions and facilities.
