docs.historyIntro: Normafa's story combines a famous tree, over a century of hiking and winter sport, and recent redevelopment. The name itself is tied to a beech that lightning felled in 1927.

children.text: Normafa is named after a beech tree on Svábhegy. Older Swabian residents called it Viharbükk, the storm beech. According to the hegyvidek.hu page, the actress Róza Schodelné Klein sang an aria from Bellini's Norma under the tree in 1840 because its appearance recalled a scene from the opera, and the name then spread to the surrounding meadow. A We Love Budapest article says the name was linked to Norma after 1840, and Wikipedia calls the tree allegedly a beech planted by King Matthias Corvinus. Lightning felled the tree in 1927 and a plaque commemorating it was erected in 1967.

Svábhegy has attracted hikers since the 17th century, first for its hunting grounds and then for the pilgrimage site at Zugliget. The cogwheel railway opened in 1874 and was extended to Széchenyi-hegy in 1890. Skiing is recorded from 1895, a toboggan run built before the First World War hosted sledding competitions, and car races were held on Svábhegy by 1920. Two ski jumps, one small and one large, were built in the 1920s and hosted domestic and international competitions. The district's page says the flourishing sporting life was halted by the Second World War but soon revived. The first electric ski lift opened on Kis-Normafa in 1971; it, like the jumps, has been demolished.

The Hotel Olimpia, opened in 1972 on the Normafa plateau, was later demolished, and the Eötvös Loránd Park now occupies its site. A multi-year improvement project by the local government completed its first phase by November 2015, including repaving the main path to János Hill and upgrading the playground on Anna Meadow. In February 2020 We Love Budapest reported that a new car park and visitor centre were planned, with the Eötvös Loránd Park on the site of the neglected Olympia Hotel under way. These reports are from different dates, so check what has been completed.

stories.title: The tree of King Matthias

children.text: According to local legend, the beech that gave Normafa its name sprouted when King Matthias was born, and some people believe the king once napped in its shade. Wikipedia words the tradition differently, as a beech allegedly planted by Matthias Corvinus in the 15th century.
These are traditions recounted on the sources named here, and no document is cited for either version.

docs.name: Bartók Béla Boulevard
docs.description: A long Buda road climbing gently from the Gellért area through Móricz Zsigmond körtér towards the Feneketlen-tó lake, now lined with cafés, galleries and bookshops. It has carried several names since the 1870s and has been called Bartók Béla út since 1945.

children.text: Bartók Béla út is a main road in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, it runs for about 2.96 kilometres between Szent Gellért tér and Vasút utca, crossing Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Kosztolányi Dezső tér on the way. It is one of the busiest radial roads of southern Buda. For visitors the interesting stretch is the one that rises gently from the Hotel Gellért area towards the Feneketlen-tó, the Bottomless Lake.

The street was not always named after the composer. The first section, from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér, was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920, and the outer section towards Kelenföld railway station was Átlós út from 1890 to 1920. In 1920 both were renamed Horthy Miklós út. The name Bartók Béla út dates from 1945. Building along the road followed the 1913 zoning plan, and it is lined mostly with residential blocks of three to five storeys.

Transport shaped the street early. A tram first ran along it in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér, and in 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway began running from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út. The tram depot at Kelenföld has operated since 1912. The same article notes that cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, and that the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016.

In recent years the road has been described as a success story. A We Love Budapest walk published in January 2022 calls it once neglected but now full of cafés, restaurants, galleries and boutiques. It mentions the Hadik café, an old literary café where Frigyes Karinthy, Dezső Kosztolányi and Tibor Déry met, and Pagony, described as Hungary's largest children's bookstore. It also lists small galleries including Godot Gallery, Zsófi Faur Gallery, Artphoto Gallery and Dokubrom, which shows archive photographs edited by the Fortepan team.

The walk in that article ends at the Feneketlen-tó, where it lists the Figaró Magic Shop, run by the Szabó family since 1969. By the lake's playground it also notes a statue of a teddy bear, Mackó, by the sculptor László Molnár, there since 1961. The Hungarian Wikipedia article adds that a programme called Bartók-negyed, started after the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Szent Gellért tér.
Good to know
Szent Gellért tér at the Danube end is the natural starting point; the We Love Budapest walk begins at Fővám tér on the Pest side and crosses Liberty Bridge.
The Feneketlen-tó park at the far end of the walk has tennis courts, a running track and an outdoor gym.
Cafés, shops and galleries change often, so check each venue's own page for current opening times before planning a stop.
Trams run along the street; check the BKK journey planner for current routes and service.

docs.historyIntro: Bartók Béla út grew from a Buda road that carried two different names before the First World War and was renamed twice more. Rail and tram lines reached it in the 1890s, long before the cafés and galleries of today.

historySections.heading: Fehérvári út and Átlós út, 1874 to 1920

children.text: According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, the section from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920. The section from the körtér to Vasút utca, near Kelenföld railway station, was called Átlós út, but only from 1890 to 1920. Both names describe a road leading out of Buda towards the south and west rather than a boulevard of the kind it became. Building along the route followed the zoning plan of 1913, which set the pattern of the residential blocks of three to five storeys that line most of it today.

historySections.heading: Rails and trams reach the road, 1898 to 1942

children.text: Transport arrived early. A tram ran along the street for the first time in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér. In 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway started from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út, splitting after Albertfalva into one branch for Budaörs and Törökbálint and another for Budafok and Nagytétény. Trams 19 and 49 began service in 1910, and the Kelenföld tram depot has operated since 1912. In 1942 the HÉV was shortened to the building known as the Gomba at the körtér, which was completed that year.

historySections.heading: New names and recent renewal, 1920 to today

children.text: In 1920 the Council of Public Works renamed Fehérvári út and its continuation, Átlós út, as Horthy Miklós út. In 1945 the road was renamed Bartók Béla út. The cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, the reconstruction reached Kelenföld railway station in 2005, and the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016. After the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, the Bartók-negyed programme strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between the körtér and Szent Gellért tér, the same stretch that now holds many of the street's cafés and galleries.

stories.title: The composer's will and the street's name

children.text: The Hungarian Wikipedia article suggests that the choice of Bartók's name in 1945 may have been symbolic. It notes that the composer opposed Nazi-aligned ideas and emigrated from Hungary in 1940, and that in his 1940 will he stated that his name should not be used for public spaces in Hungary while places in Budapest were named after Hitler and Mussolini.

docs.name: National Dance Theatre
docs.description: Hungary's National Dance Theatre now stands in Millenáris Park in Buda, in a converted former factory that opened in February 2019. Before that it was based in the former Carmelite monastery and church in Buda Castle, a building that had been a theatre since the 1780s.

children.text: The National Dance Theatre, in Hungarian the Nemzeti Táncszínház, is a dance venue that hosts performances by resident and guest companies. Its current address, according to its own website, is Kis Rókus utca 16-20 in Buda, and the new building opened on 15 February 2019 in Millenáris Park. The venue is separate from the Hungarian National Dance Ensemble, a folk dance company that performs at other stages.

A February 2019 report describes the theatre as a three-nave former factory, part of the former Ganz electro-technical works that the park was converted from. The Budapest firm ZDA designed it, industrial features are kept visible and a pavilion-like lobby sits partly in the park. The report mentions a 368-seat main hall and a 120-seat hall for studio productions, while the theatre's own site lists two theatre halls and a chamber hall plus rehearsal rooms. The lobby has a suspended ceiling of about 13,000 wooden pieces, and the report calls the venue the home of nearly 40 dance companies.
The theatre's programme features productions by companies such as Fitos Dezső Társulat and Duda Éva Társulat. The programme changes, so the official calendar is the place to confirm what is on.

Before the move, the theatre was based in the former Carmelite monastery and church in Buda Castle, a building with a long theatre history of its own. Wikipedia says the Carmelites received the plot in 1693 and finished the church by 1736. After Joseph II dissolved the order in 1784, the church was converted into the Castle Theatre in 1786 to plans by Wolfgang von Kempelen. The first Hungarian-language play there was staged on 25 October 1790. Sources disagree about when the dance theatre left the Castle building, so the exact years should be treated with care.
Good to know
Check the official site for the current performance calendar and tickets, since the programme changes.
Older listings may still give the former Castle District address, so use the Millenáris address when planning your route.
Millenáris Park itself is a conversion of the former Ganz works, so the surroundings are worth a look before or after a performance.

docs.historyIntro: The National Dance Theatre's story runs through two very different buildings: the former Carmelite church in Buda Castle, which was a theatre from the 1780s, and a converted factory at Millenáris Park, which opened in 2019.

historySections.heading: From Carmelite church to Castle Theatre

children.text: Wikipedia says the site first held a Franciscan church of St John, built in 1269-1270, which became a mosque under Ottoman rule and was destroyed in the 1686 siege of Buda. The Carmelites received the plot in 1693, laid the foundation stone in 1725 and finished the church by 1736. After Emperor Joseph II dissolved the order in 1784, the church was converted into the Castle Theatre in 1786 to plans by Wolfgang von Kempelen, with the high altar turned into the stage. The first play in Hungarian was staged there on 25 October 1790.

historySections.heading: War damage, closure and the Várszínház

children.text: The theatre reopened in 1918 but closed in 1924 after a gallery collapsed, and it remained shut for about five decades, according to Wikipedia. Bombing in the Second World War damaged the building and collapsed the balcony, and it was renovated in 1947. It reopened on 13 February 1978 as the Várszínház. It housed the Népszínház until 1982 and then served as the National Theatre's chamber theatre until 1 December 2001. A Hungarian account says the National Dance Theatre began operating in the building on that date.

Sources disagree about when the dance theatre left the Castle building: one 2019 report says it was based there from 2001 to 2014, while Wikipedia says the building was the theatre's home from 2001 to 2019 and that the government took it over in 2014 before the Prime Minister's office moved in during 2019. A 2019 news report said the theatre had to leave so that the prime minister could work from the Castle. The new building in Millenáris Park, at Kis Rókus utca 16-20, opened on 15 February 2019 according to the theatre's own site. It occupies a converted former factory from the Ganz works.

docs.name: Müpa Budapest
docs.description: A riverside arts complex in Ferencváros combining the Béla Bartók National Concert Hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum under one roof. It opened in 2005 as the Palace of Arts and was renamed Müpa in 2015; its main hall is known for adjustable acoustics and a large organ.

children.text: Müpa Budapest is a concert, theatre and museum complex at Komor Marcell utca 1 in Ferencváros, near Rákóczi Bridge. Between 2005 and 2015 it was called the Palace of Arts, in Hungarian the Művészetek Palotája. It was built between 2002 and 2005 to designs by Zoboki, Demeter and Partners, and it was officially opened on 14 March 2005. The National Theatre, which opened in 2002, stands next door as part of the Millennium City Center development.

Wikipedia says the concert hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum were built in parallel over 28 months. The complex has about 10,000 square metres of ground area and 70,000 square metres of floor space. The Ludwig Museum's own site describes a simple, clear exterior with large glass areas and few decorative elements, and an undulating main wall inside clad mainly in walnut.

The Béla Bartók National Concert Hall is the largest section, with about 1,656 seats according to Wikipedia, although other sources give 1,699. Its acoustics were designed by Russell Johnson and can be adjusted using 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. The hall's organ was inaugurated on 22 May 2006 and has 92 stops, 5 manuals and about 6,700 pipes. It was built by Orgelbau Mühleisen with the Pécs Organ Building Manufactory and is described as one of the largest organs in Europe.

The Festival Theatre occupies the eastern third of the building and seats 452. The Ludwig Museum, a museum of contemporary art, takes the Danube-facing side of the complex and was previously housed in Buda Castle. Wikipedia says the complex won the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence in 2006 and the FIABCI audience award in 2007.
Good to know
Check the official Müpa site for the current concert, dance and theatre calendar and tickets, since several halls run different programmes.
Wikipedia says the building is served by the H6 and H7 suburban railway lines; confirm the best route with a current journey planner.
The Ludwig Museum is inside the complex but is a separate institution, so check its own page for its exhibitions.

docs.historyIntro: Müpa Budapest was built between 2002 and 2005 as the Palace of Arts, with a concert hall, a theatre and a museum built in parallel. It was renamed Müpa Budapest in 2015.

children.text: Wikipedia says the Palace of Arts was built from 2002 to 2005 to designs by Zoboki, Demeter and Partners, with the general contractors Trigránit and Arcadom Építőipari Zrt. The concert hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum were built in parallel over 28 months. The building has about 10,000 square metres of ground area and 70,000 square metres of floor space. It stands in Ferencváros near Rákóczi Bridge, next to the National Theatre, which opened in 2002, and both are part of the Millennium City Center development.

The complex was officially opened on 14 March 2005. Its Béla Bartók National Concert Hall has acoustics designed by Russell Johnson, adjustable with 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. The hall's organ was inaugurated on 22 May 2006. It has 92 stops, 5 manuals and about 6,700 pipes and was built by Orgelbau Mühleisen with the Pécs Organ Building Manufactory. Wikipedia says the complex won the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence in 2006 and the FIABCI audience award in 2007.

historySections.heading: From Palace of Arts to Müpa

children.text: Between 2005 and 2015 the building was known as the Palace of Arts, and it was then renamed Müpa Budapest. The Ludwig Museum, a museum of contemporary art, occupies the Danube-facing side and was previously housed in Buda Castle, according to its own website. The Festival Theatre, in the east wing, seats 452, and the main lobby connects the three main parts of the complex.

docs.name: Budapest Music Center
docs.description: A concert hall, jazz club, music library and record label in a converted 1890 building at Mátyás utca 8. The organisation was founded in 1996 by trombonist László Gőz and moved into its own premises in 2013, presenting classical, contemporary and jazz music.

children.text: The Budapest Music Center, usually shortened to BMC, is a concert promoter, record label and music information centre at Mátyás utca 8. According to its own site it was founded in 1996 by trombonist and former academy professor László Gőz, with the aim of presenting contemporary Hungarian music in a collective and coordinated way. Its record label, BMC Records, was founded in 1998 and has issued more than 370 releases across classical, contemporary and jazz music.

The building has a story of its own. A case study by the software company Graphisoft says it began as a one-storey neoclassical residential building from 1890 with street-facing shops on the ground floor. Preparation, design and implementation took close to 10 years, and the centre opened in spring 2013. The architects were Art1st Design Studio. The original elevations were conserved and refurbished, with a new metallic corner element rising above the main cornice, and the main entrance was moved to the street corner.

The concert hall sits in the former inner courtyard and is linked to the street by a large lobby, and its exposed original brick walls contribute to its sound. The Opus Jazz Club, opened in 2013, occupies two storeys on the street side and is acoustically separated from the hall so both can run at once. The first floor holds the library and recording studios, and an attic conference room, a roof terrace and an event hall complete the building.

The Hungarian Music Information Center and Library collects and shares information on Hungarian classical and jazz artists. BMC's site says its database covers about 3,700 artists and orchestras and 33,000 compositions, and the library has more than 100,000 scores, books, CDs and LPs. BMC also says it holds about 500 events a year, only some of them public concerts.
Good to know
Check the BMC site for the current concert and jazz club calendar, tickets and any library visiting arrangements, since the venue also hosts private events.
The Opus Jazz Club and the concert hall can host separate events at the same time, so check which room your event is in.
The address is Mátyás utca 8, so use a current journey planner to plan your route.

children.text: BMC's own about page says it was founded in 1996 by trombonist and former academy professor László Gőz. Its aim was to present contemporary Hungarian music in a collective and coordinated way. BMC works as a concert promoter, a record label and an information centre. Its record label, BMC Records, was founded in 1998, and BMC's site says it has released more than 370 albums in classical, contemporary and jazz music on CD and in digital formats.

historySections.heading: From an 1890 house to a music centre

children.text: A Graphisoft case study says the building began as a one-storey neoclassical residential building from 1890, with shops on the ground floor facing the street. Preparation, design and implementation took close to 10 years, and most of the transformation was financed from private resources. The centre opened in spring 2013. The architects were Art1st Design Studio. The original elevations were conserved and refurbished, the entrance was moved to the street corner, and the concert hall was built in the former inner courtyard with its exposed brick walls kept.

BMC says the building houses a concert hall, the Opus Jazz Club, the music library, BMC Records and the Peter Eötvös Contemporary Music Foundation. The Opus Jazz Club also opened in 2013. Since 2014 the information centre and library has published monographs on Hungarian composers. The Graphisoft case study adds that the founder issued a written statement forbidding future owners from changing the building's content or function, or selling or transforming it.

docs.name: Castle Garden Bazaar
docs.description: A neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, stairways and gardens by Miklós Ybl at the foot of Castle Hill, beside the Danube. Built in the 1870s and 1880s, it later served as a rock-concert venue, then as a ruin, before its restoration and reopening in 2014.

children.text: The Castle Garden Bazaar, Várkert Bazár in Hungarian, is a neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, staircases and gardens on the Danube side of Castle Hill, at Ybl Miklós tér. It was built between 1875 and 1883 to plans by Miklós Ybl. According to the building's own history page, the idea arose in the early 1870s of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of the hill. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as a listed monument and part of the Budapest World Heritage site.

A history of Buda Castle describes Ybl's design as an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant to hold shops, stores and workshops, and the neo-Renaissance gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace above. The sculptor Alajos Stróbl got the first studio in the arcade, in 1884, and about eighty other artists followed over the next century.

In the second half of the twentieth century the bazaar found a different life as the Budai Ifjúsági Park, the Buda Youth Park, which hosted pop and rock concerts from 1961 to 1984. Visit Hungary names bands such as LGT, Edda, Piramis, P. Mobil, Omega and Beatrice, and says inscriptions by Edda and LGT on a stone wall survived the later restoration. A P. Mobil concert on 23 September 1984 is described as the end of the Youth Park. The building was closed that year and decayed, and it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world.

A government decree of 2011 launched its reconstruction. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and the second, with an event centre, underground garage and Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014. Excavations during the work found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries that operated here from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, and, according to the building's own history page, several hundred carved stone and cast-iron bullets, probably from the 1686 recapture of Buda. Restorers also found an old lock with its broken key still inside, which has since been shown in several exhibitions.

The gardens are the part most visitors walk through. The Visit Buda Castle page mentions a Triton Fountain, a rose garden and stretches of old castle walls, and describes the building by the Danube bank as a home for exhibitions and cultural events. Do not confuse the bazaar with the Várkert-kiosk, a separate Ybl building nearby; the Buda Castle history notes that only these two of his works there survive.
Good to know
The gardens lie at the foot of Castle Hill beside the Danube bank, so they combine easily with a visit to the Castle District above.
Check the official Várkert Bazár site for current exhibitions, events and visiting conditions, as the building hosts cultural programmes.

When the building reopened in 2014, the Budapest History Museum's exhibition Ostromok és hétköznapok showed archaeological finds from the excavations in the southern palaces; check the official site for what is currently on show.

historySections.heading: Ybl's complex below the palace, 1875 to 1883

children.text: The building's own history page says the idea of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of Castle Hill arose in the early 1870s, and that Miklós Ybl was given the task of drawing the final plans. The neo-Renaissance complex was built between 1875 and 1883. A history of Buda Castle describes an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant for shops and workshops, and the gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace. Ybl died in 1891, before the palace reconstruction he had planned was finished.

historySections.heading: Studios, schools and a Youth Park, 1884 to 1984

children.text: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the north wing housed a craftswomen's training workshop from 1883 to 1888, the Historical Portrait Gallery from 1890 to 1895 and a women's painting school from about 1890 until 1918. From 1884 the sculptor Alajos Stróbl had a studio in the arcade, the first of about eighty artists who worked there over the next century. The building was heavily damaged in the Second World War. From 1961 it became the Budai Ifjúsági Park, a venue for pop and rock concerts. A staircase wall collapsed during an Edda concert in 1980, and the Youth Park ended in 1984, when the building was closed.

After 1984 the building decayed, and a Visit Hungary article says it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world. Several plans for its reconstruction and reuse were drawn up before Government Decree 1375 of 2011 launched the reconstruction, with work beginning in summer 2013. Excavations found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries and, according to the building's own history page, several hundred carved stone and cast-iron bullets, probably from the 1686 recapture of Buda. The Triton fountain was restored. The first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and a second phase, with an event centre, an underground garage and a Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014.

stories.title: Franz Joseph and the view he rarely saw

children.text: Visit Hungary records a story told about the gardens: according to legend, Emperor Franz Joseph rarely enjoyed the Danube view that the Neo-Renaissance gardens were designed to keep open, because he never stayed overnight in the Castle. The article presents this as a legend, not as a documented fact.

docs.name: Clark Ádám Square and the 0 km Stone
docs.description: The roundabout at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, named after the engineer Adam Clark and home to the limestone 0 km stone from which Hungary's main roads are numbered. The Buda Castle Funicular and the tunnel under Castle Hill start here.

children.text: Clark Ádám tér is the square at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, below Castle Hill. Visit Buda Castle calls it a symbolic starting point: the limestone 0 km stone stands here, beside the lower station of the Buda Castle Funicular, and the kilometre numbering of several of Hungary's main roads is counted from it. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it marks the start of the first-class main roads except routes 1 and 8, and that the square lies at the entrance of the Buda tunnel.

The square has had several names. In the 1860s it was also called Népszínház tér, after the Buda People's Theatre that stood there, and from the mid-1870s Lánchíd tér, Chain Bridge Square. In 1912 it was renamed after Adam Clark, the Scottish engineer who designed the Chain Bridge and the tunnel. Hungarian Wikipedia calls it Budapest's first uniform neo-Renaissance square.

War and rebuilding changed it. The Budai Takarékpénztár building, designed by Miklós Ybl, was hit by a bomb in the Second World War. Hungarian Wikipedia says it was demolished in 1949 while the roundabout was being built, whereas We Love Budapest says the damaged parts came down in 1948 and a remaining torso only in 1990; a hotel now stands on the site. The Lánchíd Palota is the only original building left standing on the square. The square and the area around the 0 km stone were renovated in July 2014.

The stone itself is a limestone sculpture about three metres tall, with a zero sign and the letters KM on its pedestal. English Wikipedia credits the present sculpture to Miklós Borsos and dates it to 1975. It was not the first monument on the spot: in 1932 a statue of the Virgin Mary by Körmendi, put up by the Hungária Automobil Club, was the first monument here. Sources differ on its fate: English Wikipedia says the Second World War destroyed it, while We Love Budapest says it survived the siege but was removed by the communist authorities. From 1953 until the present sculpture replaced it, a sculpture of a worker stood here.
Good to know
The square is the lower terminus of the Buda Castle Funicular; check the official funicular page for its current operating status and tickets.
From the stone you can walk onto the Chain Bridge or into the Castle Hill area; the Buda tunnel entrance is at the square.
The roundabout is busy with traffic, so use the marked crossings when approaching the stone and take photographs from the small park around it.

docs.historyIntro: The Zero Kilometre Stone at Clark Ádám Square is the point from which distances in Hungary are measured, and the spot has held several monuments in its time.

children.text: The present sculpture was erected in 1975 and is the work of Miklós Borsos. It is a three-metre limestone monument that represents Kilometre Zero in Hungary, and its pedestal carries the inscription 'KM' for kilometres. It stands in a small park at Clark Ádám Square, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, below Buda Castle.

historySections.heading: A spot with a changing monument

children.text: The country's road zero point is said to have first been marked at the threshold of the Buda Royal Palace. HVG says the milestone was later moved near the newly opened Chain Bridge, and English Wikipedia dates this to 1849, although the source it cites does not mention the move. A Madonna statue by Eugene Kormendi was set up on the spot in 1932; English Wikipedia says it was destroyed in the Second World War, but other sources say it survived the siege and was removed later. A sculpture of a worker stood there from 1953 until the present monument replaced it.

docs.name: Hungarian Heritage House
docs.description: A national institute for Hungarian folk culture based in the former Budai Vigadó on Corvin Square, built in 1898-1900. It runs folk dance houses, craft courses, concerts, exhibitions and archival work, and it is also the base of the Hungarian State Folk Ensemble.

children.text: The Hungarian Heritage House, in Hungarian the Hagyományok Háza, is an institute of national significance that works to preserve the folk traditions of the Carpathian Basin. It was established in 2001. Its mission includes bringing back small cultural elements that have faded or are fading and keeping them alive in today's cultural life. Its activities include stage folk dance, handicraft classes, folk craft arts, archiving of folklore footage, live storytelling and folk arts education for young people.

Its home is the former Budai Vigadó, an entertainment hall in Buda at Corvin tér 8, standing on Fő utca between Batthyány tér and Clark Ádám tér. The institute's own page says it was built between 1898 and 1900 by Aladár Árkay and Mór Kallina and was designed as a cultural complex for Buda's middle class, with a theatre, library, cafe and restaurant. It has an eclectic exterior with a relatively simple facade and rich Art Nouveau ornamentation inside, including a columned hall with a wide marble staircase and an ornamented lounge.

The house runs a permanent dance house series in its glass-roofed atrium. The institute says the first Budapest dance house was held in May 1972, based on the experience of the dance houses of Szék, a village in Transylvania. Its own dance houses focus on teaching, with courses on a region's dances followed by a ball with regional musicians. The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble, which marked its 70th anniversary around the time of the institute's 20th, is part of the house.

Other activities include folk craft training, folk music and dance camps and a museum, according to the institute's own website. The Buda Castle District attractions listing describes it as a place where folk tradition appears in a living, present-day form, with dance performances, concerts, exhibitions, craft programmes and community events.
Good to know
Check the Heritage House website for the current dance house series, exhibitions, concerts and tickets, since programmes run by season.
The institute's page suggests metro line 2 to Batthyány tér followed by a short walk south on Fő utca, or bus 86 to Szilágyi Dezső tér, or tram 19 or 41 to Halász utca.
The Hungarian Heritage House is a different institution from museums nearby, so look for the Corvin tér 8 address when you navigate.

docs.historyIntro: The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 in the Budai Vigadó, a Buda entertainment hall built in 1898-1900. It draws on the dance house movement that began in Budapest in 1972 and on the Hungarian State Folk Ensemble founded in the early 1950s.

children.text: The Heritage House's own page says its building was the historic Vigadó, an entertainment hall, of Buda. It was built between 1898 and 1900 by Aladár Árkay and Mór Kallina as a cultural complex for Buda's middle class, with a theatre, library, cafe and restaurant. The exterior is eclectic with a relatively simple facade, while the interior has rich Art Nouveau ornamentation, including a columned hall with a wide marble staircase. The page does not describe the building's later history or restoration, so those details should be checked separately.

historySections.heading: Dance houses and a state folk ensemble

children.text: The Heritage House's page on its dance house says the first Budapest dance house was held in May 1972, based on the experience of the dance houses of Szék in Transylvania. UNESCO's own page says the táncház method was selected in 2011 for its Register of Good Safeguarding Practices, as a Hungarian model for transmitting intangible heritage. The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble is described as the first professional folk dance ensemble in Hungary. Miklós Rábai was chosen in 1950 to establish its dance chorus, and its inaugural performance, with the Moiseyev Ensemble, took place on 4 April 1951 at the Opera House.

The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 as an institute of national significance based in the Budai Vigadó on Corvin Square. Its mission is to preserve folk traditions of the Carpathian Basin and bring back small cultural elements that have faded or are fading. A February 2021 report said the institute marked 20 years in 2021, a double jubilee with the 70th anniversary of the Folk Ensemble, which also works from the building. Its activities include stage folk dance, handicraft classes, archiving of folklore footage and folk arts education.

docs.name: Vienna Gate
docs.description: A rebuilt gateway at the northern end of the Castle District, where several well-known streets meet. The present gate dates from 1936, marking 250 years since the recapture of Buda, and replaced older gates that stood here since the Middle Ages.

children.text: The Vienna Gate, Bécsi kapu in Hungarian, stands at the northeastern corner of Vienna Gate Square at the northern end of the Castle District. It is the gate that linked the Castle to the road to Vienna. Visit Buda Castle calls it one of the most atmospheric entrances to Buda Castle and notes that several well-known Castle District streets begin at the square. Nearby it lists the Hungarian National Archives, the Lutheran church of Buda Castle and a notable grapevine.

A gate has stood here since the Middle Ages, and the names show its past. In the Middle Ages it was the Porta Sabbati, or Szombat-kapu, the Saturday Gate, after the weekly markets held in front of it. In the Ottoman period it was called Beç kapusu, and it was later also known as the Zsidó-kapu, the Jewish Gate. The Castle District heritage site says the medieval layout is known only from Baroque and late Ottoman plans, which show a tower where the wall sections met, with the passage through its ground floor.

The gate was rebuilt several times. A new one was built in 1723 and remained in use until 1849; another followed in 1850. In the early nineteenth century one of its two side gates was removed, and before the 1896 millenary festival the whole gate was pulled down. The present gate was built in 1936 to mark the 250th anniversary of the recapture of Buda from the Ottomans, and it resembles the destroyed one.

Wikipedia names the architect as Jenő Kismarty-Lechner and says the sculptor Béla Ohmann made the inscriptions, ornaments and reliefs, including a running angel. Memorials to the 1686 recapture stand on both sides: an angel statue on the left and a tablet on the right. Wikipedia describes the gate as more symbolic than functional. Two parts of the Bastion Promenade are connected across its top, and automatic barriers at the gate help control traffic within the Castle.
Good to know
Walk through the gate to see the angel statue and the tablet commemorating the 1686 recapture on either side.
The Lutheran church of Buda Castle and the Hungarian National Archives are close by on the square.
Several of the best-known Castle District streets start at the square, so it works well as an entry point for a walk through the district.

It was called the Szombat-kapu, the Saturday Gate, because markets were held in front of it every Saturday. The Ottomans called it Beç kapusu, and it later became known as the Zsidó-kapu, the Jewish Gate.

docs.name: The Tabán
docs.description: A green slope between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, on the site of the old Tabán quarter of winding streets, taverns and Serbian, Greek and German residents. The district was largely demolished in the 1930s, and today a quiet park near Döbrentei Square marks its place.

children.text: The Tabán is a park in Buda's 1st district between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, near Döbrentei Square. The Visit Buda Castle page calls it a quiet place for a walk, a picnic or a pause while sightseeing, and says it occupies the site of a quarter of winding streets, restaurants and wine taverns that many called the Montmartre of Budapest.

The area has long been settled thanks to its sheltered valley, the thermal waters at the foot of Gellért Hill and a ford across the Danube. After the 1686 liberation of Buda, refugees arrived from Greece, Bosnia and Serbia, and Wikipedia says that in the 18th century the residents included Serbs, Greeks, Vlachs, Germans, Croats, Slovaks and Romani people. The Serbs were called Rácok, which gave the district the name Rácváros.

In the early 20th century its houses were considered unhealthy, and the Tabán was demolished in the 1930s because of overcrowding and poor public health. Hungarian Wikipedia says the planned new district was never built because of the Second World War, and that the area was landscaped as a public park in the 1960s. Wikipedia also records the 1956 memorial near Naphegy and Kereszt streets and the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History near Apród Street. The Rác Thermal Bath near Döbrentei Square was listed as closed on the Visit Buda Castle page, so check its current status.
Good to know
The park is near Döbrentei Square, at the foot of the Tabán, and lies between Buda Castle and Gellért Hill, so it suits a walk between the two.
The Rác Thermal Bath is nearby but has been closed for refurbishment for many years, and its reopening is still only a plan, so check the operator before counting on it.
The Semmelweis Museum of Medical History is near Apród Street, and the 1956 memorial is near Naphegy and Kereszt streets.

docs.historyIntro: The Tabán was a quarter of Buda that stood for centuries on the river side of Castle Hill and was largely demolished in the 1930s. The park there today replaced it.

children.text: Wikipedia says the area has been inhabited since Neolithic times thanks to a sheltered valley, thermal waters at the foot of Gellért Hill and a ford over the Danube, and that the Romans replaced the Celts in the 1st century BC. In the Middle Ages the Tabán lay outside the walls and became a suburb of Buda, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Turks developed thermal medicinal baths there and brought in settlers from the Balkans. After the 1686 liberation of Buda refugees arrived from Greece, Bosnia and Serbia, and the Habsburg authorities resettled roughly 600 Serbian families in the Lower Town; a 1696 census recorded more than 1,000 Serbian families. The district was also known as Raitzenstadt, the town of the Serbs.

Franciscans from Bosnia founded the parish Church of St Catherine of Alexandria in the 17th century, and it was rebuilt in Baroque style between 1728 and 1777. The Serbian community's Church of St Demetrius was built in Baroque style from 1742, consecrated in 1751 and given a copper spire in 1775. The Great Tabán Fire of 1810 burned out the church, and the 1838 flood damaged it again. By the 19th century the Tabán was a bohemian quarter with many restaurants, bars and brothels, its narrow hillside streets giving it a Mediterranean feel, and Kereszt Street was its centre.

Because of overcrowding and poor public health, the Tabán was demolished in the 1930s: The English Wikipedia article on the Church of St Demetrius dates the main clearance to 1933 to 1934 and the last surrounding buildings to 1938, while Hungarian Wikipedia says the houses were demolished between 1933 and 1936. Hungarian Wikipedia says the planned new district was never built because of the Second World War, and that the area was landscaped as a public park in the 1960s. The Church of St Demetrius survived the clearance but was seriously damaged in the siege of 1944 and 1945 and the ruin was demolished in 1949. The Tabán school was destroyed in January 1945. Today the Tabán is a park, with the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History and a 1956 memorial nearby.

docs.name: Matthias Fountain
docs.description: A neo-Baroque bronze fountain group by Alajos Stróbl in the Buda Castle palace forecourt, showing King Matthias Corvinus on a hunt. It was inaugurated in 1904, damaged in the Second World War, and is sometimes nicknamed the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.

children.text: The Matthias Fountain, Mátyás kútja, is a monumental fountain group in the western forecourt of Buda Castle, set against the northern facade of the former Castle Church. Visit Buda Castle places it in the Hunyadi Courtyard of the palace and describes it as Alajos Stróbl's sculptural composition evoking the legend of the Renaissance ruler, with cascading water. English Wikipedia calls the style neo-Baroque and says it is sometimes called the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.

The scene is a hunting party led by King Matthias Corvinus. The king stands on the highest rock in hunting dress with a crossbow in his right hand and a huge dead stag at his feet. Below him a henchman blows a horn, the leader of the hunting group sits on a boulder with his back to the viewer, and three hounds complete the central group. The bronze figures stand on heaps of rocks, with water running down between the boulders. The central niche forms a triumphal arch bearing the king's personal coat of arms.

Two figures sit at the sides of the basin. On the right is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, protecting her tame fawn from the hunters. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. On the left is Galeotto Marzio, an Italian chronicler who lived at Matthias's court, with a sighthound at his feet and a falcon on his fist.

Stróbl began work in 1899 after King Franz Joseph approved the composition. According to Wikipedia, the stag was modelled on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where Stróbl had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent the hounds that served as models. The henchman figure won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the king's presence, and Alajos Hauszmann, master builder of the palace reconstruction, is credited with erecting it.

The Second World War destroyed the middle dog, which Jenő Grantner later reconstructed. The more elaborate original balustrade and mansard roof were simplified after the war damage, and the fountain was restored in 2010.
Good to know
Look for the details at the basin: Szép Ilonka and her fawn on the right, Galeotto Marzio with his falcon on the left.
The fountain is part of the palace grounds; check the official Buda Castle pages for current access to the courtyards.
The Savoyai Terrace and the Hungarian National Gallery are also in the palace area, so the two sights combine easily.

docs.historyIntro: The Matthias Fountain was made by Alajos Stróbl between 1899 and 1904 as part of the great reconstruction of the Buda palace. It lost a figure in the Second World War and was restored in 2010.

historySections.heading: The palace that needed a fountain, 1875 to 1912

children.text: English Wikipedia's history of Buda Castle says the rebuilding of the palace spanned 1875 to 1912. Miklós Ybl drew a master plan in 1885 and work began in 1890, and after his death in 1891 Alajos Hauszmann took over. Hauszmann designed the north wing, which doubled the Baroque palace on the Danube side. The same history places Alajos Stróbl's fountain in the western forecourt near the rear facade of that wing, as part of Hauszmann's work. The fountain's own article credits Hauszmann as master builder of the palace reconstruction and as the man who erected the fountain.

According to English Wikipedia, King Franz Joseph approved the scheme, and Stróbl began work in 1899. He modelled the stag on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where he had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent him the hounds that served as models. The figure of the henchman won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the presence of the king. It shows King Matthias Corvinus in hunting dress above a dead stag, with Szép Ilonka and the chronicler Galeotto Marzio at the sides of the basin.

The group suffered in the Second World War, when the middle dog sculpture was destroyed. The sculptor Jenő Grantner reconstructed it. Wikipedia adds that the original balustrade and mansard roof, which had been more elaborate, were simplified after the war damage. This matches the wider history of the palace, which was reduced to ruins in the siege of 1944 and 1945 and rebuilt in the following decades. The fountain was restored in 2010, and it stands today in the palace forecourt that Visit Buda Castle calls the Hunyadi Courtyard.

stories.title: Szép Ilonka and the king

children.text: One of the figures at the basin is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, shown protecting her tame fawn. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. According to the ballad, Ilonka and Matthias fell in love when he was hunting without revealing who he was; when she learned his true identity she assumed the love was impossible and died of a broken heart. This is a literary legend, not a documented event.

docs.name: Savoyai Terrace
docs.description: A broad terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of Buda Castle, with views of the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges. Its centrepiece is József Róna's equestrian statue of Prince Eugene of Savoy, installed in 1900.

children.text: The Savoyai Terrace lies in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of the Buda palace. Visit Buda Castle says it offers a stunning view of the Danube, the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges of Budapest, and that it features an equestrian statue of Eugene of Savoy. Wikipedia lists the Hungarian National Gallery, founded in 1957, among the palace wings labelled A to D.

The terrace is named after Prince Eugene of Savoy, born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, which the same article says ended roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary.

The statue is the work of the sculptor József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, so it waited in Róna's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did, judging by photographs. It was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace. That account describes its style as Viennese neo-Baroque, chosen to harmonise with the horseshoe-shaped Baroque staircase behind it.

The palace around the terrace changed greatly in the twentieth century. English Wikipedia says fighting in the siege of 1944 and 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque staircase was demolished in the 1950s and not restored, but the statue survived the siege relatively intact and returned to its original place after restoration.
Good to know
Come for the view: the terrace looks across the Danube towards the Parliament, with Gellért Hill and several bridges in sight.
The Matthias Fountain and the Hungarian National Gallery are in the same palace area, so the three sights fit into one visit.
Check the official Buda Castle and Hungarian National Gallery pages for current access conditions and events on the terrace.

children.text: Prince Eugene of Savoy was born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today, he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, a victory the same article credits with ending roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary. He also owned the island of Csepel, where he built a castle at Ráckeve, and Promontor, today's Budafok, was part of his estate.

The equestrian statue is the work of József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, which waited in the sculptor's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did so on the basis of photographs. The statue was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace in Buda. A list of equestrian statues in Hungary also gives it as by József Róna, in the Buda Castle, 1900.

historySections.heading: Siege, ruin and return, 1944 to the 1950s

children.text: The palace around the statue changed greatly after the siege of Budapest. English Wikipedia says that fighting between 29 December 1944 and 13 February 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque horseshoe staircase behind the statue was demolished in the 1950s and not restored. The statue itself came through the siege relatively intact and, after restoration, returned to its original place. Today the terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery, with the statue at its centre, looks out over the Danube towards the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the city's bridges.

docs.name: Tóth Árpád Promenade
docs.description: A tree-lined walk along the castle wall in Buda Castle District, laid out on the line of an old defensive passage. It looks out toward the Buda hills, Tabán and Gellért Hill, carries the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, and is known for the Japanese ornamental cherries that bloom along it in spring.

children.text: The Tóth Árpád Promenade (Tóth Árpád sétány) runs along the castle wall on the western side of the Buda Castle District. Time Out Budapest describes it as a route with centuries of history that began as a defensive passage and later became a walkway. Today it is a quiet, green stretch of the district that most visitors use as a slow alternative to the busier squares around Matthias Church.

The views are the main reason to come. Visit Buda Castle speaks of vistas toward the Buda hills and the city, while Time Out highlights the outlook over the Tabán district and Gellért Hill. In spring, Japanese ornamental cherry trees blossom along the path, and both sources single this season out as the most photogenic time to walk it.

The name is more recent than the walkway. According to a Hungarian city-culture article, the area behind the castle wall was occupied by gardens until 1936, when they were cleared and the Bástya sétány (Bastion Promenade) was created. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was divided into sections, and the Tóth Árpád sétány is one half of the former Bástya sétány. It is named after the poet Árpád Tóth (1886-1928), a lyric poet associated with the Nyugat circle; the Castle District heritage site says the lane received its present name in 1946. None of the pages consulted explains why he was chosen.

Along the walk you can find a statue of Artúr Görgei at the Fehérvári rondella, according to Time Out, and the promenade is within a few minutes of Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate (Bécsi kapu) and the Fisherman's Bastion. Visit Buda Castle also places it near Kapisztrán tér and the Military History Institute and Museum, which makes it an easy addition to a Castle District day.
Good to know
Spring, when the ornamental cherry trees bloom, is the season both Time Out and Visit Buda Castle recommend for the promenade.
Time Out suggests starting at the Castle, walking down toward Tabán and finishing near Gellért Hill.
Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate and the Fisherman's Bastion are all a few minutes' walk away, so the promenade combines well with a Castle District visit.

docs.historyIntro: The promenade along the western castle wall began as a defensive passage and became a public walk, taking its present name in the 20th century. The documented record is thin, and the sources read give few dates.

historySections.heading: A defensive passage on the wall

children.text: Time Out Budapest describes the Tóth Árpád Promenade as a route with a history of several centuries that grew out of a former defensive passage along the castle wall, on the western side of the Castle District. The page gives no construction dates and does not say who built the passage or when it first became a place for walking. The English Wikipedia article on Buda Castle describes a reconstruction of the castle's fortifications from the 1950s to 1966, and its article on the Bastion Promenade says the promenade was heavily damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt between 1966 and 1970.

historySections.heading: From Bástya sétány to a named promenade

children.text: A Hungarian city-culture article records that in 1936 gardens still occupied the ground behind the wall, and that they were removed to make way for the Bástya sétány, the Bastion Promenade. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was cut into several sections. The Tóth Árpád sétány is described as the other half of the former Bástya sétány, while the Babits Mihály sétány came from the same division. The promenade now bears the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, who lived from 1886 to 1928 and wrote for the journal Nyugat. The pages consulted do not explain why he was chosen.

docs.name: Garden of Philosophers
docs.description: A small sculpture garden on the side of Gellért Hill, where eight life-size bronze figures by Nándor Wagner face a shared centre. Religious founders and thinkers stand together in a work meant to show what cultures have in common. It was a gift from the sculptor's widow and was unveiled in 2001.

children.text: The Garden of Philosophers (Filozófusok kertje) is a quiet sculpture group on the western side of Gellért Hill, between Orom utca and Hegyalja út and behind the Rudas Baths. It is the work of the sculptor Nándor Wagner, and Visit Buda Castle describes it as an eight-figure group that highlights values which religions and cultures share. The life-size bronze figures face each other, looking toward the geometric centre of the group.

A guide from the XpatLoop site names the figures. Five stand in a ring around a sunken pool: Abraham, Jesus, Buddha, Laozi and Akhenaten. Abraham is the only one not standing, and crouches with his head in his hands. Behind the ring stand Mahatma Gandhi, Bodhidharma and Saint Francis of Assisi. Each figure focuses on a small globe, which the guide says represents divine essence. Wikipedia describes Wagner's wider concept as having a further ring of lawgivers, but the Budapest sources describe eight figures, which is what stands here.

Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and left Hungary after the 1956 revolution, living first in Sweden and then in Japan, where he died in 1997. According to Wikipedia he conceived the work in Mashiko, Japan, as a spiritual message for future generations. The Budapest set was a gift from his widow and was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site.

The group has had a difficult history. Hungarian magazine HVG reported in 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma (named Dharma in the article), had been stolen after an earlier attempt the previous October that damaged the figures. The article notes that plaster moulds for recasting exist in Japan. Közterkép and a Budapest city blog report that the three figures were later recast from moulds provided by Wagner's widow and that the full set of eight was back in place by 2010. A separate small sculpture of Prince Buda and Princess Pest stands nearby.
Good to know
The garden lies on a hillside between Orom utca and Hegyalja út, behind the Rudas Baths, so expect an uphill walk from the riverside.
Three figures were stolen in 2007, but they were recast and the full set of eight was back in place by 2010, and a 2023 guide describes all eight.
It combines naturally with a visit to the Rudas Baths and the other sights on Gellért Hill.

docs.historyIntro: The Garden of Philosophers on Gellért Hill is a bronze sculpture group created by Nándor Wagner and given to Budapest by his widow. It was unveiled in October 2001 and has been damaged by thieves since.

historySections.heading: Wagner and the idea of a philosophical garden

children.text: Nándor Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and studied at the Budapest art academy. After the suppression of the 1956 revolution he was admitted to Sweden, where he worked in Lund, and later settled in Mashiko in Japan, where he met his wife, the art student Chiyo. According to Wikipedia he created the Garden of Philosophy there as a spiritual message for present and future generations and said it was not made to earn money. XpatLoop reports that he unveiled the first statue, Laozi, in 1977 and the others during the 1980s in Japan.

historySections.heading: A gift to Budapest, unveiled in 2001

children.text: Wagner died in 1997. Wikipedia says three sets were cast, for Japan, Hungary and the United States, and that the Hungarian set was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. The Hungarian magazine HVG describes the Budapest group as a gift from the sculptor's widow, and XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site. The Budapest sources describe eight life-size bronze figures facing a shared centre.

HVG reported in April 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma, were stolen from the hill, with damage estimated at about thirty million forints, according to the director of the Budapest Gallery. The article says that the previous October someone had removed five large bronze arc pieces that stood around the statues and had cut notches in the figures with a saw so that they could be broken off, but that an eyewitness interrupted them. It also notes that plaster moulds for recasting the statues exist in Japan. Közterkép says the three figures were recast in Japan in 2009 from moulds provided by Wagner's widow, and a Budapest city blog says the Budapest and Buda Castle district municipalities paid for the replacements, which completed the group again by 2010.

docs.name: Cave Church
docs.description: A church built into natural and artificial caves on the side of Gellért Hill, linked to the Pauline order. Founded after Hungarian pilgrims visited Lourdes in the 1920s, it was walled up under communism and reopened as that era ended; thermal water keeps the interior mild.

children.text: The Cave Church is built into the southeastern side of Gellért Hill, partly in a natural cave and partly in man-made chambers. Visit Buda Castle describes it as set in natural and artificial cave cavities and links it to the Pauline order. Visitors enter an outer cave and then follow a tunnel-like corridor to the deeper man-made church, where Masses and prayers are held. Visit Hungary says hot springs through the hill keep the interior at about 20 degrees Celsius all year.

The church grew out of a pilgrimage. According to We Love Budapest and Visit Hungary, Hungarian pilgrims who visited Lourdes in the 1920s proposed building a cave chapel inspired by the grotto there. We Love Budapest says it was consecrated in 1926, with the main altar in the outer cave and benches on the rock terrace outside; Visit Hungary gives 1931 as the year the construction was completed, so the sources differ. A legend recorded by We Love Budapest tells of a hermit named Iván who healed the sick with the bubbling waters at the cave's entrance.

In 1934 the Pauline order returned to Hungary after about 150 years in exile, bringing sixteen monks from Poland, according to We Love Budapest. Volunteers enlarged the cave with controlled explosions, and a neo-Romanesque monastery was built on the Danube side of the hill. During the Second World War the Pauline fathers sheltered civilians and refugees, sometimes disguising them as monks.

Under communist rule the monastic orders were abolished, the monks were forced out, the entrance was walled up with concrete and the cross above it was torn down. Sources differ on the date: We Love Budapest says the wall dates to 1960, Visit Hungary says only the 1950s, and Wikipedia and Aleteia say the cave was sealed in 1951. The wall was demolished as communist rule ended (Wikipedia gives 1989, Visit Hungary the 1990s), and the Pauline order restored the church. A section of the wall still stands on the right side of the entrance as a reminder.

Inside, the features named by the two sources include a bronze altar with a Polish eagle, a green pyrogranite altar made by the Zsolnay manufactory, a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, a statue of Saint Stephen at the entrance and a ceramic relief of Saint Gellért. A relic believed to be part of the tibia of Saint Paul the Hermit, the Pauline order's most important relic, is also kept here.
Good to know
This is an active place of worship where Masses and prayers are held, so be considerate of worshippers.
Check the official Pauline Cave Church page for current visiting arrangements and the times and languages of services.
Look at the right side of the entrance for the preserved section of the concrete wall from the communist era.
The church is set in the side of Gellért Hill, so it combines naturally with other sights on the hill.

historySections.heading: A church fashioned from the hillside

children.text: The Pauline order developed the cave church in the early twentieth century; the sources give 1926 for its consecration and 1931 for the completion of construction. The distinctive interior connects Christian worship with the natural rock of the hill above the Danube.

During the Second World War, monks provided refuge here to people in danger. The church was closed and sealed with a concrete wall in 1951, according to Wikipedia and Aleteia. The wall came down as communist rule ended, and sources date the reopening between 1989 and 1992.

docs.name: Trinity Square
docs.description: The main square of the Castle District, where Matthias Church, the Fisherman's Bastion and the Baroque Holy Trinity Column meet. The column was inaugurated in 1713 after a plague epidemic, and the square took its open shape only after the Ottoman rule ended in 1686.

children.text: Trinity Square, Szentháromság tér, is called the most significant square of the Buda Castle District by the district's heritage site. It lies where Tárnok, Szentháromság and Országház streets meet Hess András tér. Visit Buda Castle says the square, the richly decorated Holy Trinity Column, Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion together create a setting that invites photography and strolling.

It is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. The Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were joined only by a narrow lane, with a row of houses directly in front of the church. After the houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the area between church and Town Hall was opened up. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene, the town's defender, was completed in 1718.

The Holy Trinity Column is the square's centrepiece. The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a column against the plague, the foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb. The present column was built between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713. The sculptor was Fülöp Ungleich, and Antal Hörger made the reliefs and coats of arms.

A hexagonal obelisk carries statues of Saint Roch, Saint John, Saint Christopher, Saint Augustine, Saint Joseph and Saint Sebastian, with reliefs of King David praying in repentance, the horrors of the epidemic in the Castle and the column itself. The Holy Trinity group crowns the top. The original sculptures are now in the Kiscelli Museum in Óbuda, and replicas stand on the monument.

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church, the Jesuit buildings were cleared, and the former Ministry of Finance rose on the north side, opening the square towards the Fisherman's Bastion. The heritage site notes that the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.
Good to know
Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion stand on or beside the square; check their official sites for visiting conditions and tickets.
Walk around the Holy Trinity Column to find the six saints and the three reliefs described above.
The square is the heart of the Castle District, so it is a convenient base for nearby sights such as the Hospital in the Rock and the Vienna Gate.

docs.historyIntro: Trinity Square in the Buda Castle District took its open form only after the Ottoman occupation ended in 1686. Its Holy Trinity Column was inaugurated on 11 June 1713 as a thanks-offering after the plague.

historySections.heading: Houses before 1686 and the open square after

children.text: The Buda Castle District heritage site stresses that this is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. Before then, the Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were linked only by a narrow lane, and a row of houses stood directly in front of the church. When these houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the space between church and Town Hall was opened up. In the eighteenth century the parish church was run by the Jesuits, with a monastery on the north side and a three-storey seminary on the south, and a Baroque Town Hall stood at the corner of Tárnok and Szentháromság streets.

The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a Holy Trinity Column to protect the town from recurring plague, in gratitude for the end of an epidemic. The foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706 by the architect Ceresola Vereio and the stone carver Bernát Ferretti. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb, and the magistrate ordered a larger and more decorative replacement. The present column was erected between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713, made by Fülöp Ungleich with reliefs and coats of arms by Antal Hörger. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene was completed on the square in 1718.

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church. The northern side of the church was cleared, the former seminary to the south was demolished, and the south-eastern side of the square opened towards the Fisherman's Bastion. On the north side the former buildings were cleared and the former Ministry of Finance was built. The heritage site shows photographs of the Jesuit convent being demolished around 1900 and of Matthias Church in ruins in 1945. It says the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of town replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.

docs.name: St Elizabeth Church — Rózsák tere
docs.description: The Roman Catholic parish church of St Elizabeth of Hungary stands on Rózsák tere in Erzsébetváros. Designed by Imre Steindl, the architect of the Hungarian Parliament, it has two 76-metre neo-Gothic towers, a richly furnished interior and a statue of the saint in front, from which the Square of Roses takes its name.

children.text: St Elizabeth's Church stands on Rózsák tere, the Square of Roses, in Budapest's seventh district, Erzsébetváros. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, and the parish gives its address as Rózsák tere 8. Its two towers, each 76 metres high according to Visit Hungary, make it easy to spot above the surrounding streets.

The building exists because the first church was too small. The independent parish of Erzsébetváros was founded in 1881 and built a modest eclectic church to plans by Győző Czigler, but the district grew quickly. A building committee was formed in 1889, and on 28 July 1892 the neo-Gothic design of Imre Steindl was accepted. Steindl is best known for the Hungarian Parliament Building, and Visit Hungary notes that visitors can see similarities between the façades of the two buildings.

Construction began in September 1893. King Franz Joseph I laid the foundation stone in person on 20 October 1895, and the church was consecrated on Ascension Thursday, 16 May 1901. Visit Hungary gives the floor area as 1,800 square metres and the capacity as 2,560 people, which explains why the church feels so large for an ordinary parish.

Inside, the furnishings were mostly made by well-known Hungarian craftsmen. Visit Hungary lists the main altar, the pulpit, the baptismal font, a Wedding Altar, the Altar of Archangel Gabriel, a Requiem Altar and an altar of St Anthony of Padua. Bombs hit the church in the Second World War; the parish says the damage was repaired by 1949, and a full renovation of the exterior and interior ran from 1995, with the exterior finished by 2004 and the interior by 2007.

In front of the church stands a statue of St Elizabeth by József Damkó, placed there in 1932 on the 700th anniversary of the saint's death. The square is named after the roses that are her traditional attribute. Visit Hungary dates the statue and the renaming to 1931, so sources differ by a year. On 29 April 2023 Pope Francis met poor people, refugees and charity representatives in the church during his visit to Hungary.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, rozsaktere.hu, or ask the parish for Mass times and when visitors can enter the church.
Look at the façade and towers from the square and compare them with the Hungarian Parliament, also by Imre Steindl.
Read the story of the roses before you go: Visit Hungary explains the tradition that gave the square its name.
Remember that the first, smaller church of the parish still exists as a separate building, now used by the Greek Catholic Church.

docs.historyIntro: The church on Rózsák tere was built for a parish created in 1881 that quickly outgrew its first building. Its present neo-Gothic form dates from 1893 to 1901 and was designed by Imre Steindl.

historySections.heading: A parish and a church too small

children.text: The independent parish of Erzsébetváros was founded in 1881 by the Archbishop of Esztergom together with the city leadership. The faithful built a first, smaller church in eclectic style to plans by Győző Czigler, but it soon proved too small for the district. A church-building committee was founded in 1889, and on 28 July 1892 the neo-Gothic design of Imre Steindl was accepted; Samu Pecz and Sándor Aigner did not win the competition. When the new church was finished, the first one was handed over in 1905 to the Greek Catholic Church, and today it is the Church of the Protection of the Mother of God.

Digging of the foundations began on 23 July 1893, and construction began on 11 September 1893. King Franz Joseph I placed the foundation stone in person on 20 October 1895. The church was consecrated on Ascension Thursday, 16 May 1901. Steindl was also the designer of the Hungarian Parliament Building, and Visit Hungary notes that the façades of the two buildings show similarities. The same source gives the floor area as 1,800 square metres, the two towers as 76 metres high, and the capacity as 2,560 people.

historySections.heading: War damage, restoration and the Square of Roses

children.text: In the Second World War the church was hit by a bomb. Visit Hungary reports that the stained-glass windows were shattered, one arch was destroyed and the pedestal of the statue in the square was damaged; the parish says the restoration of the bomb damage was completed in 1949. A full renovation took place between 1995 and 2007, with the exterior completed by 2004 and the interior by 2007. In 1932 József Damkó's statue of St Elizabeth was placed in front of the church on the 700th anniversary of the saint's death, and the square was named Rózsák tere after the roses that are her attribute; Visit Hungary dates this to 1931. On 29 April 2023 Pope Francis met poor people, refugees and charity representatives in the church.

stories.title: The miracle of the roses

children.text: According to the traditional story told about Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, she was carrying bread to the hungry when someone stopped her and asked what she was hiding. Afraid she would be forbidden to continue her charity, she said she had roses. When she was made to show what she carried, the bread was said to have turned into roses.
This is a religious legend about charity, not a documented historical event. Visit Hungary notes that Elizabeth is often shown with a rose in her apron, and the roses give the square its name.

docs.name: St Anne's Church — Batthyány Square
docs.description: St Anne's is the Baroque parish church of Felsővízváros, the upper part of Buda's Víziváros, on Batthyány tér across the Danube from the Parliament. Begun in 1740 and completed in 1761 according to most sources, it is entered by steps down from the square, and the parish is known for its Jehmlich organ.

children.text: St Anne's Church is the Roman Catholic parish church of Felsővízváros, Upper Víziváros, at Batthyány tér 7 in Budapest's first district. English Wikipedia places Batthyány Square on the Buda bank directly opposite the Hungarian Parliament Building and describes the church as one of Budapest's most beautiful Baroque buildings. Its dedication is to Saint Anne.

The parish itself is older than the present building. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the parish, it was founded in 1390, destroyed by the Ottomans in 1540 and re-founded in 1687, with baptismal registers starting in 1693. In 1724 the Buda city council bought a property on the site and had it converted into a chapel and parish house with a tower. The Jesuits served the parish, and as the congregation grew, work on a new church began in 1740.

The builder first commissioned was Kristóf Hamon. After his death, Máté Nöpauer of Brno finished the church in 1761, according to the same article. Wikidata records both men as architects and gives 1740 to 1761 as the construction period, while a caption on Wikimedia Commons dates the church to 1762, so the exact completion year varies by source. The Jesuits ran the parish until the order was suppressed in 1773; priests of the Esztergom archdiocese then took over, and in 1787 Archbishop József Batthyány split the parish in two.

A detail worth noticing is the level of the square. A We Love Budapest article on the history of Batthyány tér explains that landfill added in 1870, during the regulation of the Danube, left some older entrances below street level, so you reach St Anne's by going down a staircase rather than up. The same article places the church on the south side of the square, beside the market hall.

Inside, the parish website highlights the church's Jehmlich organ, which it describes as of European renown and recently repaired. The parish also runs a choir. The congregation was mostly German-speaking until the late 18th century, according to the Hungarian Wikipedia article, and the parish remains active today.
Good to know
St Anne's is a working parish church. Check the parish website, felsovizivaros.plebania.hu, for Mass times and for when visitors can go in.
Look at the steps down from the square: they come from the 1870 landfill described in a We Love Budapest article on the square's history.
Combine the visit with Batthyány tér itself and the view across the Danube to the Parliament.
If you are interested in the organ, the parish site lists music events and concerts.
