docs.historyIntro: St Anne's parish in Buda's Víziváros dates back to the Middle Ages, but the Baroque church seen today was built between 1740 and 1761 under the Jesuits. It stands on Batthyány tér, facing the Danube.

children.text: According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the parish, it was founded in 1390, destroyed by the Ottomans in 1540 and re-founded in 1687, and baptismal registers began in 1693. In 1724 the Buda city council bought a property on the site and had the mason master Henrik János Fiedler convert it into a chapel and parish house with a tower. The article itself notes that some earlier dates for the property conflict with the parish's foundation dates, so the early history is not fully settled. The Jesuits served the parish in the 18th century.

Construction of the church began in 1740 to serve a growing congregation. The builder commissioned was Kristóf Hamon. After his death, Máté Nöpauer of Brno completed the church in 1761, according to the Hungarian Wikipedia article. Wikidata lists both men as architects and gives the construction period as 1740 to 1761, and English Wikipedia says the church was built by the Jesuits between 1740 and 1761. A caption on Wikimedia Commons dates the church to 1762, so sources differ on the exact year.

historySections.heading: Parish changes and the raised square

children.text: The Jesuits ran the parish until their order was suppressed in 1773. Priests of the Esztergom archdiocese then took over, many of them former Jesuits, until 1803. In 1787 Archbishop József Batthyány split the parish, and the southern part became a separate parish under the Capuchins. The congregation was mostly German-speaking until the late 18th century. In 1870 landfill added during the regulation of the Danube left older entrances on the square below street level, which is why St Anne's is reached by steps down. In 1950 the reorganisation of Budapest moved the northern part of the parish area into District II and the southern part into District I.

docs.name: Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption
docs.description: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption sits at the Pest end of Elisabeth Bridge, which was designed as an arch so the church could stay. A Gothic hall church that served as a mosque under Ottoman rule, it still has a mihrab, and Roman fort remains were found beneath it in 2014 to 2016.

children.text: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption, in Hungarian the Belvárosi Nagyboldogasszony Főplébánia, stands at Március 15. tér 2 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, and its own website has a section for visitors as well as for parishioners. The parish gives the church's age as more than 950 years, although the date of the first Christian church is unknown.

What you see today is mostly a Gothic hall church with three aisles and an ambulatory, built from around 1370 to 1490 under King Louis the Great and later kings. The south tower dates from the reign of Matthias. Visit Hungary records that Matthias was elected king here in 1458 and Ulászló in 1490, and that the church's earliest layers go back to Roman times: a renovation in 2014 to 2016 uncovered remains of the Roman fort Contra Aquincum.

During Ottoman rule, from 1541, the church was used as a mosque, and a mihrab, the prayer niche, still survives in the wall. After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686 only the Gothic sanctuary was usable. Archbishop György Széchényi paid for a vault and conservation work on the nave in the following decades. The result is a building where Gothic, Ottoman and Baroque elements sit side by side.

The church is closely tied to Pest's public life. Count István Széchenyi lay in state here in 1860, Franz Joseph took the royal oath in front of the church in 1867, though sources differ on whether this was before or after his coronation, and Visit Hungary says Franz Liszt was a frequent guest and occasional conductor between 1858 and 1871. When Elisabeth Bridge was planned in the 1890s, demolishing the church was considered; instead the bridge was designed as an arch so the church could stay.

Look for the sanctuary vault, painted by Imre Steindl in 1889, and the 14th-century Madonna fresco found behind the main altar in 2010. The church was heavily damaged in 1944, losing its high altar and a tower spire; the new spire was finished by 1957. The 2014 to 2016 excavations ended when Cardinal Péter Erdő blessed the church on 14 August 2016. The parish site also mentions lookouts in the Baroque towers, which opened to visitors in 2020.
Good to know
This is an active parish. The parish website, belvarosiplebania.hu, has the current visiting arrangements, Mass times, tower lookout information and a virtual tour.
Groups should register in advance with the parish, which lists a separate contact for guided visits.
Stand on the bridge side and look at how Elisabeth Bridge curves around the church, which the Visit Hungary history describes as deliberate.
Look for the mihrab inside, a reminder of the Ottoman period.

docs.historyIntro: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption has a history of more than 950 years, according to its parish. It has been a Gothic hall church, a mosque and a Baroque-restored parish church, and excavations in 2014 to 2016 found Roman fort remains beneath it.

historySections.heading: From the first church to the Gothic hall

children.text: The parish says the church was already standing in 1046, when Saint Gellért was martyred at the Pest ferry, though the date of the first Christian church is unknown; Visit Hungary instead says Gellért was buried here in 1046 before his remains were moved. The parish records that, according to a canon's chronicle, Louis of Thuringia likely became engaged to the future Saint Elizabeth of Hungary here in 1211. The Mongol invasion destroyed the original church in 1242. Under King Louis the Great, from about 1370, a new three-aisled Gothic hall church with an ambulatory was built, and the south tower dates from the reign of Matthias. Visit Hungary records that Matthias was elected king here in 1458 and Ulászló in 1490.

From 1541, under Ottoman rule, the church was used as a mosque, and a mihrab, the prayer niche, remains in the wall. The parish says it was one of the few churches in Pest that stayed in Catholic hands during the period. After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686, only the Gothic sanctuary was usable. Between 1686 and 1725, Archbishop György Széchényi funded a vault and conservation work on the nave. Over the following centuries the building was restored several times, usually by leading architects working in the style of their day, which is why Visit Hungary says its façade and interior mix styles from different eras.

historySections.heading: A civic landmark, war damage and excavation

children.text: Count István Széchenyi's lying-in-state was held here in 1860, and in 1867 Franz Joseph took the royal oath before the church. In 1889 Imre Steindl painted the sanctuary vault. In the 1890s demolition was considered when Elisabeth Bridge was planned, but the bridge was designed as an arch so the church could stay. Bombing in 1944 damaged the vaults, roof and walls, destroyed the high altar and one tower spire; the new spire was finished by 1957. In 2010 a 14th-century Madonna fresco was uncovered behind the main altar, and in 2014 to 2016 excavations found remains of the Roman fort Contra Aquincum. Cardinal Erdő blessed the church on 14 August 2016.

stories.title: An engagement in 1211

children.text: The parish's history says that, according to a canon's chronicle, Louis of Thuringia likely became engaged to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary in this church in 1211. Visit Hungary similarly states that the engagement of the four-year-old Elisabeth was held here.
The parish itself hedges the claim with the word likely, so it is best read as a recorded tradition from a chronicle rather than a certain fact.

docs.name: Deák Square Lutheran Church
docs.description: A plain neoclassical Lutheran church at Deák Ferenc tér 4, designed by Mihály Pollack and built between 1799 and 1808, with a Doric-pilastered façade rebuilt by József Hild in 1856. It is an active Lutheran parish church and stands next to the Evangelical National Museum.

children.text: The Deák Square Lutheran Church, in Hungarian the Deák téri evangélikus templom, stands at Deák Ferenc tér 4 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Lutheran, or Evangelical, parish church and still hosts services and concerts. A We Love Budapest listing calls it the city's oldest and largest Protestant church, and notes that the Evangelical National Museum operates next to it.

The architect was Mihály Pollack, one of the main builders of neoclassical Pest. A We Love Budapest article on Pollack says he designed the church in the late 1790s with master builder János Krausz and took over the project after Krausz died. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period as 1799 to 1808. The building was not used as a church at once: from July 1809 to spring 1811 it served as a military clothing store, and it was consecrated at Pentecost in 1811.

The exterior is deliberately plain. The façade has four Doric pilasters, a cornice with triglyphs and metopes, and a triangular pediment, under a large convex metal roof. József Hild rebuilt the main façade in 1856. Pollack's design was compact and unadorned, which the We Love Budapest article says sparked debate at a time when late Baroque still shaped architecture.

Inside is a single rectangular nave with a double gallery, completed in 1820. Pollack designed the altar, which carries a painting by Ferenc Lochbichler based on Raphael's Transfiguration, and Lőrinc Dunaiszky made the pulpit and the red marble baptismal font. The church was changed over time: in 1875 the classicist tower was removed for structural reasons and the barrel vault was replaced with a coffered ceiling.

In the courtyard, two bronze reliefs commemorate the 500th anniversary of Luther's birth and the 300th anniversary of Bach's birth. A marble plaque on the façade records that Lajos Kossuth had his sons baptised here. The church also sheltered many people during the great flood of 1838.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, deakter.hu, for services, music events and when visitors can enter.
The Evangelical National Museum is next door but is a separate institution; check its own site for opening times and tickets.
Walk around to the courtyard side to see the bronze reliefs of Luther and Bach mentioned in the Hungarian Wikipedia article.
Compare the plain façade with the more ornate churches elsewhere in the city centre.

historySections.heading: Building a Lutheran church in Pest

children.text: Mihály Pollack designed the church in the late 1790s, working with master builder János Krausz and taking over the project after Krausz died, according to a We Love Budapest article on Pollack. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period as 1799 to 1808. The church was finished before it could be used for worship: from July 1809 to spring 1811 it served as a military clothing store. It was consecrated at Pentecost in 1811, and the double gallery was completed in 1820. Pollack also designed the altar, which carries a painting by Ferenc Lochbichler after Raphael's Transfiguration.

historySections.heading: Floods, new façade and altered interior

children.text: During the great flood of 1838 the church sheltered many people. József Hild rebuilt the main façade in 1856, giving it four Doric pilasters, a triglyph and metope cornice and a triangular pediment; Károly Benkó directed construction work from 1867. The church was damaged in a bombardment associated with Hentzi, as Hungarian Wikipedia puts it; the article gives no year. In 1875 the classicist tower was removed for structural reasons, and the barrel vault was replaced with a coffered ceiling.

Hungarian Wikipedia says the church was also damaged in the Second World War and during the construction of the M2 metro line. A small computer-controlled chime was installed around 2000, and the most recent exterior renovation mentioned in the article took place in 2003. In the courtyard two bronze reliefs commemorate the 500th anniversary of Luther's birth and the 300th anniversary of Bach's birth, and the Evangelical National Museum operates next to the church.

docs.name: Saint Emeric Cistercian Church
docs.description: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church at Villányi út 25 is a neo-Baroque parish church consecrated in 1938 and designed by Gyula Wälder. Its twin towers face Feneketlen Lake in Szentimreváros, and it stands beside the Cistercian school; the parish has again been run by the order since 1989.

children.text: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church, in Hungarian the Budai ciszterci Szent Imre-templom, stands at Villányi út 25 in Szentimreváros, part of Budapest's eleventh district, Újbuda. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, dedicated to Saint Emeric, and the parish has again been run by the Cistercians since 1989. The parish office is at Himfy utca 9.

The church was designed by the architect and university professor Gyula Wälder for the Cistercian order. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its style as neo-Baroque and says it was built in 1938, the jubilee year of Saint Emeric, and consecrated that year by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. Wikidata gives the date as 6 November 1938. It belongs to a larger complex: the Cistercians settled in Buda in 1912, and the Feneketlen Lake article says Wälder planned a church, monastery, gymnasium and boarding school near the lake, with construction beginning in 1927.

The site relates closely to the lake. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, Feneketlen Lake began as a clay pit worked for a brickworks, and its origin is usually dated to 1877; the brickworks closed in 1889. When the surrounding park was landscaped in 1958 to 1960, the designer Mihály Mőcsényi aimed to make the church's twin towers visible as a reflection on the water, turning that view into a landmark of the district. The church and the Budai Ciszterci Szent Imre Gimnázium stand on the north side of the lake, across Villányi út.

Hungarian Wikipedia lists a main altar with a painting, a pulpit, side altars, a painted coffered ceiling, porcelain Stations of the Cross, a statue of Mary and a baptismal chapel with the Batthyány-Strattmann baptistery. The interior was renovated in 1972 to 1975 and the exterior in 1976 to 1979, and the façade and roof were reconstructed in 2019 to 2020, when the towers also received clocks. The parish website lists a sanctuary renovation project for 2026.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, szentimre.hu, for Mass times, visiting arrangements and the current renovation work on the sanctuary.
Walk to the lake first and look back across the water at the twin towers, the view the park designer planned.
Feneketlen Lake is a short walk away; Hungarian Wikipedia describes the park around it, with an open-air stage, a running track and sculptures.
The church is beside an active Cistercian school, so show consideration for pupils in the surrounding streets.

docs.name: Saint Margaret Parish Church — Lehel Square
docs.description: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, popularly the Lehel tér church, is a neo-Romanesque parish church in Újlipótváros designed by István Möller and modelled on the Zsámbék church ruin. Built from 1931 to 1933, it has frescoes by Henrik Heintz and stained glass by Miksa Róth.

children.text: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, the Church of Saint Margaret of the House of Árpád, is popularly known as the Lehel téri templom, the Lehel Square church. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in Budapest's thirteenth district. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its address as Váci út 34, 1132 Budapest, in the Újlipótváros neighbourhood, and says it stands on Szent Margit tér, a small square separated from Lehel tér on 29 May 2019.

The parish grew out of a Chapel Association founded in 1919. A parish community formed in 1920 under Gyula Zaymus, and in 1923 it became an independent parish. The church was built between 1931 and 1933 to plans by István Möller, who based them on the ruins of the church at Zsámbék; the master builder was Ferenc Wihart. It was consecrated on 15 October 1933 by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. The total cost was about one million pengő, which the community paid off through donations.

The style is neo-Romanesque, and Hungarian Wikipedia links the thick walls, square towers and portal to the medieval atmosphere of the Zsámbék model. The interior has frescoes by Henrik Heintz, statues by György Nemes Ősz, and stained glass and a rose window by Miksa Róth. A planned altarpiece by Ferenc Chiovini, St Stephen's Missionary Journey, was never completed.

The church took the name Árpád-házi Szent Margit in 1944, after the canonisation of Margaret; before that it was dedicated to Blessed Margaret. It suffered minor damage in the Second World War and was repaired with donations. In 1975 a new liturgical space was designed by Gyula Bárdos, and from 1988 to 1994 the roof, stained glass and interior painting were renovated.

The church sits at the edge of a busy junction. Hungarian Wikipedia describes the neighbouring Lehel Csarnok market hall, built in 2002 to a design by László Rajk Jr. and nicknamed the Kofahajó, on the site of the old Lehel market. The article on Lehel tér lists the M3 metro, which has a Lehel tér station.
Good to know
This is a working parish church. Check with the parish for current Mass times and when visitors can enter.
Maps may show the church under either Lehel tér or Szent Margit tér, and the street address is Váci út 34.
Look at the rose window and stained glass by Miksa Róth, and the frescoes by Henrik Heintz.
The Lehel Csarnok market hall next to the church is a short walk away.

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records that the Chapel Association was founded in 1919 and that a parish community, Lipótváros II, was formed in 1920 under Gyula Zaymus. In 1923 it became an independent parish, and part of Terézváros was attached to it.

István Möller designed the church, basing his plans on the ruins of the church at Zsámbék, and the master builder Ferenc Wihart carried out the work. Construction took place between 1931 and 1933, and Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi consecrated the church on 15 October 1933. The floor area is 918 square metres. The total cost was about one million pengő, which the community paid off through donations. The interior frescoes are by Henrik Heintz, the statues by György Nemes Ősz, and the stained glass and rose window by Miksa Róth.

historySections.heading: A new name, war damage and renovation

children.text: The church took the name Árpád-házi Szent Margit in 1944, after the canonisation of Margaret; it had previously been called Árpád-házi Boldog Margit. In the Second World War it suffered minor damage, which was repaired with donations from believers. In 1975 a new liturgical space was designed by Gyula Bárdos, and between 1988 and 1994 the roof, stained glass, interior painting and electrical wiring were renovated. On 29 May 2019 Szent Margit tér was separated from Lehel tér, and the church now stands on that square.

docs.name: Saint Ladislaus Church — Kőbánya
docs.description: Ödön Lechner's Kőbánya church mixes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk motifs. Built from 1894 to 1899 and consecrated in 1900, it has Zsolnay tiles and altars, and among Budapest churches only St Stephen's Basilica is taller than its 83-metre tower.

children.text: The Kőbánya Saint Ladislaus Church, in Hungarian the Kőbányai Szent László-templom, stands at Szent László tér 25 in Budapest's tenth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, owned by the Kőbánya local government according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Budapest City Archives describe it as a church by Ödön Lechner, built on the site of a former rowing lake. Lechner's father owned a brick factory on Maglódi Street, and the archive notes that Lechner lived in Kőbánya at the time.

The commission was complicated. According to the City Archives, Lechner received the commission in 1891, and his first design, in an unusual Byzantine style with Eastern ornament, had to be revised at the client's request. A second version was also rejected. A third, eclectic and Secessionist, was approved, but Lechner was removed from the project when he judged the deadline unachievable; about a hundred artists then petitioned that the interior should be by the same architect as the exterior. Hungarian Wikipedia counts the designs differently and says Lechner prepared the final design in September 1893.

Construction ran from 1894 to 1899. The cross was blessed on 12 August 1897, and the faithful took possession of the church on 2 April 1899. It was consecrated in June 1900; Hungarian Wikipedia's text gives 27 June, St Ladislaus's day, while its infobox says 28 June. Lechner's style combines Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk elements. The tower is 83 metres high, and in Budapest only St Stephen's Basilica is taller.

Look for the colourful Zsolnay roof tiles outside and the Zsolnay majolica altars and pulpit inside. One side altar was donated by the brewer Antal Dreher, and the stained glass and mosaics are attributed to the workshop of Miksa Róth. The Second World War damaged the building badly, with the original stained glass destroyed, and the Hussar tower burned in 1957.

A long restoration followed. Hungarian Wikipedia dates the complete renovation to 1974 to 1994, while a We Love Budapest article says major reconstruction began in the 1980s and ended in 2001, so sources differ. A statue of Saint Ladislaus by Károly Antal stands in front of the church.
Good to know
This is an active parish. Check the parish website, szentlaszlo.net, for Mass times and visiting arrangements before you go.
Kőbánya is away from the central tourist area, so plan your route and travel time in advance with the city's public transport planner.
Look up at the roof tiles and the tower; the Zsolnay ceramics are the church's most distinctive features.
Read the Budapest City Archives article on the church's design history, which explains why Lechner's plans changed.

docs.historyIntro: The Kőbánya church was designed by Ödön Lechner after a difficult commission and built between 1894 and 1899. It was consecrated in 1900 and is today owned by the Kőbánya local government.

children.text: According to the Budapest City Archives, Ödön Lechner received the commission for a parish church in 1891, on the site of a former rowing lake. His first design, in an unusual Byzantine style with Eastern ornament, had to be revised at the client's request, and the second version was also rejected even though it followed the requested pointed-arch form. The third, eclectic and Secessionist, was approved, but Lechner was removed from the project because he judged the deadline unachievable. Hungarian Wikipedia gives a different account: it says Elek Barcza was first commissioned, that Lechner took over, and that his final, fifth design dates from September 1893.

Construction ran from 1894 to 1899, with Lechner as site supervisor and János Szabó as contractor according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The cross was blessed on 12 August 1897, and the faithful took possession of the church on 2 April 1899. About a hundred artists petitioned the council that the interior should be designed by the same architect as the exterior; the interior works went to Ottó Tandor, who designed the altars, pulpit and baptismal font. The church was consecrated in June 1900; the article's text gives 27 June, the feast of Saint Ladislaus, while its infobox gives 28 June.

The building suffered serious damage in the siege of Budapest in the Second World War. Visitor information from We Love Budapest says the Zsolnay roof and towers were damaged and that stained glass by Miksa Róth was destroyed and later recreated by Tibor Bráda from the original plans. In 1957 the Hussar tower burned down. Hungarian Wikipedia says a complete renovation began in 1974 and ended in 1994, and that the church regained protected monument status in 1991; We Love Budapest says major reconstruction began in the 1980s and finished in 2001. A proposal to rename Kőbánya Szentlászlóváros, made around the time northern Transylvania returned to Hungary, was never carried out.

stories.title: Lechner's changing designs

children.text: The Budapest City Archives describe how Lechner's proposals were revised more than once. His first design was Byzantine in character, the second was rejected although it was pointed-arch in form, and a third, eclectic and Secessionist design was approved. The archive states that Lechner was then removed from the project over the deadline, and that about a hundred artists petitioned for the interior to be designed by the same architect as the exterior.
Hungarian Wikipedia counts the designs differently, so sources do not agree on the exact sequence.

docs.name: Óbuda Synagogue
docs.description: The Óbuda Synagogue at Lajos utca 163 is a neoclassical synagogue consecrated in 1821 and designed by András Landherr. After decades as a warehouse and television studio it was rededicated in 2010 and is again an active Orthodox prayer house maintained by EMIH, a Chabad-linked community.

children.text: The Óbuda Synagogue, in Hungarian the Óbudai zsinagóga, stands at Lajos utca 163 in Óbuda, Budapest's third district. Its website calls it the capital's oldest functioning Jewish prayer house, and says it is maintained by the EMIH, the Unified Hungarian Israelite Community. The congregation is Orthodox, and Hungarian Wikipedia says Chief Rabbi Slomó Köves has led it since 2010. It is a living place of worship with a weekly schedule of prayer and study.

Jews resettled in Óbuda in the early 18th century under the protection of the Zichy family. The synagogue's history page says that by 1727 they could hold public worship, and that in 1738 construction began on the first synagogue. A Baroque synagogue by Máté Nöpauer followed in 1767 to 1769, but its walls cracked because of poor foundations and unstable soil. In 1817 the Buda Building Committee chose to rebuild it while keeping most of the walls.

The present building is the result. Hungarian Wikipedia credits András Landherr with the design, work began around 1820, and the synagogue was consecrated on 20 July 1821. It received a new south façade with a columned porch of six Corinthian columns and a tympanum inscribed with a Hebrew verse from 1 Kings. The main hall has 662 fixed seats, 364 for men and 298 for women, and a wooden Torah reading table in the centre surrounded by four Empire-style obelisks.

The 20th century was hard on the building. About 3,000 Óbuda Jews died in the Holocaust, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and from the 1960s the building was sold and used in turn as a museum, a warehouse and a television studio; Magyar Televízió used it as Studio 5 from 1978. In spring 2010 EMIH took it over, and it was rededicated on 5 September 2010. Restoration work included repainting about 25,000 small Stars of David on the vaults, and the restored synagogue was formally reopened on 12 April 2016.
Good to know
This is an active synagogue and prayer house. Check obudaizsinagoga.hu for current visiting arrangements, services and events before you go.
Respect the prayer schedule: the site lists daily services and a Shabbat programme, so visits should be arranged around them.
Across the street, at the corner of Lajos utca and Zichy utca, a We Love Budapest article places the oldest house in the third district, now an exhibition space of Budapest Galéria.
Pair the visit with a walk around Óbuda; English Wikipedia says that when the synagogue was built, Óbuda's was the largest Jewish community in Hungary.

docs.historyIntro: The Óbuda Synagogue was consecrated in 1821 as a rebuilding of an earlier Baroque synagogue. From the 1960s it was sold and used as a museum, warehouse and television studio, and it was rededicated for worship in 2010.

historySections.heading: A Jewish community under Zichy protection

children.text: Jews settled in Óbuda in the early 18th century, mainly from Moravia; a 1712 census lists 24 families, or 88 people. They lived under the protection of the Zichy family, and by 1727, according to the synagogue's history page, they could hold public worship, acquire property and run their own courts in exchange for a protection payment. By 1737 the community had 43 families, and in 1738 construction began on the first synagogue, which Countess Zichy ordered enlarged in 1746. A Baroque synagogue by Máté Nöpauer followed in 1767 to 1769, but its walls cracked because of poor foundations and unstable soil.

In 1817 the Buda Building Committee assessed the cracked synagogue and chose to rebuild it while keeping most of the walls. Architect András Landherr began work around 1820. The building received a new south façade, a columned porch and a new roof, and was consecrated on 20 July 1821. The main hall has 662 fixed seats, 364 for men and 298 for women. In 1900 the synagogue was renovated by architect Gyula Ullmann with Art Nouveau elements, and electric lighting was installed.

historySections.heading: Deportation, a studio and the return of worship

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records about 3,600 members in 1944, down from 5,500 in 1929, and says around 3,000 Óbuda Jews died in the Holocaust. After repairs in 1946 and 1947, the Jewish school was closed by the state in 1948, the Óbuda congregation merged into the Budapest congregation in 1949, and the building was listed as a protected monument in 1957. From the 1960s the building was sold and used as a museum, a warehouse and, from 1978, a Magyar Televízió studio. In spring 2010 EMIH took over the building, which was rededicated on 5 September 2010 and reopened for worship on 8 September. The restored synagogue was formally reopened on 12 April 2016.

stories.title: The flood of 1838

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records that in the great flood of 1838 the water reached the Ark in the Óbuda Synagogue, and that members of the community rowed in to rescue the Torah scrolls.

docs.name: Serbian Orthodox Church — Downtown Pest
docs.description: The Church of Saint George on Szerb utca is the Serbian Orthodox parish church of central Pest and, according to Wikipedia, the only Serbian Orthodox church in the capital today. Its Baroque building dates from 1733, its tower from 1752, and its garden wall holds old Serbian gravestones.

children.text: The Serbian Orthodox Church of Saint George stands at Szerb utca 4, less than a hundred metres from Váci utca in the inner city. Its full Hungarian name is Szent György nagyvértanú szerb ortodox templom, and it belongs to the Eparchy of Buda of the Serbian Orthodox Church. English Wikipedia describes it as the only Serbian Orthodox church in the Hungarian capital today, and it is a protected monument. The street takes its name from the community: Szerb utca means Serbian Street.

Serbian worship in Pest is older than the present building. A Serbian place of worship stood here during the Ottoman period, and some sources suggest a church on the site even before 1526. After Habsburg forces took the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. The authorities permitted a new one in 1695, which Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated in 1698. The Baroque church seen today was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg, and the bell tower followed in 1752. Archaeological research in 1959 confirmed that it stands on the site of an older church.

Inside, the church follows the traditional layout of an Orthodox church, and Hungarian Wikipedia notes a wooden railing between the women's area and the men's area, which sits one step lower. The iconostasis seen today dates from 1850. The original, by Stefan Tenecki, was damaged in the flood of 1838 and was replaced by a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist.

The surroundings are part of the character of the place. A Baroque garden is enclosed by a stone wall, and the gravestones of Serbs who were buried in Pest are built into it. A Copf-style gate on Szerb utca dates from 1776, and at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca a ceramic image of Saint George slaying the dragon sits in a niche in the wall.

The church also records how small the community's footprint became. The larger Church of Saint Demetrius, damaged in the Second World War, was demolished in 1949, which left this church as the city's only Serbian place of worship. It is still in active use: in 2021 the parish celebrated its patron saint with a hierarchal liturgy led by Bishop Lukijan of Buda, a procession around the church along Szerb utca and a programme in the courtyard.
Good to know
This is a working Serbian Orthodox church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting, and do not assume the interior or garden is open to visitors.
It is under a hundred metres from Váci utca, so it fits easily into a walk through the inner city.
From the street, look for the ceramic image of Saint George at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca and for the tower added in 1752.

docs.historyIntro: The Serbian Church of Saint George in central Pest was built in 1733 on the site of an older Serbian place of worship. It is the surviving centre of a Serbian community that settled in Pest after the Ottoman period.

historySections.heading: Serbs in Pest under Ottoman and Habsburg rule

children.text: English Wikipedia records that a Serbian place of worship stood on the site during Ottoman rule, and that some sources suggest a church existed even before the Battle of Mohács in 1526. A source from 1655 records a separate cemetery beside the Kecskemét Gate, and between 1660 and 1664 the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi noted that the Serbs of Pest had their own church. After Habsburg forces captured the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. A new church was permitted in 1695, and Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated it in 1698. Hungarian Wikipedia says the new church of 1695 to 1698 stood on the foundations of a medieval church.

A project for a new Baroque church was prepared in 1731, and Hungarian Wikipedia says the earlier church was demolished that year. The present church was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg. The Baroque bell tower was completed in 1752, when the main facade also reached its present form. The Copf-style gate on Szerb utca was made in 1776. The original iconostasis was by Stefan Tenecki; after the flood of 1838 damaged it, a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist was installed in 1850.

historySections.heading: Change and survival in the twentieth century

children.text: In 1932 the street level was raised and a new wrought-iron gate was made, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. After the Second World War the community's more significant church, Saint Demetrius, was demolished in 1949 following war damage, which left the church on Szerb utca as the only Serbian place of worship in the city. In 1959 archaeological research confirmed that the present building stands on the site of an older church. The church is protected by the Hungarian National Office for Cultural Heritage and remains in use by the Eparchy of Buda.

docs.name: Queen of Heavens Church — Újpest
docs.description: The Queen of Heavens Church, or Egek Királynéja-templom, is the main Roman Catholic parish church of Újpest. Built between 1875 and 1881 to plans by József Kauser in a neo-Gothic style, it stands on Szent István tér, the main square of a town founded only in 1840.

children.text: The Queen of Heavens Church, in Hungarian Egek Királynéja-templom, stands at Szent István tér 13 on the main square of the former town of Újpest, today Budapest's 4th district. It is the district's main Roman Catholic parish church. Since 1993 the parish has belonged to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest; before that it was part of the Diocese of Vác.

Újpest is a young town by Budapest standards. It was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Its Catholics were first a filial of Dunakeszi and later attached to the parish of Fót, until Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the congregation an independent parish in February 1870. A parish house and Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875 with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He served until his death in 1905.

The church was built between 1875 and 1881 in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by the architect József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Hungarian Wikipedia notes that two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure.

The bells carry some of the church's recorded history. There were originally five, and the middle bell, which weighed 310 kilograms, was lost in the Second World War; its place in the bell frame remains empty. Four bells hang in the tower today. The largest, named for King Saint Stephen, weighs 1,010 kilograms and was cast in 1924 by Ferenc Walser. The other three were cast in 1888 by Walser as well.

The square around the church tells the story of the town. It was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928, and it became Újpest's main square after the town hall opened in 1900. A Reformed church built in 1878 stands on one side, and the town hall and the Újpest market are also on the square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check access and service times with the parish rather than assuming the interior is open to visitors.
Szent István tér also holds the Reformed church of 1878, the town hall by Henrik Bőhm and Ármin Hegedűs, and the Újpest market, so the square is worth a short walk in itself.
Újpest lies outside the central districts, so plan the journey with the public transport journey planner before you set out.

historySections.heading: A new town and its parish

children.text: Újpest was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Until 1845 its Catholics were a filial of Dunakeszi, and then they were attached to the parish of Fót. In February 1870 Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the Újpest congregation an independent parish. A parish house and a Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875, with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He held the post until his death in 1905.

The church was built between 1875 and 1881, in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure. Ferenc Walser cast the bells, three in 1888 and the largest, dedicated to King Saint Stephen, in 1924. A fifth, middle bell was lost in the Second World War.

The square in front of the church was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928. It became the main square of Újpest after the town hall opened in 1900, and a Reformed church, built in 1878, stands on the same square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950, and in 1993 the parish passed from the Diocese of Vác to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest.

docs.name: Holy Family Church — Terézváros
docs.description: The neo-Gothic Holy Family Church at Szondi utca 67 was built in 1930 and 1931 for a fast-growing Terézváros. Heavily damaged on New Year's Day 1945, it was rebuilt and reconsecrated in 1948, and its high altar was later clad in marble paid for by the composer Zoltán Kodály.

children.text: The Holy Family Church, Szent Család-templom in Hungarian, stands at Szondi utca 67 in Terézváros, Budapest's 6th district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest. Unlike the older churches of central Pest, it is a twentieth-century building: Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew sharply between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church here.

The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930 and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the church's builder. Hungarian Wikipedia calls the style neo-Gothic. The Budapest library's description is more detailed: an eclectic design based on medieval church architecture, with Romanesque-style elements on the facade and English Gothic details, such as a large Tudor-arched window between the towers.

On 1 January 1945 the church was severely damaged. Sources differ on the cause, one speaking of a bomb and another of a chained explosive, but they agree that the furnishings were lost, including the altars, pulpit and confessionals, and that the organ was partly destroyed. Two things survived: the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church on 18 May 1948.

Later additions give the interior its present character. In 1955 the composer Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and a statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985. A columbarium for urns was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996, the building was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003, and the organ was rebuilt in 2006.
Good to know
This is a working parish church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
The columbarium in the basement and courtyard is part of the site, so ask the parish which areas are open to visitors.
From the street, look for the large Tudor-arched window between the two towers, which the library description picks out as an English Gothic detail.

docs.historyIntro: The Holy Family Church was built in 1930 and 1931, destroyed in large part on New Year's Day 1945 and rebuilt by 1948. Its history is the story of a district church that was built, lost its furnishings and was gradually refitted.

historySections.heading: A church for the interwar city

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew significantly between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church at Szondi utca 67. The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930, and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the builder of the church.

On 1 January 1945, during the Second World War, the church was struck and severely damaged. Hungarian Wikipedia speaks of a bomb, and the Budapest library's description of a chained explosive. The altars, pulpit, confessionals and lighting were destroyed, and the organ was partly destroyed. Only the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux survived. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and on 18 May 1948 Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church.

In 1955 Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and insulation work was carried out in the 1970s. A statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985, and a columbarium was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996. The church was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003 and the organ was restored in 2006.

docs.name: Armenian Catholic Church — Újbuda
docs.description: The Armenian Catholic church at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros serves Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholic community and is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s, and the parish centre was renovated with state support in 2022.

children.text: The Armenian Catholic church stands at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros, in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. Its Hungarian name is Fogolykiváltó Boldogasszony és Világosító Szent Gergely-templom, and it is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It follows the Armenian rite and belongs to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, according to GCatholic. Wikimedia Commons describes it as one wing of the parish building rather than a freestanding church.

A study published by the Budapest City Archives explains how the community came to be here. Most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. After the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, many Hungarian Armenians moved to Hungary, and the community sought its own church and its own priest. For a very long time Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.

The Orlay utca site came later. According to the same study, in the 1960s the Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár gave up his family's properties and collected donations among Armenians in Hungary and Western Europe. With the money he bought a villa on Orlay utca, where a pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. The study quotes a community member who said that people went to the Orlay utca chapel as if to their first family.

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed it, that the Hungarian government funded the work through the Hungary Helps Program, and that the centre is to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.
Good to know
This is a working Armenian Catholic parish, not a conventional sightseeing stop. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
Orlay utca is in Szentimreváros in the 11th district, so it fits a visit to that part of Újbuda.
The Budapest City Archives study shows a wrought-iron gate on Orlay utca, but do not assume the chapel or the parish centre is open to visitors.

docs.historyIntro: The Armenian Catholic church on Orlay utca grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s for Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholics. Its history is tied to the Transylvanian Armenians who settled in the capital in the twentieth century.

historySections.heading: A community that settled in Budapest

children.text: According to a study by the Budapest City Archives, most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. They arrived in a first wave among the civil servants of the period after 1850, and in a second wave after the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, when many Hungarian Armenians who had lost their livelihoods moved to Hungary. The community then wanted its own church and its own priest. For a very long time, however, different Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.

The same study says that in the 1960s the Armenian Catholic Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár started a fundraising effort, giving up his family's properties and collecting donations among Armenians in Hungary and in Western Europe. He succeeded in buying a villa on Orlay utca, where an Armenian Catholic pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. Interviews in the study describe the Orlay utca chapel as a place where people felt at home, as if it were their first family.

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre in Budapest was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed the premises and that the Hungarian government paid for the renovation through the Hungary Helps Program. The renovated section is intended to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.

docs.name: Pozsonyi Road Reformed Church
docs.description: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church, known as the Hálaadás or Thanksgiving church, stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros. Built between 1936 and 1940 to designs by Imre Tóth and Jenő Halászy, it has a classical portico, a separate tower and Bauhaus-influenced interiors, and its basement once sheltered people in hiding.

children.text: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros, in Budapest's 13th district, between Pozsonyi út, Garam utca, Gogol utca and the Újpesti rakpart. The parish describes the site as just north of Margaret Bridge, facing Margaret Island. It is a Reformed, or Calvinist, church, known as the Hálaadás temploma, the Church of Thanksgiving.

The congregation began in a first meeting house on Tutaj utca, consecrated in 1926, and outgrew it. The Reformed Church received the new plot from the municipality; it was marshy ground that had to be taken into account in the building. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937.

Sources describe the design in different words. WeLoveBudapest calls the church neoclassical, with Bauhaus features in the interior and the ancillary buildings, unusual aisle windows, a separate bell tower and Greek-style columns. The parish describes a classical building with a full-width portico, a central cross and a tall separate tower. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the style as Bauhaus. Construction took about four years, with stoppages caused by money shortages and the approaching war. Sulfurous water surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, and the tower was built on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940.

The church was badly damaged in 1944, when it stood between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until the building was restored in 1972. During the later war years the basement sheltered deserters, resistance members and mainly Jewish families, and pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the construction, was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.

Today the church is used for services, religious classes and Bible lessons, and WeLoveBudapest reports a basement theatre hall seating more than two hundred people. Hungarian Wikipedia says the crypt, with a stage and event hall, is rented out for various events.
Good to know
The parish website shows a liturgical calendar but no visiting hours, so check access and service times with the parish before going.
The church faces Margaret Island and stands just north of Margaret Bridge, which makes it easy to combine with a walk by the Danube.
The basement theatre hosts performances, so ask the parish whether anything is on during your visit.

docs.historyIntro: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church was built between 1936 and 1940 for a congregation that had outgrown its first meeting house. Its history includes severe war damage in 1944 and a rescue effort in its basement.

historySections.heading: From Tutaj utca to a design competition

children.text: The Reformed congregation first met at the corner of Tutaj utca and Visegrádi utca, and the parish website says its first permanent meeting house on Tutaj utca was consecrated in 1926. It outgrew that site and received a new plot from the municipality, on marshy ground. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Lajos Simkovics, a civil engineer, supervised the works.

Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937, with Bishop László Ravasz recorded by the parish as laying it. The ground was raised with soil and more than three hundred piles were driven. Construction took about four years because of stoppages caused by the approaching war, shortages of money and sulfurous water that surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, especially of the tower, which stands on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940, before the Second World War broke out.

The church came through most of the war largely unscathed but was severely damaged in 1944, standing between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until 1972, when the building was restored. After the war the basement served as a warehouse for about fifty years and was later returned to use as a theatre. Parish information says repairs were completed by 1972, and a destroyed facade pillar was restored for the church's fiftieth anniversary.

stories.title: Hiding in the basement

children.text: WeLoveBudapest reports that during the later war years the basement of the church sheltered deserters, wanted resistance members and mainly Jewish families who had false papers. Pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the church's construction, and members of his congregation were involved.

According to the article, the basement had its own toilet, so those hiding did not need to come up, they received food, and a child was born there. No one was discovered by the Germans, the Arrow Cross or the Soviets. Bereczky received the Righteous Among the Nations award.

docs.name: Rumbach Street Synagogue
docs.description: Rumbach Street Synagogue, designed by Otto Wagner and consecrated in 1872, is an octagonal Moorish Revival synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of Erzsébetváros. After decades of decay it was restored and reopened in 2021, and, according to its official site, it is still a synagogue that also hosts concerts and events and serves as an exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives.

children.text: Rumbach Street Synagogue stands at Rumbach Sebestyén utca 11–13 in Erzsébetváros, in the area of the former Pest ghetto. Hungarian Wikipedia gives it a second name, the Little Synagogue, to tell it apart from the Dohány Street Synagogue. It was built for traditionalist Jews of the Status Quo Ante community, the congregation formed around the 1869 schism in Hungarian Jewry, although the building's official site says the Neolog community commissioned it with fittings suited to traditional liturgy. The Center for Jewish Art records Otto Wagner, then an emerging Viennese architect, as its designer.

Sources give slightly different dates for the start of construction: English Wikipedia says 1869, and Hungarian Wikipedia says 1 May 1870. The work was paid for by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit followed in May 1873. The building is of brick, in a neo-Moorish style, and the prayer hall has an octagonal plan.

The facade is symmetrical. Its two octagonal side sections are said to represent the biblical pillars Jachin and Boaz, and, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, they are topped with lotus-flower carvings and continue in small domed towers that resemble minarets. Sources describe the colours of the restored facade differently, so the exact palette is left unstated here; according to Hungarian Wikipedia, its central part carries the two tablets of Moses. Inside, an octagonal dome rests on eight slender iron columns with Alhambra-style capitals, and the walls carry gold, blue and red reliefs. English Wikipedia calls the design an homage to the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, though not an exact copy.

The building's later history was hard. In 1941 Jews were gathered in it before being deported to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and a plaque commemorates them. Worship ended in 1959, the roof over the Torah ark collapsed in 1979, the building was evacuated in 1980 and it was looted in 1982. After years of state ownership it passed to the Mazsihisz Jewish federation in 2005, and works began in 2017. The König-Wagner architects' office led the restoration, using Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the building was officially reopened on 10 June 2021.

The building's official site says it is still a synagogue, that it also hosts concerts, lectures and events, and that it serves as an external exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives; the Center for Jewish Art likewise records that in 2021 it was open to the public as a synagogue, museum and concert hall. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it can still be used for ritual purposes and also hosts concerts, cultural events and conferences, and that a hydraulic mechanism in the middle of the octagon can raise or lower the Torah reading platform. Modern chairs have replaced the original wooden benches.
Good to know
Visiting arrangements depend on its mix of uses as a synagogue, museum and event venue, so check the current official information for opening times and tickets before you go.
It is also a synagogue, so ask the organisers what applies on the day of your visit.
Under the dome, look for the eight slender iron columns with their Alhambra-style capitals and the gold, blue and red reliefs.

docs.historyIntro: Rumbach Street Synagogue was built for the Status Quo Ante community in the early 1870s and then spent decades in decay before a restoration that ended in 2021. Its history follows the changing fortunes of Jewish Pest.

historySections.heading: Building for the Status Quo Ante, 1869 to 1873

children.text: English Wikipedia says the building was begun in 1869, during the schism in Hungarian Jewry, and Hungarian Wikipedia gives the start of construction as 1 May 1870, with the Jewish congregation applying for the building permit only on 14 June 1870. Otto Wagner designed the synagogue, and the work was funded by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit was issued on 10 May 1873. It was intended for traditionalist Jews who found the Neolog synagogues too liberal.

In 1941 Jews were gathered in the building before Hungarian authorities deported them to Kamianets-Podilskyi in occupied Ukraine, where Germans murdered them. A plaque commemorates them. During the Second World War only the residential part of the building suffered minor damage. After 1956 about eighty congregants remained, and the synagogue was no longer used for worship from 1959. In 1979 the roof above the Torah ark collapsed, and the women's gallery later collapsed as well. The building was declared life-threatening and evacuated in 1980, and unknown perpetrators looted it in 1982.

In the 1980s a state construction company bought the building from the congregation, and in the 1990s preservation work restored the sanctuary but left the renovation unfinished. The Mazsihisz Jewish federation received the building in 2005, and from 2006 it was open to visitors without its interior fittings. Works began in 2017, designed by the König-Wagner office on the basis of Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the Hungarian ICOMOS committee gave the restoration an award in 2019. The renovated building was officially opened on 10 June 2021.

docs.name: Kazinczy Street Orthodox Synagogue
docs.description: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue is the great Orthodox synagogue of Pest's Jewish Quarter, built in 1912 and 1913 by the Löffler brothers in an Art Nouveau style influenced by Ödön Lechner. A Hebrew inscription crosses its brick facade, and the complex around it has included a school and a ritual bath.

children.text: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue stands in Erzsébetváros, in the heart of the old Jewish Quarter, and was built for the Orthodox Jewish community of Pest. In the late nineteenth century Pest's Jewish community had divided into three branches, the Neolog, the Status Quo Ante and the Orthodox. The congregation's own site gives the address as Kazinczy utca 29–31, as do the BKK listing and Wikipedia, while a few visitor sites give 27–29; the building itself dominates the narrow street.

The architects were the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. A competition was announced on 25 June 1909, and a jury favoured another design, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and chose the Löfflers' plans, which were approved in detail on 8 November 1910. The school and the community headquarters were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912, and in July 1913 the architects submitted a revised facade design, which Hungarian Wikipedia describes as plainer and cheaper, although English Wikipedia describes the change as making the main facade more ornate. The use permit was issued on 29 September 1913.

The style is Art Nouveau, or Secession, shaped by Ödön Lechner's national style and by late Viennese Secession. The brick facade has a wrought-iron main gate flanked by two smaller entrances, coloured artificial stone decoration and a two-line Hebrew inscription from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17). Inside, according to the sources, there are women's galleries, a central reading platform and a carved ark, with Transylvanian motifs in the wood carving, Zsolnay porcelain inlays on the columns of the eastern wall and windows by Miksa Róth. It can seat over a thousand people.

During 1944 and 1945 the building lay within the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of its furnishings were destroyed, and the complex was restored after 1945. By the end of the twentieth century the main synagogue had deteriorated and become unsafe to use. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the building's west corner. The mikveh, or ritual bath, which operated here from 1928, reopened in 2004 after renovation.

Sources describe the synagogue today as the religious and cultural centre of Pest's Orthodox community. Hungarian Wikipedia says the main synagogue can be visited, but another source mentions renovation works and fundraising for repairs, so the position may have changed.
Good to know
This is an active Orthodox synagogue. Check access and visiting arrangements directly with the community and the official sources before you plan a visit.
One source gives the way here as metro line M2 to Astoria or M4 to Rákóczi tér, then a short walk to Kazinczy Street.
From the street, look for the Hebrew inscription along the top of the facade, a verse from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17).

docs.historyIntro: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue was built in 1912 and 1913 for Pest's Orthodox Jewish community, after a design competition that the congregation decided against its jury. Its history runs through war damage, decline and a long search for a way to keep the community worshipping.

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia says the idea of an Orthodox synagogue in Erzsébetváros emerged in 1909, on a site on Kazinczy utca that belonged to the Pest Autonomous Orthodox Congregation. A design competition was announced on 25 June 1909. The jury chose the design of József Porgesz and Sándor Skultetzky, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and selected the design of the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. The detailed plans were approved on 8 November 1910.

The school and the community headquarters of the complex were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912. In July 1913, because of delays and unexpected costs, the Löffler brothers submitted a revised facade design, which Hungarian Wikipedia describes as plainer with lower material costs (English Wikipedia describes the change as more ornate). The official use permit was issued on 29 September 1913. A mikveh, or ritual bath, began operating in the building in 1928.

In 1944 and 1945 the building lay in the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of the furnishings was destroyed, and the complex was restored and the furnishings reconstructed after 1945. In the following decades the main synagogue deteriorated, and by the end of the twentieth century it was unheatable and unsafe. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the corner of the site by the engineer Sándor Bokor. The mikveh reopened in 2004 after renovation funded by private donations.

docs.name: Újlak Synagogue — Frankel Leó Street
docs.description: The Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, known earlier as the Újlak Synagogue, is a neo-Gothic brick synagogue consecrated in 1888 and later enclosed by a 1920s residential building. It is the home of an active Neolog congregation in Buda's 2nd district, and it appeared in the 1999 film The Taste of Sunshine.

children.text: The synagogue at Frankel Leó út 49 is in Újlak, in Budapest's 2nd district on the Buda side. Its present name is the Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, and Újlak Synagogue is its former name. It belongs to the Buda Jewish Community, follows the Neolog movement and the Ashkenazi prayer rite, and has Tamás Verő as its rabbi. The community's website, frankel.hu, publishes its weekly prayer times and contact details.

The foundation stone was laid in 1887, the building was completed in 1888 and it was consecrated on 8 August 1888. Sándor Fellner designed it in the neo-Gothic style, on the site of an earlier synagogue that was about a hundred years old. It originally stood free of other buildings, with its entrance on what was then Zsigmond utca, now Frankel Leó út, among single-storey houses, a kosher butcher shop and community apartments. It measures about 21.5 metres by 19 metres and was built for about 400 worshippers.

In the 1920s a residential building was constructed around the synagogue. It was handed over on 1 August 1928 and was designed by Dezső Jakab and his son-in-law Aladár Sós, on the initiative of a former community president, Berthold Beer. The synagogue itself was rebuilt at the same time, given reinforced concrete floor slabs and joined to the residential building, so that today it sits inside the block.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a three-bay facade of clinker brick with plaster detailing, stepped gables, pointed-arch windows and stone Tablets of the Law at the top. Inside are a wooden bimah, two seven-branched menorahs, an ark decorated with the Star of David and the Tablets of the Law, three women's galleries lit by pointed-arch windows and triple cross vaults. Marble plaques on the walls commemorate Holocaust victims and former chief rabbis.

At the end of the Second World War the synagogue was used as a stable, and the Jewish residents of the building were deported in 1944. A black marble plaque in the courtyard, unveiled in 2014, commemorates them. The residential building and the synagogue survived the siege of Budapest almost intact. The synagogue was used as a prayer house again under socialism and was completely renovated in 2000. It was also a filming location for Szabó István's 1999 film A napfény íze, The Taste of Sunshine.
Good to know
This is an active community synagogue inside a residential building. Use the contact details on frankel.hu to ask about access, and check prayer and service times there.
A memorial plaque for the residents deported in 1944 is in the courtyard, so ask the community before entering the building.
The synagogue is at Frankel Leó út 49 in Újlak, so it combines with a walk through that part of the 2nd district.

docs.title: The Danube, at your pace
docs.eyebrow: RIVERSIDE WALKS & A CITY SEEN FROM THE WATER
docs.summary: Riverside walks, bridges and a city seen from the water.

heroImage.alt: The Chain Bridge lit up at night over the Danube with Buda Castle glowing behind
heroImage.creditTitle: Széchenyi Chain Bridge in Budapest at night.jpg

docs.intro: The Danube is what holds Budapest together. Buda rises in hills on one bank and Pest spreads out flat on the other, and almost every classic view in the city is a view across the water. You can see the river from a bridge, a promenade, a hilltop terrace or a boat, and each gives you a different city.
highlights: Walk a stretch of either embankment before choosing a boat.
Check the exact departure pier and route for any cruise.
Evening departures vary with season and sunset.

sections.title: Walk both banks

children.text: Treat the riverfront as a route rather than a single stop. On the Pest side the embankment runs past the Chain Bridge, the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences towards the Parliament, and the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial sits on the same stretch. On the Buda side the road below Castle Hill starts at Clark Ádám Square, the foot of the Chain Bridge and the funicular.
Each bank is the viewpoint for the other. The Pest promenade looks up at Castle Hill and the Bastion; the terraces on Castle Hill look back across to the Parliament and the Pest skyline.
Pest bank: Chain Bridge → Gresham Palace → Shoes on the Danube Bank → Parliament.
Buda bank: Clark Ádám Square → the foot of Castle Hill → the Castle Garden Bazaar.
Leave time to stop: most of the good moments here are unplanned.

sections.title: Cross the bridges on foot

children.text: The Chain Bridge is the obvious first crossing, linking Széchenyi István Square in Pest with Clark Ádám Square in Buda. Walking it rather than riding over gives you time to look downstream and upstream, and the bridge ends make natural starting points for either side of the city.
If you have time for a second crossing, pick one further along the river and compare the angle: every bridge frames the Parliament, Castle Hill and Gellért Hill a little differently.

sections.title: See the city from the water

children.text: A river cruise changes the scale of the city and puts the Parliament and Castle Hill in one frame. Formats differ widely: shorter daytime sightseeing trips, evening cruises when the riverside landmarks are lit, and longer trips with dinner or drinks.

GoToBudapest does not take bookings. Compare the route, departure pier, duration and what is included directly with each operator, and check accessibility for your own needs. Our guide explains how to choose between daytime, evening and dinner formats.

sections.title: Take a green break on the river

children.text: Two places let you leave the pavements without leaving the water. Margaret Island is a green island in the middle of the Danube for walks and a slower pace, and Kopaszi-gát is a waterside green area on the Buda side.

sections.title: Practical notes

children.text: Embankments are largely flat, but Castle Hill and Gellért Hill are steep, and surfaces can be uneven. Wind off the river can make evenings feel cooler than the forecast, so carry a layer outside summer. Opening times, boat departures and seasonal services change; confirm them with the operator before you travel.

faqs.question: Do I need a cruise ticket to enjoy the Danube?
faqs.answer: No. The public riverfront and bridges offer excellent views without booking a boat.

faqs.question: Are all cruises the same?
faqs.answer: No. Check the route, boarding pier, operating dates, inclusions and cancellation conditions for the specific departure.

docs.title: Soak up the city
docs.summary: Build a slower day around a thermal-bath visit.

heroImage.alt: Bathers in the outdoor pools beneath the colonnades of the Széchenyi Thermal Bath

docs.intro: Bathing is part of how Budapest rests. Some baths are grand historic complexes, some are small Ottoman-era-style Turkish baths, and others are open-air pools that only run in season. The best visit is the one that suits the rest of your day, so choose the bath around the neighbourhood you are already exploring.
highlights: Pair Széchenyi with City Park.
Check Rudas session arrangements carefully.
Gellért Bath is closed for renovation.

sections.title: Pair a bath with a neighbourhood

children.text: Széchenyi Thermal Bath sits in City Park, so it fits naturally with a slow day around Heroes' Square and the park. On the Buda side, Rudas, Lukács and Veli Bej are close to the river and Gellért Hill, which makes them an easy follow-on to a morning on Castle Hill. Palatinus is on Margaret Island and works well after a walk on the island.
Thinking in neighbourhoods keeps travel time down and leaves the baths as the relaxed part of the day instead of an extra errand.

sections.title: Choose the kind of bath you want

children.text: Large thermal complexes combine several pools, steam and sauna areas. Turkish-style baths such as Rudas and Veli Bej offer a quieter, more traditional atmosphere, and both have sessions and access areas that vary by day and time, so check which one applies to your chosen date.
Open-air pools and beaches such as Palatinus, Lupa Beach and the Római Open-Air Bath are seasonal. Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a family-oriented water-park setting rather than a historic bath.

sections.title: Check the status before you plan

children.text: Gellért Thermal Bath is currently closed for renovation. The operator states that reopening is planned for 2028, which is not a confirmed date, so build your bath day around another venue. Seasonal baths can be closed outside their season and may change dates from year to year.

sections.title: Before you go

children.text: Bring swimwear and a towel unless the venue says it provides them, and check which facilities your ticket covers. Age rules, mixed or single-gender sessions, pool access and dress requirements differ between baths. GoToBudapest does not show ticket prices or availability, so confirm everything on the bath's own website.
Choose one bath rather than two: it is meant to be slow.
Check the day-specific session and access information.
Plan how you will get there and back before you get wet and tired.

faqs.question: Is Gellért Bath open?
faqs.answer: No. The operator reports a renovation closure with a planned reopening in 2028, which is not a confirmed date.

faqs.question: Are Budapest thermal baths suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Admission rules differ by venue and area. Check the operator's age restrictions before buying tickets.

docs.title: A taste of Budapest
docs.summary: Market mornings, cafés and Hungarian flavours.

heroImage.alt: Shoppers walking between stalls under the iron roof of the Great Market Hall

docs.intro: Budapest is a city of long breakfasts and unhurried cafés. You do not need a list of restaurants to eat well here: start with a market, learn a few dishes, plan one grand café stop and let the rest of your wandering decide where you end up.
highlights: Browse the Great Market Hall with time to look around.
Pair Vörösmarty Square with a café stop.
Check menus, reservations and current hours directly.

sections.title: Start with the market

children.text: The Great Market Hall is a covered market hall for exploring food stalls and the atmosphere of a city market. Go earlier in the day for the best sense of how it works as a market, and treat it as a place to look, taste and ask questions as well as to buy.

sections.title: Plan one grand café stop

children.text: Budapest's historic cafés are destinations in their own right. The New York Café is known for its richly decorated interior, and Café Gerbeaud sits on Vörösmarty Square in the middle of downtown Pest. Both are popular, so allow for queues at busy times and check opening hours.
Pair a café stop with a walk: Vörösmarty Square and Váci Street are short walks apart, and Andrássy Avenue leads onwards from the centre.

sections.title: Sweet and spirited stops

children.text: For a food-flavoured museum visit, the Szamos Chocolate Museum is centred on the Szamos confectionery tradition, and House of Unicum tells the story of the Unicum brand and its production heritage. Check visit formats and age rules for the spirits-related venue directly.

sections.title: What to look for on a menu

children.text: Hungarian classics worth knowing by name include gulyás (a soup or stew), pörkölt (paprika-based stew), halászlé (fish soup), lángos (fried flatbread) and kürtőskalács (chimney cake). Cooking varies from place to place, so ask staff what they recommend.
Ask about ingredients and allergens directly; menus and recipes change.
Opening hours vary, and many places close on certain days.
GoToBudapest does not rate or recommend individual restaurants.

sections.title: Food history indoors

children.text: If the weather turns, the Hungarian Agricultural Museum in Vajdahunyad Castle and the Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism explore the country's agricultural, commercial and hospitality history.

faqs.question: Is this a list of the best restaurants in Budapest?
faqs.answer: No. It selects food-related places from the attraction directory and does not rank or review restaurants.

faqs.question: Should I book cafés?
faqs.answer: Check each café's current reservation policy and opening hours; they vary by venue.
