docs.title: The Castle District

heroImage.alt: The Holy Trinity Column on Trinity Square, with Matthias Church on the right and the rebuilt former Ministry of Finance on the left

docs.intro: Castle Hill is Budapest's old Buda: cobbled lanes, courtyards, gateways and terraces above the Danube, with Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion at its heart. It rewards a slow half-day, and it is the best place to look back across the river at Pest.
highlights: Allow half a day for a relaxed first visit.
Fisherman's Bastion has separately ticketed upper areas.
Build in time for the backstreets and viewpoints beyond the main photo stop.

sections.title: Choose your way up

children.text: The funicular connects Clark Ádám Square, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, with the Castle area. You can also walk up, either by the stairs and paths from the river or through the Vienna Gate side, or take a bus: BKK lists routes 16, 16A and 116 for the upper Castle area, so check the current journey planner for your starting point. Whichever you choose, expect slopes.

sections.title: Begin at Trinity Square

children.text: Trinity Square is the centre of the district and sits beside Matthias Church. Take time to look at the details of the building, then continue to Fisherman's Bastion, whose terraces overlook the Danube and the Pest riverbank. The lower walkways and the upper lookout have different access arrangements, so check admission details for the level you want.

sections.title: Walk towards the palace

children.text: South of the church the hill opens into the Buda Castle palace complex. The Hungarian National Gallery and the Budapest History Museum are both inside it, and the Matthias Fountain and Savoyai Terrace are outside. Check museums and venues separately, because opening times and tickets are not shared.

sections.title: Find the quieter corners

children.text: Away from the main viewpoints the hill is calmer. The Tóth Árpád Promenade runs along the Castle wall, the Castle Garden Bazaar and the Tabán below the hill are green spaces, and the Medieval Jewish Prayer House introduces Buda's medieval Jewish heritage. The Hospital in the Rock is an underground museum beneath the hill.
Mary Magdalene Tower is currently listed as temporarily closed; check before planning an interior visit.
The Vienna Gate is a convenient entrance or exit on the northern side.

sections.title: Make it comfortable

children.text: Wear shoes with grip, because cobbles, steps and slopes are the norm. Leave time for the descent rather than rushing it, and confirm access arrangements for your own mobility needs before you go.

faqs.question: Is the Castle District free to visit?
faqs.answer: Walking the public streets is free. Museums, church interiors and the upper lookout at Fisherman's Bastion may require separate admission.

faqs.question: How much time should I allow?
faqs.answer: A half-day is a useful editorial allowance for the main viewpoints and quieter lanes. Add time for any museum or guided visit.

docs.title: Downtown Pest

heroImage.alt: The Hungarian Parliament Building seen across the Danube in daylight
heroImage.creditTitle: Hungarian Parliament Building from across the Danube, 2025-01-11.jpg

docs.intro: Pest is the flat, grand half of the city: wide boulevards, apartment blocks, cafés, concert halls and the Danube promenade. Most of the central sights are within walking distance of each other, which makes it ideal for a day without a fixed plan.
highlights: A mostly walkable city-centre area.
Combine St. Stephen's Basilica, the Chain Bridge and the riverside.
Váci Street and Vörösmarty Square bring cafés and shopping into the mix.

sections.title: Begin on the riverfront

children.text: Start by the Danube. The Hungarian Parliament stands on the Pest bank at Kossuth Square, and the promenade south of it passes the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial, a riverside memorial to people murdered during the Holocaust, which deserves a respectful visit. Further on you reach the Chain Bridge, the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences around Széchenyi István Square.

sections.title: Basilica to Andrássy Avenue

children.text: St. Stephen's Basilica is a good starting point for the streets of the centre. From the area, Andrássy Avenue is the grand route out towards City Park, lined with the Hungarian State Opera, the Liszt Academy of Music and the House of Terror Museum and ending at Heroes' Square.
Opera and concert halls publish their own performance calendars and visitor programmes.
The House of Terror Museum addresses Hungary's experience of twentieth-century dictatorships; allow time and emotional space for it.

sections.title: Café, square and shopping street

children.text: Vörösmarty Square is a natural meeting point, home to Café Gerbeaud, and it connects to the pedestrian Váci Street. Pause for a coffee and cake before carrying on, or head for the New York Café for a more theatrical stop.

sections.title: Jewish heritage

children.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue is a significant synagogue and Jewish heritage site in central Pest. Check visiting arrangements, any dress requirements and security procedures with the site before you go, and treat it as a place of worship and memory.

sections.title: When it rains

children.text: Downtown has plenty of indoor options. The Hungarian National Museum traces the country's history, and the Great Market Hall makes an easy covered stop for food and atmosphere.

faqs.question: Is Downtown Pest the same as the Jewish Quarter?
faqs.answer: No. The historic city centre is primarily District V; the Jewish Quarter is mainly in neighbouring District VII and deserves a separate visit.

faqs.question: Can I see the main sights on foot?
faqs.answer: Many central sights are close enough for a walking day. Allow extra time for stops, accessibility needs and any booked interiors.
